- list 3 of 3China’s Xi Jinping launches new AI alliance: What is it?
The action is part of a wider US effort to reduce reliance on Chinese technology in industries linked to artificial intelligence, energy and data centres.
Power inverters connect solar panels, batteries and other electricity sources to the grid and to data-centre equipment. Humanoid robots and four-legged robot dogs are increasingly being used in factories, warehouses and research facilities.
The FCC said the devices could create supply-chain and cybersecurity risks, particularly if foreign actors were able to compromise or control them.
“These devices could create supply chain vulnerabilities that could disrupt US economic and national security,” the agency said.
The restrictions are expected to affect Unitree, a Chinese robotics company that has worked with Nvidia on robots powered by the US chipmaker’s technology.
The Pentagon recently added Unitree to a list of companies it alleges have links to China’s military. Beijing has denied those allegations.
‘Stop smearing Chinese companies’
China’s embassy in Washington criticised the latest move and urged the US to stop targeting Chinese companies.
It said Beijing “urges the United States to heed the objective and rational voices of the business communities in both countries” and “stop smearing Chinese companies and threatening them with sanctions”.
China’s government will “take all necessary measures in response to any action that causes material harm to its interests”, the embassy added.
The FCC action also covers new Chinese-made power inverters. Huawei and Sungrow are among the leading Chinese suppliers in that sector.
The restrictions do not affect products already approved for sale in the US, although the FCC can revoke those approvals in some cases.
The decision comes as US President Donald Trump’s administration pushes companies to expand advanced manufacturing in the United States. Tesla, Figure AI, Agility Robotics and Boston Dynamics are among the firms developing or assembling humanoid robots in the country.
Tesla has said it plans to increase production of its Optimus robot. Figure AI and Agility Robotics already operate US facilities producing robots for industrial use.
The move could add to tensions between Washington and Beijing, which are already at loggerheads over advanced chips, artificial intelligence, trade and control of strategic technology supply chains.

title: Greetings from an isolated region in northern Pakistan's Hindu Kush mountains
summary: Chitral borders Afghanistan and isn't easy to reach. Breathtaking views abound in this remote mountainous region — as do rockslides and avalanches.
full_text:
Greetings from an isolated region in northern Pakistan's Hindu Kush mountains
The rawness of Pakistan's mountain regions is one of their main selling points. High-elevation passes feature on Instagram pages of adventure travel influencers, who promote their journeys along some of the world's most dangerous roads. Jeeps and buses can get stalled for hours while workers clear rockslides that clog entire stretches of highway. During one of my trips to the mountains, we had to wait at a safe distance while a boulder blocking the road was blown up with dynamite.
The intensity of the elements, along with sketchy infrastructure, can make traversing Pakistan's mountains feel like a grand adventure. That's mostly how I felt as I moved through Chitral, a district in the Hindu Kush range, during a reporting trip earlier this summer. There are currently no flights to this part of the country, so people are entirely dependent on passable roads. In winter, when the heavy snows come, it's hard to get around this area at all.
But for the people I met in Chitral, including my local reporting partner, Siraj Uddin, these unpredictable mountains are home, and they spoke matter-of-factly about managing floods, landslides and avalanches. They find ways to carry on. After pausing in Upper Chitral to take this photo during one long day on the road, that's what I did too.

full_text:
BreakingUS sanctions Chinese, Hong Kong shipping firms over Iranian oil deliveries
Six targeted tankers allegedly carried crude to China as Washington links economic campaign to US Navy enforcement
The United States on Wednesday sanctioned a group of mainland Chinese and Hong Kong shipping companies accused of operating vessels that transported Iranian oil to China, extending Washington’s economic campaign against Tehran alongside its naval blockade.
The US State Department said eight companies were designated for operating vessels that moved Iranian crude oil and petrochemical products to China and the United Arab Emirates as part of Iran’s sanctions-evading “shadow fleet”.
Six of the eight vessels identified by the US Treasury Department were specifically accused of carrying Iranian crude to China, in some cases transporting millions of barrels during 2026.
“Today’s designations support the US Navy’s enforcement of a blockade on Iranian ports and coastline,” State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said.
The action also targeted two Iranian companies accused of forcing commercial vessels passing through the Strait of Hormuz to purchase maritime insurance against risks, including seizures, that Washington says are created by Tehran itself.
The South China Morning Post has contacted the Chinese embassy in Washington for comment.

full_text:
BreakingFauci refuses to answer questions at heated Senate hearing on Covid-19 origins
Republicans press former health official over Wuhan research funding as Democrats accuse committee of pursuing political vendetta
The extraordinary appearance reopened one of Washington’s most politically divisive disputes: whether the pandemic began through natural transmission from animals or a laboratory-related incident in Wuhan, and whether US officials adequately scrutinised research conducted there with American funding.
Fauci, who led the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases and became a prominent face of the US government’s Covid-19 response during the pandemic, was subpoenaed to appear on Wednesday before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on the virus’s origins.
“I have appeared multiple times for hearings in the Senate and the House, usually under oath, and sat for several days-long transcribed sworn interviews, answering questions about the very issues that are now the subject of this hearing,” Fauci said in his opening remarks.
Committee chair Rand Paul, a Republican from Kentucky, has repeatedly accused Fauci of covering up evidence supporting the lab-leak theory tied to the Wuhan Institute of Virology in China.
“Can you explain to the committee why you chose to fund this dangerous research in China?” Paul asked.

summary:
The death of a six-year-old girl after receiving an experimental gene-editing therapy has been described by scientists as a tragedy that highlights the need to improve trial safeguards.
But some in the biotechnology industry fear Chinese policymakers may curtail the regulatory flexibility that scientists have long enjoyed in initiating clinical trials – a key mechanism behind China’s competitive edge in frontier treatments.


“I hope this tragedy does not have a lasting negative impact on...
full_text:
Is China’s biotech boom at risk? Fear of policy backlash after death in gene-editing trial
Scientist says child’s death reveals ‘serious failures in risk assessment, transparency and institutional oversight’
“I hope this tragedy does not have a lasting negative impact on China’s investigator-initiated clinical-research system, but there is a real risk of a regulatory backlash,” said Wang Haoran, chief executive of Neoland Biosciences, based in Shandong province.
“China has advanced rapidly in several frontier areas, partly because the mechanism has provided greater flexibility for carefully supervised early clinical exploration. That speed has increased the sense of urgency across the biotechnology industries in the United States and Europe.
“This case appears to reveal serious failures in risk assessment, transparency and institutional oversight. Stronger safeguards are clearly necessary, especially for first-in-human gene-editing treatments involving children.”
The girl, identified only as Mei, died days after receiving a bespoke therapy designed to correct a neurodevelopmental genetic mutation in March last year, according to a joint investigation by Retraction Watch and the journal Science published on July 23.

title: The population of an endangered Australian bat suddenly dropped by up to 16%. No one knows why
summary:
Exclusive: Scientists say about 5,000 fewer southern bent-wing bats have been recorded at a key maternity site for the species

A sudden decline in critically endangered bats is troubling experts, who recorded about 5,000 fewer southern bent-wing bats than usual at Naracoorte’s “bat cave” this summer.

These tiny russet-toned microbats roost in caves and forage for insects over long distances across south-west Victoria and south-east South Australia.

Continue reading...
full_text:
A sudden decline in critically endangered bats is troubling experts, who recorded about 5,000 fewer southern bent-wing bats than usual at Naracoorte’s “bat cave” this summer.
These tiny russet-toned microbats roost in caves and forage for insects over long distances across south-west Victoria and south-east South Australia.
Through summer, the Naracoorte cave in South Australia – one of three maternity sites for the species – becomes home to the largest population when the bats return to give birth and raise their young.
Over the past five years, the peak population at Naracoorte has averaged 28,600 adults, but last summer, that fell by about 14-16%.
“We’ve lost quite a lot of the adults,” said bat ecologist Nicola Bail, who coordinates the species recovery team at Zoos Victoria.
“We’re really not sure what the cause of this decline is, but it is really concerning, especially with so many threats operating in the range of the southern bent-wing bat.”
Population counts at the World Heritage listed site date back to the 1960s, when as many as 200,000 bats were recorded. Severe declines since then have seen southern bent-wing bats listed as one of Australia’s eight critically endangered mammals.
“They’re still hanging on. They’re a real little fighter,” Bail said.
But the recent drop, which includes some of the lowest male survival rates in a decade, would have long-term ramifications. Southern bent-wing bats depend heavily on adult survival, she said. The bats are known to live up to 22 years, with females producing only one young a year.
Associate prof Jasmin Hufschmid, from the University of Melbourne, said the bats were “gorgeous little creatures” that played an “invaluable” role controlling agricultural pests and insects that spread disease.
“They’re very important animals for us, but we just don’t really see it because they’re really small, they’re out at night,” said Hufschmid, who researches bat health but was not involved with the counts at Naracoorte.
Possible explanations for the decline include habitat clearing, drought, fewer flying insects that the bats eat, or human disturbance at non-breeding caves, many of which are located on private land.
A spokesperson for South Australia’s environment department said collisions with wind turbines and the potential introduction of disease like white-nose syndrome – which has not been detected in Australia – also posed risks to the species.
Cassie Hlava at the Limestone Coast Landscape Board, is coordinating a federally funded project that is working with landowners, restoring caves and replanting corridors of native grasses and flowering natives. This includes planting wattles, eucalypts, hakeas and banksias – places for moths to gather and breed, boosting the food supply for hungry bats.
Southern bent-wing bats are unique to the area, she said. “We know they’ve been here around 500,000 years. We’d like to keep them in this landscape, and we would like more people to get involved in habitat restoration on their properties to support the bats.”
“The recent decline is a huge concern,” she said. “The numbers are already quite low. So when you have a drop of 5,000 bats within a year, it’s really concerning that the species is being pushed towards extinction.”

title: Australians value batteries and EVs, but renewables industry must earn trust of regions, summit told
summary:
Clean Energy Council calls for a national, legislated scheme to funnel benefits of hosting renewables projects back to local councils

Organised campaigns against wind and solar energy have proved “extremely effective” in undermining community support for renewable energy but enthusiasm for electric vehicles has jumped following Donald Trump’s attack on Iran, according to a detailed snapshot of Australian attitudes to the clean energy transition.

The survey found levels of “deep support” for clean technologies were highest for home batteries and rooftop solar and also improving for major infrastructure projects such as transmission lines, which have been a target for critics of renewables.

Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter

Continue reading...
full_text:
Organised campaigns against wind and solar energy have proved “extremely effective” in undermining community support for renewable energy but enthusiasm for electric vehicles has jumped following Donald Trump’s attack on Iran, according to a detailed snapshot of Australian attitudes to the clean energy transition.
The survey found levels of “deep support” for clean technologies were highest for home batteries and rooftop solar and also improving for major infrastructure projects such as transmission lines, which have been a target for critics of renewables.
But support for onshore wind and solar farms had dropped from last year, with Australians reporting receiving more negative than positive messages about windfarms.
Rebecca Huntley, a social trends expert who leads the annual Clean Energy Solutions Index, said anti-wind campaigns promoted by conservative groups had been “extremely effective” in undermining community support.
“All that these campaigns need to do is create the perception that other people think [windfarms] are a bad idea,” she said.
“It isn’t difficult at this stage to get people to think renewable energy is a good idea. But you can get people to think there is no social licence for a fast transition.”
As the data was revealed at the renewable energy industry’s annual summit in Sydney, the Clean Energy Council told the industry it had a “fundamental problem” with a lack of trust in regional and rural communities.
The council called for a nationwide legislated scheme for local councils to receive money from renewables companies for every megawatt hour of electricity generated by projects over their lifetime.
Huntley measured the level of “deep support” for a range of renewable technologies by asking if people personally supported them; if they thought they were good for Australia; if they were willing to talk positively to others about them; and how they perceived others felt about the same technology.
She said Australians tended to overestimate the amount of opposition to a clean energy transition, compared with how they personally felt.
This was creating a perception gap, she said, which was undermining support for a fast transition away from coal and gas.
The index also showed people grossly underestimate how much electricity is already being generated from renewables.
Well over half (62%) of Australians think renewables supply less than 30% of electricity in the main eastern market, but the actual figure is 46%.
Huntley said Trump’s war on Iran and subsequent fuel crisis had been a boon for electric vehicles.
But she said renewable projects were facing an “existential threat” because the companies behind them were failing to properly share benefits with regional and rural towns hosting them.
Renewables companies needed to look back at previous resource booms such as coal, gas and gold that had helped build community infrastructure such as community halls and arts centres.
“The question the industry needs to ask is: in 50 years as Australians wander around renewable energy zones, what can they point to that was built off the back of wind turbines?” she said.
Jackie Trad, the chief executive of the Clean Energy Council, told the industry’s annual summit on Tuesday: “The fundamental problem this industry has is trust. We do not have enough of it in the places where we build – regional and rural Australia.
“Our intentions are sincere. Our product is clean. But go looking for the research that says regional communities trust the renewable energy industry, and you will not find it. It does not exist.
“And in this business, what communities believe determines what gets built.”
Trad said the current “patchwork of community benefit funds, grants and negotiated payments” needed to be replaced with a national legislated scheme.
She said: “Regional Australia is being asked to host the machinery of our energy security. The least we can do is make sure the towns that host it share squarely in the wealth it creates.”

title: Atlassian tightens tracking of staff AI use as other technology firms encourage ‘tokenmaxxing’
summary:

full_text:
Software firm Atlassian has sought to tighten tracking of its staff’s AI spending by introducing “wallets” with monthly caps of up $2,000 for each employee, amid an explosion in costs at other tech companies.
The move by Atlassian, which recently cited AI as part of the reason behind cutting 1,600 staff, bucks the trend of others in the tech sector who encouraged employees to use as much of the technology as possible, dubbed “tokenmaxxing”. Some companies have reportedly introduced leaderboards for employees who used the most AI in their work.
Tokens refer to the measurement of a response AI gives to a prompt. OpenAI has said one token is about four characters, and something like the US Declaration of Independence amounts to 1,695 tokens. OpenAI’s flagship model, GPT-5.6 Sol, has a charge of US$5 for every 1m tokens, while Anthropic’s Claude Fable and Mythos models are US$10 for every 1m tokens.
Under tokenmaxxing, the costs quickly add up.
Uber reportedly blew through its AI budget in four months, and Amazon has reportedly told employees to stop using AI just for the sake of using AI.
While Atlassian never encouraged tokenmaxxing or had unlimited AI budgets, the Australian company this month introduced an “AI wallet” for staff in the research and development team.
According to an internal memo seen by Guardian Australia, employees have between $500 and $2,000 monthly spend in the wallet, which can be used across four AI products, including Claude Code. Employees receive notifications as they approach their limit on their wallets, and usage is paused when the money runs out.
Employees can request additional funds. It’s understood Atlassian has not turned down any request for additional funds so far.
A company spokesperson said it was transforming into an “AI-first company” by supporting people building and experimenting with the technology.
“Atlassian provides a significant budget for our builders to leverage multiple AI tools,” the spokesperson said.
“AI tooling budgets are set by role based on how different teams work.”
They said the wallet also represented a boost in the amount employees could spend.
A June PureProfile survey of 500 senior Australia staff at companies using AI, conducted on behalf of search AI company Elastic, found that 80% were concerned that high usage was being mistaken for productivity gains.
It found 32% had reported pausing, cancelling or winding back AI deployments, due to cost.
Elastic’s ANZ manager, Jeremy Pell, said a monthly cap on AI spend was “smart” and more organisations should be doing it.
“Right now, only 9% of Australian organisations currently have any limits on token or API consumption when it comes to AI agents or autonomous workflows, so any organisation that adopts this practice is an outlier,” he said.
Arun Chandrasekaran, a distinguished vice-president analyst at research firm Gartner, said wallets were a simple way to “incentivise the right behaviour” and stop people from using AI ineffectively.
He said such expenses were becoming an important issue among businesses, with the cost explosion being driven by AI agents that autonomously undertake tasks on behalf of the user.
“You suddenly have these systems that are all trying to do independent tasks that are spawning smaller agents, that are creating their own prompts and initiating requests for the model,” he said.
“So while the AI model prices have been falling for the last three years, the volume of tokens that particularly the AI agents are starting to send to the models … is significantly increasing.”
Chandrasekaran said companies are figuring out how to drive the cost down, including using less powerful models for simpler tasks, and looking at using open weight – where people can download and run the models on their own systems – or open source models.

title: Bird flu is spreading locally and Australia faces more wildlife deaths. How bad could it get?
summary:
Authorities say local transmission of H5 bird flu virus among South Australian birds signals ‘shift in the situation’

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australia has entered a new phase in dealing with the incursion of deadly H5N1 bird flu, with authorities confirming on Wednesday that local transmission of the highly virulent strain had taken place.

“We have had what is suggestive of local transmission for the first time,” Julie Collins, the federal minister for agriculture, fisheries and forestry, said on Wednesday afternoon, after 11 new suspected detections were reported in South Australian birds.

Continue reading...
full_text:
“We have had what is suggestive of local transmission for the first time,” Julie Collins, the federal minister for agriculture, fisheries and forestry, said on Wednesday afternoon, after 11 new suspected detections were reported in South Australian birds.
“We will expect to see increased evidence and deaths of wildlife … given there has been some local transmission,” she said. “This small shift in the situation will be very disappointing to many, but is certainly not an unexpected development as the last continent to detect H5 bird flu.”
Now that authorities believe transmission of H5 strain is occurring locally, what does this mean for Australia’s wildlife, and how bad could things get?
What’s the current status of H5N1 bird flu in Australia?  On Wednesday morning, South Australian authorities announced 11 new suspected bird flu detections in greater crested terns in the state’s south-east, including four cases on Kangaroo Island. That brings Australia to a total of 27 confirmed detections.
Julie Collins, the agriculture minister, said the Consultative Committee on Emergency Animal Diseases – comprising federal and state and territory authorities – had met on Wednesday and agreed that “some local transmission has occurred between a number of greater crested terns that are resident in South Australia”.
Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Dr Beth Cookson, Australia’s chief veterinary officer, said genetic sequencing showed all confirmed cases detected to date were related to sub-Antarctic strains  of the virus.
Clare Scriven, the SA minister for primary industries, said earlier on Wednesday: “This is concerning but not unexpected. We knew that eventually when bird flu arrived in Australia it would spread. It has spread on every other continent around the globe.”
To date, there have been no H5 detections in poultry or agricultural industries in Australia. “The risk to human health remains low,” Collins said.
How could bird flu affect wildlife on Kangaroo Island? One of the Kangaroo Island bird flu detections was at Seal Bay, home to the country’s third-largest Australian sea lion population. Conservationists have expressed fears for the sea lion population there.
Alexia Wellbelove, campaigns director at the Australian Marine Conservation Society (AMCS), said Australian sea lions were “now on the frontline of the potential wildlife crisis”.
About 80% of the Australian sea lion population is found in South Australia; the endangered mammal has seen populations decline by 60% in four decades , with remaining numbers about 12,000.
“In South America, this virus killed 30,000 sea lion pups in just six months following transmission from birds to marine mammals,” Wellbelove said. “On our own Heard Island, it killed more than 13,000 elephant seal pups  in a single season … we now have to face the very real possibility of similar devastation here at home, in a species already teetering on the edge.”
Scriven said on-beach tours at Seal Bay were temporarily paused to keep people separate from the “very vulnerable” animal population and to reduce the risk of spreading infection.
What can be done to stop the spread of bird flu?  Not much, unfortunately. Cookson said on Wednesday: “We do know from the overseas experience that once the virus becomes more widespread in wild bird populations it will not be possible to avoid losses in susceptible wildlife in the natural environment.”
Authorities had anticipated the arrival of H5N1 in Australia through migratory birds “for a number of years”, she said. They will continue to focus on surveillance, to confirm where the virus is circulating and to “reduce the impacts where possible”.
Collins said the federal government had invested more than $113m preparing for the virus’s arrival. “We have also, working with states and territories, now released a further $24m.”
Without listing specific animals, Cookson said the government was taking “a number of actions in high-priority conservation species, including site- and species-specific planning”. There would also be a focus on protecting captive breeding populations, and implementing farm biosecurity measures to “limit contact between wild birds and poultry”.
Groups including the AMCS and the Invasive Species Council have called on the federal government to establish a $200m national wildlife resilience fund, “focused on emergency protection and recovery for our most at-risk species”.
How bad could bird flu get in Australia? Worldwide, the H5N1 variant has caused  “unprecedented levels of ongoing outbreaks”, killing millions of wild birds and tens of thousands of mammals.
Large-scale deaths have not yet occurred in Australia, but the major concerns relate to potential wildlife impacts: more than 150 native bird species  have been assessed as being at “very high risk” of extinction or major decline if they are infected – including the red goshawk, fairy tern, plains-wanderer, shy albatross, black swan and western hooded plover.
More than 10 mammal species are at very high risk, including the Australian sea lion, the subantarctic fur seal and the Australian fur seal.
There could also be significant impacts on the poultry industry. Globally, an estimated 140m farmed birds  have died or been culled since January last year. In the United States, the virus was linked to a 220% spike  in egg prices in the first quarter of 2025. Western Australia’s Chamber of Commerce and Industry has warned  that if the virus were to reach commercial flocks, it could push egg prices above $10 a carton. Mass culls could be necessary, and the RSPCA has called for fast-tracked research into more humane killing methods, such as the use of nitrogen in gas or foam.
Human-to-human transmission of the virus is not common, but since 2003, there have been 1,000 reported cases of H5N1 in humans globally, with a 48% fatality rate .

title: Icac hits paydirt as Reformers’ ‘shit sheets’ are given a very public airing
summary:
Dirt files are always damaging – not least those originating in the secretive rightwing Reformers sub-faction of the party

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

From time to time, dirt files – crudely known as shit sheets – flutter around the corridors of power in state and federal parliaments.

They can be enormously damaging even if never published. While there might be speculation as to their origin, rarely is there confirmation – especially if the dirt file emanates from your own side.

Continue reading...
full_text:
From time to time, dirt files – crudely known as shit sheets – flutter around the corridors of power in state and federal parliaments.
They can be enormously damaging even if never published. While there might be speculation as to their origin, rarely is there confirmation – especially if the dirt file emanates from your own side.
But on Wednesday, the New South Wales Independent Commission Against Corruption hit paydirt, uncovering a document – and a text trail indicating its origin – that painted a very unflattering portrait of the former NSW police minister David Elliott.
Equally, it paints an unflattering picture of politics in the NSW Liberal party and potentially serious perversion of the system.
Icac is investigating allegations that members of a secretive rightwing sub-faction of the NSW Liberals – the Reformers – took undeclared political donations, including from banned donors like developers and hoteliers, and in amounts that exceeded donation caps.
We have already heard allegations that Catholic Schools NSW, a charity that distributes funding to the state’s catholic schools, made undeclared payments totalling $260,000 and that the hotelier Michael O’Hara also contributed more than $150,000.
The counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC has also hinted there will be further revelations about $2m paid by the fugitive developer Jean Nassif to the key players.
Nassif’s largesse to the Reformers almost certainly had less to do with the conservative values on abortion and same-sex marriage that motivated other financial backers. It is alleged by Dwyer it had much more to do with getting rid of the then building commissioner David Chandler and critics of Nassif’s buildings such as the former Baulkham Hills MP David Elliott.
In the witness box on Wednesday the most junior of the Reformers, Dylan Whitelaw, was asked about the work he did on a 2021 document titled “David Elliot shit sheet.docx”, while working at a public relations company owned by two other Reformers, Christian Ellis and Jeremy Greenwood.
Whitelaw admitted he had compiled a document at the request of Greenwood and had included references to unflattering articles about Elliott, such as when he was photographed as police minister firing an illegal firearm at a corrections department firing range.
“I think it comes back to the standard factional warfare that occurs inside political parties. ‘Distaste’ maybe is the incorrect word, but the right wing of the Liberal party had hatred of the centre-right or the Alex Hawke faction, of which Mr Elliot was a leading figure,” Whitelaw told Icac.
But Whitelaw said he did not recall writing a section that suggested Elliott had engaged in an extramarital affair. It might have been added later, Whitelaw said. He had heard of the existence of photos but had not seen them.
“The allegation around Mr Elliot and the affair was something that Mr Greenwood and Mr Ellis kept very, very secretive,” Whitelaw said.
Elliott, who is not under investigation by Icac, issued a statement to the Sydney Morning Herald on Wednesday denying the affair.
“As most of Sydney knows I’m a devoted husband of 30 years to a beautiful woman who doesn’t deserve to be treated like this by the party she has sacrificed so much for,” he said in the statement.
“Needless to say I’m looking forward to the possibility of providing my own observations should the commission see fit to invite me to give evidence.”
But was it just factional rough and tumble?
“I want to suggest to you, Mr Whitelaw … that this document was prepared at the instruction of Mr Greenwood by you to further certain interests that Mr Nassif had,” counsel assisting Juliet Curtin said.
“At the time, I had no idea. At the time, it would appear to me as just standard factional warfare. On reflection, absolutely, that’s what it appears to be,” Whitelaw replied.
More signs of dirty tricks emerged in relation to Chandler. In 2022, Whitelaw was working for the planning minister, Anthony Roberts, reporting to chief of staff Christopher Spence.
Whitelaw gave evidence that Spence was excited about a video he had received from an undisclosed source. Whitelaw said Spence claimed the video showed Chandler in an unflattering light.
Whitelaw said Spence told him he gave the video to the Liberal MP Eleni Petinos to use in a parliamentary committee, but Spence later said “Eleni fucked it up”.
Neither Spence nor Petinos have been named as subjects of the Icac Investigation.
Meanwhile, the federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, faced more questions about whether he had contributed to the Reformers, as indicated in text exchanges shown as evidence.
In one, Whitelaw told the Reformers WhatsApp group that the head of Catholic Schools NSW Dallas McInerney had told him Taylor was tipping in $15,000 plus $3,000 a month. Another screenshot of a text from McInerney indicated he planned to “shake down Angus for $10k”.
“I’m not going to give a running commentary on all of this. I’m not a party to the proceedings, but no payment was made,” Taylor said on Wednesday.
Asked about the text message, he said: “No payment was made and I’ll let the commission do its job.” Taylor is not under investigation by Icac.
Icac is also curious to discover why, around the time of the text exchanges about financial support from Taylor in March 2021, the monthly amount being paid by Catholic Schools to Ellis and Greenwood’s company Beckington increased by $3,000 a month.
Whitelaw said he did not know. But he was sure he never received a bonus of $8,000 that was also referred to.

title: Body found in suitcase in Athens 11 days ago that of 38-year-old British woman
summary:
Greek authorities identify remains after reported discovery in a derelict building by homeless man

A body found in a suitcase in an abandoned building in central Athens has been identified as a 38-year-old British woman, with Greek authorities saying she had been dead for several weeks.

Eleven days after the macabre find, police said they were able to shed some light on the mystery of a body that until Wednesday had remained unidentified, after appealing to foreign law enforcement agencies.

Continue reading...
full_text:
A body found in a suitcase in an abandoned building in central Athens has been identified as that of a 38-year-old British woman, with Greek authorities saying she had been dead for several weeks.
Eleven days after the macabre find, police shed some light on the mystery of a body that until Wednesday had remained unidentified, after appealing to foreign law enforcement agencies.
“The remains, we can confirm, have been identified as belonging to a British woman,” one well-placed source said. “Her next of kin have been informed,” they said, adding it had been ascertained the victim had been born in Scotland in 1988.
The woman, whose body was found wrapped in cloth and placed in a bin bag inside the suitcase, was described as 5ft 4in tall with auburn hair gathered back in a bun. She was wearing a black T-shirt and shorts but had no tattoos or other distinguishing marks.
Police were alerted after a homeless man reportedly discovered the suitcase on 18 July in a derelict building in Kypseli, a district popular among foreign nationals in downtown Athens, according to the public broadcaster ERT.
The woman had reportedly flown to the region from the US, arriving in Greece, on 29 June, from Cyprus.
Greek homicide officers sent fingerprints to Interpol after drawing a blank on local databases. US authorities had provided evidence on the basis of the DNA that police released on Wednesday.
Detectives cordoned off the building on Evelpidon Street as they investigated the circumstances of the woman’s death.
Police spokesperson Konstantina Dimoglidou had previously said CCTV was being examined to try to trace the woman’s movements before her death. Authorities were treating the incident “as a criminal act, given how the body was found”, she told Skai TV.
Airlines are also believed to have been approached as investigators try to reconstruct the Briton’s journey to Greece and determine if she was travelling alone. Officials in Greece and Cyprus were scouring flight logs and hotel bookings.
Local media, citing the results of a postmortem, said the victim had been dead for eight days before the discovery. There was “no evidence” of a struggle or signs of injury.
Greek officials did not rule out UK investigators also joining the inquiry.
The British embassy acknowledged it had been informed but made no further comment.
Greece is no stranger to British tourists dying in what is a popular holiday destination – often by drowning or as a result of road accidents – “but incidents like this are very rare”, officials said.

title: A ​decade on the Iberian ​frontline​ has shown me that Europe’s ​climate ​emergency​ is ​impossible to ​deny
summary:
What once felt exceptional now arrives with grim regularity​ all over the continent, and it will only get worse

• Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

Spain has changed immeasurably since I arrived here 10 years ago to begin work as the Guardian’s Madrid correspondent.

Over that time, the push for Catalan independence has exploded, sputtered and faded out; the Covid pandemic has hit with unimaginable ferocity, before seeming to linger for a face-masked eternity; and Podemos and Ciudadanos – the two upstart parties that once seemed likely to alter the Spanish political landscape irrevocably – have risen and fallen.

full_text:
Spain has changed immeasurably since I arrived here 10 years ago to begin work as the Guardian’s Madrid correspondent.
Over that time, the push for Catalan independence has exploded, sputtered and faded out; the Covid pandemic has hit with unimaginable ferocity, before seeming to linger for a face-masked eternity; and Podemos and Ciudadanos – the two upstart parties that once seemed likely to alter the Spanish political landscape irrevocably – have risen and fallen.
But one change has been so insistent, so undeniable and so painfully visible, that it has come to eclipse all others. A decade ago, perhaps naively, I could never have imagined how much time I would spend reporting the effects of the climate emergency here and in Portugal. Nor would I ever have imagined that things would get this bad, this fast.
The facts, however, speak for themselves. Europe is the fastest-heating continent, warming at a speed more than twice that of the global average, and the Iberian peninsula has become the sometimes scorched, sometimes sodden, frontline of the climate crisis. The wildfires still burning here and in France – which have led to the evacuation or confinement of approximately 330,000 people since last week – are merely the latest manifestation of all that.
It’s hard to think of a better example of all this than the autumn of 2024. At the end of September that year, the photographer Gonçalo Fonseca and I trudged around the northern Portuguese municipality of Albergaria-a-Velha, trekking through a landscape of blackened trees, burnt-out cars and ruined, roofless houses.
The fires that had inflicted the damage the previous week killed nine people, injured dozens more and razed 100,000 hectares of land across northern and central Portugal. They had been fuelled by strong winds, dry conditions and unseasonably hot temperatures of more than 30C (85F). It all inevitably brought back memories of the calamitous blazes of 2017, which claimed 66 lives.
João Oliveira, the head of the civil protection agency in Albergaria-a-Velha, showed me a picture on his mobile phone of a towering tidal wave of grey smoke preparing to engulf the town.
An annual fixture
He said there was no comparison whatsoever with the fires of previous years, adding: “The amount of energy the fire created, the amount of damage it did and the intensity and violence of the fire, were something we’d never seen before.”
Four weeks later, I parked my car on the edge of the eastern Spanish town of Utiel, pulled on my wellingtons and headed to see the aftermath of the deadly floods that had hit the Valencia region 48 hours earlier, killing more than 230 people. Ruined houses, wrecked cars, people speechless on the streets, and an inches-deep carpet of thick, sticky mud everywhere.
The only reference points I had for what I saw there and in the town of Chiva were the super El Niño I witnessed in northern Peru in 1998, and the devastation I reported on a month after the Nepal earthquake in April 2015. But these days, the kind of danger and destruction I thought I’d never see in Europe is becoming an almost annual fixture on the peninsula – and beyond.
Helena Smith, the Guardian’s correspondent in Greece, points out that warnings have long sounded from her part of the continent.
“I still vividly recall Eleni Myrivili – who is now the UN’s global chief heat officer, but was then newly installed as Athens’ heat maestro – saying, ‘Heat will be the story of the next decade,’” said Helena.
“That was in 2021. The same week I had written of apocalyptic scenes on the fringes of the Greek capital and ‘infernos redolent of Dante’s hell incinerating everything in their path’. It was inconceivable it could be worse. And, yet, every year it is: testimony to the irrefutable fact that the climate emergency is our runaway train, that temperatures in Athens are set to be on a par with Bahrain; that Spain and France are the new Greece, and London the Athens I first knew, in terms of heat, in the late 90s.”
Likewise, Angelique Chrisafis, the Guardian’s Paris correspondent, told me that much of her reporting has been focused on the impact of the climate crisis – including its attendant inequalities – since May’s record-breaking heatwave.
“I remember Issam, a 10-year-old boy in the southern suburbs of Paris whose top-floor school classroom reached 40C and whose badly insulated flat was hit by blazing sun against the windows all day, often leaving his mother dizzy and struggling to breathe,” she said.
Three weeks ago, I spoke to Jeanne Henny, a British woman who would have burned to death in her car had she not risked a three-point turn on a narrow cliff road as she fled the flames in Almería earlier this month.
And on Saturday afternoon I visited people who had been evacuated from their homes west of Madrid to a municipal sports centre on the outskirts of the capital. “[The sky] turned orange and looked very apocalyptic,” one man told me. “It felt like the end of the world.”
But of all the many climate emergency stories I’ve reported over the past few years, there are two that I still think about often.
In Utiel, I met Miguel Aleixandre, a young man who told me about the night of the floods in Valencia.
As the waters rose to a height of three metres, Miguel looked out across his dark neighbourhood and saw elderly neighbours signalling with candles at their windows. They were hoping to attract the attention of the rescuers who would, in some cases, arrive too late. Then he heard the sound of windows breaking and realised that the flood waters were pouring into the houses of people who would soon drown, trapped in their homes.
Fifteen months earlier, I had stood in a petrol station in the north-western Spanish town of Tábara listening to an account of the brave but fateful decision that had cost Ángel Martín his life the previous summer.
Desperate to prevent the wildfires in the Sierra de la Culebra from devouring his town, the 53-year-old builder’s yard owner climbed into his excavator to try to dig a firebreak. Within minutes, Martín and the vehicle were swallowed by the flames and the thick, black smoke. Video showing him emerging from the inferno, his clothes consumed by the flames, went around the world.
For a week or two at least, the figure of the burning, running, stumbling man became a symbol of the human consequences of the climate emergency. Martín suffered burns to 80% of his body and died in hospital three months later.
“We still talk about him a lot,” Martín’s friend, Montse Fernández Blanco, told me. “And I remember his jokes and what a good, happy person he was. The thing is he would have done it again because that’s what he was like.”
And yet, four years after Ángel Martín ran out of the flames, and two years after people died under the flood waters in Utiel, the same arguments, denial and political point-scoring continue to hamper efforts to prepare for the decades to come – decades that are all but certain to make all this seem mild.
We can hardly say we weren’t warned.

title: Next 12 hours ‘decisive’ for wildfire near Madrid, says Spanish PM
summary:
Comments by Pedro Sánchez come as extreme heat renews pressure on firefighters tackling blazes across southern Europe

  • Europe live – latest updates

The next 12 hours will be “decisive” for a large wildfire burning near Madrid, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has said, as extreme heat renews pressure on firefighters racing to control blazes across southern Europe.

Temperatures pushed higher by climate breakdown are forecast to reach 39C on Wednesday in Bordeaux, where firefighters have kept a monster blaze in nearby pine forests from reaching the suburbs, and 37C in Madrid, west of which Spain’s largest wildfire on record is burning.

Continue reading...
full_text:
The next 12 hours will be “decisive” for a large wildfire burning near Madrid, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has said, as extreme heat renews pressure on firefighters racing to control blazes across southern Europe.
Temperatures pushed higher by climate breakdown are forecast to reach 39C on Wednesday in Bordeaux, where firefighters have kept a monster blaze in nearby pine forests from reaching the suburbs, and 37C in Madrid, west of which Spain’s largest wildfire on record is burning.
Dozens of ground crews managed to contain the Madrid fire overnight, emergency services for the region said on Wednesday morning, but a separate fire near València, where temperatures will peak at a cooler 32C, is still out of control.
In televised comments from the Navalcarnero command centre on Wednesday morning, Sánchez said the situation near the capital was improving but stressed it was the first time in Spanish history that a wildfire had been raised to “operational level 3”, with the national government taking over the disaster response.
“I believe the next 12 hours will be very important,” he said. “They are going to be decisive in consolidating the work done by the national civil protection system.”
Accompanied by strong winds, the fourth heatwave of western Europe’s scorching summer has alarmed firefighters, who warn it makes blazes harder to quell and raises the risk of fires restarting in areas that have been stabilised. The recent fires have been particularly troubling as they have burned so close to major cities.
French authorities benefited from a calm night on Tuesday that allowed flare-ups to be swiftly extinguished but warned of “unfavourable” developing weather conditions that could hamper progress. The prefecture of Gironde said 126 firefighters had been injured since the start of the fire but the total burned area remained stable at 42,000 hectares (104,000 acres) on Wednesday morning.
Wildfires have burned a record-breaking area of France, data from the European Forest Fire Information System shows, while both France and Spain have experienced record-breaking numbers of fires for this time of year. More than 330,000 people in southern Europe have been forced to flee their homes and hotels.
Officials began to lift evacuation orders on Tuesday as fires were brought under control, allowing tens of thousands of people living in towns near Bordeaux, Madrid and València to go back to their homes. Some of them returned to find burnt-out buildings and charred belongings.
José Fernández, a 74-year-old pensioner, told AFP he had “no money, no documents, no home” after he came back to the remains of what used to be his house in Pelayos de la Presa. “This place has been reduced to a total ruin.”
Europe’s wildfire season is growing hotter and longer as carbon pollution heats the continent twice as fast as the global average. Repeated heatwaves this year have dried vegetation and turned forests and shrubland into tinderboxes, alarming EU officials, who have said wildfires could still be burning in November.
Sánchez repeated calls to create a “national pact” to address the climate emergency. “These fires may or may not be caused by humans, but in any case, they increase exponentially as a result of these high temperatures, low humidity, and also the atmospheric phenomena that these fires, these large fires, cause in our forests.”
Earlier this week, the European Commission said it had sent France seven planes and four helicopters from countries as far away as Sweden and Turkey, while in Spain, it said it had mobilised six planes from Greece, Italy and Turkey, along with 134 personnel and 41 vehicles from Portugal. A Super Puma helicopter from Serbia was expected to arrive in Madrid on Wednesday, according to Spain’s interior ministry, with 40 personnel and 18 vehicles to shortly follow.
The European Union’s crisis-management team said on Wednesday it expected difficult weeks ahead, fearing a further outbreak of wildfires in Italy and Greece later in the summer.
Maria Zuber, a senior official at the EU’s emergency response coordination centre in Brussels, which coordinates the dispatch of firefighting planes, equipment and teams to countries that have asked for help, said the next few days would be “very difficult” for France and that “now we see it will go to Greece”.
Moisés Galán Santano, a wildfire expert at the ERCC, said more needed to be done to prevent wildfires and that it would be a task for many years. “The [emergency] response is not only the answer. It’s the last answer. But it’s not all the answer. We need to focus on prevention.”
Officials said prevention encompassed policies from early-warning systems to more animal grazing – to reduce vegetation – and changes to forest management.
Earlier this year, a policy paper from the European Commission set out how countries could better prevent and recover from wildfires that are expected to become bigger and more damaging across the continent. It promoted measures such as more extensive grazing, the restoration of wetlands, rivers and floodplains, better data on forest fires and raising public awareness of risky behaviour and safe evacuation.
Scientists say western Europe’s scorching summer has been deadly, costly and exacerbated by fossil fuel pollution. Rapid analyses have found June’s heatwave would have been “virtually impossible” in a world without climate breakdown, while the recent level of soil dryness in western Europe – a driver of bigger blazes – was made five times more likely. The heatwaves are estimated to have claimed at least 10,000 lives and cost grain farmers €2bn in lost crops.
Vula Tsetsi, co-chair of the European Green party, called on European institutions to take action on Wednesday and noted the European Commission had not yet published its heating and cooling plan, which was expected in April.
“Climate-driven heatwaves and wildfires are already claiming lives, destroying homes and ravaging forests at a record pace,” she said. “There is a widening gap between the scale of Europe’s heatwaves – literally hitting every EU country – and the absence of decisive European action.”

title: US-Saudi strikes in Iraq have pushed the region into ‘uncharted territory’, analysts warn
summary:
Riyadh’s decision to join the US in striking sites associated with the Iran-backed Popular Mobilisation Forces further complicates a chaotic war

US-Saudi strikes on Iran-backed militia in Iraq on Wednesday have pushed the region into “uncharted territory”, analysts have warned.

Amid stark warnings of a widening and increasingly “unpredictable” conflict, Riyadh’s decision to publicly join the US in striking sites associated with Iraq’s Popular Mobilisation Forces, killing at least 20 fighters, has added another complicating dimension to the war.

Continue reading...
full_text:
US-Saudi strikes on Iran-backed militia in Iraq on Wednesday have pushed the region into “uncharted territory”, analysts have warned.
Amid stark warnings of a widening and increasingly “unpredictable” conflict, Riyadh’s decision to publicly join the US in striking sites associated with Iraq’s Popular Mobilisation Forces, killing at least 20 fighters, has added another complicating dimension to the war.
The US-Saudi strikes on Wednesday came after a brief lull in direct US attacks on targets in Iran, with Tehran’s allies in Yemen and beyond becoming increasingly drawn in.
Iran, meanwhile, launched missiles at US military installations in Jordan, in its first attack in the region since the pause in fighting with the US began.
After the tit-for-tat strikes, the pause in fighting appeared to be at an end, with the US president, Donald Trump, saying the US would be “be hitting [Iran] hard”, even as he claimed the strikes in Iraq were coordinated with the government, despite Baghdad’s condemnation.
In Baghdad, the Iraqi presidency called the air raids on the PMF, also known as al-Hashd al-Shaabi – an armed alliance that includes powerful pro-Iran factions – as “a blatant violation of Iraq’s sovereignty, targeting its official institutions”.
The PMF is a network of Shia-majority factions that was established in 2014 to fight the Islamic State group. Their efforts were overseen by the Iranian general, Qassem Suleimani, the former head of the Quds force, the foreign operations arm of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Suleimani was killed by a US missile strike in Baghdad during Trump’s first term.
Iraqi prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi, who recently met Trump, called off a planned meeting with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Jeddah on Thursday in the wake of the strikes.
Iraq’s Harakat Hezbollah al-Nujaba, an Iran-backed militia, added that Washington’s and Riyadh’s interests and security would face consequences, as mourners shouted Shia sectarian slogans and “Death to America!” as they carried the bodies of slain fighters in body bags out of a hospital in Mosul, northern Iraq.
Iraq, which has been heavily affected by the closure of the strait of Hormuz – through which most of its oil is exported – has struggled to prevent the war between the US and Iran spilling over its borders.
Iraq’s governments have long sought to maintain a delicate balance between the US, which invaded the Shia-majority country in 2003, and Iran, which has long sought to exert influence there and has backed powerful militias that played a leading role in the fight against IS.
While Saudi Arabia has reportedly been involved in a handful of secretive strikes on Iran as part of the war, Riyadh’s overt involvement marks a new turning point in the conflict. It comes barely a week after Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels announced a blockade of Saudi ports and cargoes at the entrance to the Red Sea.
The latest serious flare up in fighting follows days in which Tehran and its proxies have targeted bases and facilities of the US and its allies, including in Saudi Arabia, despite the brief US pause.
The sense of growing chaos in the Middle East was summed up by Sanam Vakil, the director of the Middle East and North Africa programme at Chatham House.
“Everyone is trying make sense of something that is increasingly senseless. One view is that the informal [US] pause in direct strikes on Iran saw a shift from Tehran to its proxies to maintain pressure [on Washington]. But there is no longer any plausible deniability because everyone knows how the relationships are intertwined,” Vakil said.
On the Iranian side, suggested Vakil, the unpredictability of Tehran’s tactics appeared to be deliberate to pressure Trump “either into confrontation or concession” with the aim of maintaining “a stranglehold on the Strait off Hormuz”.
Vakil also said countries in the region were interpreting the chaotic context of the conflict as a historic opportunity, including to weaken Iran. And on the Saudi side, she said there was a similar desire to be unpredictable. “No one wants to stay in the status quo.”
“I think from the point of view of the Saudis,” said H A Hellyer, a senior associate fellow in Middle East studies at the Royal United Services Institute, “there is a feeling that the Iranians are doing what they are doing because they feel that the Gulf Arab states won’t move up the escalatory ladder. The Saudis want to make it clear that assessment is wrong and that if Tehran thinks the Gulf states are easy prey, they are wrong.”
The problem, added Hellyer, was that while the Saudis may have rationalised the attack on the PMF as a precisely calculated act, it may be impossible to anticipate the response.
“Because we don’t know that, we are in uncharted territory not just because of the context of the war this year, but the wider issues in the region.
“And it is risky because Tehran sees itself as having been targeted by the US and Israel in a war of existential survival. They see everything through a prism that they have to reset the of the game in the region dramatically even if they are wrong and over playing their hand,” Hellyer said.

title: Fauci Pleads the Fifth at Senate Hearing on COVID, Escalating Long-Running Clash With Republicans
summary: The hearing escalates Fauci's long-running clash with Republicans as they seek to revisit the disputed origins of the coronavirus and the U.S. pandemic response.
full_text:
Dr. Anthony Fauci, the longtime infectious disease expert who helped lead the federal government's response to the COVID pandemic, invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination on Wednesday, refusing to answer questions at a Senate hearing that Republicans had hoped would expose him to potential perjury charges and discredit his handling of the nation's pandemic response.
Appearing before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee after being subpoenaed by Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, the panel's Republican chairman and one of Fauci's most persistent critics, the former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases declined to answer questions just minutes into the hearing, saying Paul had made clear his goal was to seek his prosecution.
"The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something, anything, that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, 'behind bars,'" Fauci said in his opening statement. He accused Paul of having an "obvious obsession with calling for my prosecution" and said the Senator's release of his personal pandemic diary was intended to intimidate and embarrass him.
"Although it pains me to do so because of the respect that I have for the legislative branch of government and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress," Fauci said, "under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution to refrain from answering your questions."
The hearing marked a dramatic moment in the yearslong political battle over the pandemic. Fauci, who advised seven presidents and became the nation's most recognizable public health official during COVID, has appeared before Congress hundreds of times over four decades; Wednesday was the first time he invoked the Fifth Amendment.
The infectious disease expert has been a primary target of Republicans' continuing effort to revisit the government's response to the pandemic and the disputed origins of the coronavirus, issues that have remained central to conservative criticism of Fauci years after he left government service in 2022. Paul and other Republicans have long alleged that the National Institutes of Health funded so-called gain-of-function research at the Wuhan Institute of Virology that contributed to the pandemic, an accusation Fauci has consistently denied. Fauci has maintained that, under the government's definition of gain-of-function research, NIH did not fund such work related to the virus that caused COVID. Federal reviews have not reached a definitive conclusion about the virus's origin, and there is no evidence it was engineered and leaked from a laboratory.
Former President Joe Biden gave Fauci a preemptive pardon in the final hours of his Administration in an effort to protect him from politically motivated charges. But Paul, who has repeatedly accused Fauci of misleading Congress about federally funded virus research in China and the origins of COVID, argued the hearing was necessary regardless. "A pardon that protects a person from criminal prosecution doesn't rewrite history," the Kentucky Senator said in his opening statement. "It does not erase documents. It does not convert a misleading statement to a truthful one, and it does not prevent Congress from establishing what happened."
Ahead of Wednesday's hearing, Paul released roughly 1,100 pages from Fauci's pandemic-era diary, arguing the documents showed discrepancies between Fauci's private thinking and his public testimony.
As Paul pressed ahead with questions despite Fauci's refusal to testify, the former health official responded each time with the same statement: "On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the Fifth Amendment to the Constitution."
At one point, Paul remarked, "Let the record record that the witness has refused to answer whether there's a folder in front of him based on his Fifth Amendment right."
The hearing also unfolded amid mounting pressure from Trump Administration officials to revisit Fauci's testimony under oath. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said earlier this week that Fauci could face perjury charges if he lied during the hearing despite Biden's preemptive pardon, arguing, "There are many things that (Fauci) said that we know are lies," and adding that "if he lies again, then he could be subject to perjury prosecution."
President Donald Trump likewise weighed in before the hearing, saying on Truth Social that Fauci "made too many bad calls" during the pandemic and asserting that he "didn't let (Fauci) shut the Country down." Trump has repeatedly criticized Fauci's recommendations on masks, shutdowns, and other public health measures.
Biden's pardon shielded Fauci from federal prosecution over actions and testimony connected to his government service during the pandemic. But Republicans have argued that any false statements made in new testimony could expose him to fresh legal jeopardy, a possibility Paul openly discussed before the hearing.
Asked this week about concerns that the hearing was designed to lure Fauci into committing perjury, Paul dismissed the criticism. "There's no risk to perjury if you tell the truth," he told reporters. "The only thing he can't do is lie again."
Democrats criticized the hearing as a partisan exercise. Senator Gary Peters of Michigan, the committee's top Democrat, argued the panel should be focusing on current national security threats rather than revisiting disputes over the pandemic. "Instead of focusing on the national security challenges that we are facing in our country right now, today's hearing looks backwards," Peters said at the hearing. "Rather than building on that work to strengthen our preparedness against future disasters, we are instead relitigating the past."

title: How to Stop Being So Defensive During Arguments
summary: You don’t need a better rebuttal. You need a reset.
full_text:
Here's a reliable way to tell that an argument has gone sideways: You started out discussing who was supposed to load the dishwasher, and you're now somewhere in the vicinity of a canceled dinner in 2019, your mother-in-law, or whether anyone in this household appreciates anyone else.
"It's like, ‘Wait, how did we get here?’" says Jessica Harrison, a couples counselor in Rhode Island. "That's a sign that somebody somewhere is being defensive."
It can be difficult to recognize when you’re being defensive, because it rarely feels that way. It feels like accuracy—like you’re finally setting the record straight. Meanwhile, the actual problem—the one somebody worked up the nerve to raise—never gets solved. It’s now buried underneath four brand-new ones. As Harrison puts it: “Who can manage and conclude five arguments in one conversation?”
The instinct to defend yourself isn’t a character flaw. It’s a protective reflex that can kick in when something threatens your sense of who you are. “We have the fight-or-flight response to protect ourselves from physical danger,” says Eli Kraiem, a clinical psychologist in New York who specializes in couples therapy. “But there’s also that same component to protecting our ego or our sense of self, which not everyone is as aware of.” In other words, a relatively ordinary complaint can feel like a verdict on who you are—especially when it comes from someone you care about. The alarm sounds, and suddenly you’re presenting Exhibit A for why you are, in fact, an excellent partner who does plenty around here, thank you very much.
That protective instinct isn’t always a bad thing. Sometimes you need to set a boundary or protect yourself, says Dr. Jeff Katzman, a psychiatrist at Silver Hill Hospital in New Canaan, Conn. But when defensiveness becomes your default response during ordinary disagreements, it can take a toll over months and years. Partners drift apart while ostensibly discussing chores. Friends stop bringing things up. “Whenever we become defensive, we start to become more certain about our perspective, and we go to battle in some way,” Katzman says. “The more defensive we become, the lonelier we become.”
The goal isn’t to eliminate defensiveness entirely. It’s to recognize it sooner, respond more thoughtfully, and know how to repair the conversation when you slip up. Here’s what experts recommend.
Learn your body's tell
Defensiveness often starts in your body before you even utter a word. Reuven Rosen, a couples therapist in Columbia, Md., asks clients: “What happened in your body the moment your partner said that?”
The answers tend to be specific and physical. “There's going to be a knot in my throat, there's going to be maybe a tightness in my stomach, a tightness in my chest, maybe my heart's beating,” he says.
These sensations are easy to overlook, but they can serve as early warning signs that you’re about to interrupt, deny, or fire back. When you notice your heart racing or your chest tightening, pause and ask yourself why you’re having such a strong reaction. That brief check-in can give you a chance to choose what to say next—instead of automatically going on the defensive.
Ask what you're trying to protect
Once you notice yourself becoming defensive, reflect on this: “What am I actually trying to protect?” It’s probably not the specific point you’re arguing about. More often, it’s something personal—your belief that you’re a good partner, a dependable friend, or a competent employee.
“When we're being defensive, we're ultimately trying to protect something, whether it's a value, a moral, our character, or our confidence in being able to do something,” Harrison says.
Figuring out what feels threatened can quickly change the conversation. A request for more help around the house might come across like this: “You think I’m a bad partner.” But that’s not necessarily what the other person said—or meant. They might simply be asking you to take on more around the house.
Harrison suggests asking yourself: “Am I protecting my character or my values right now, or am I actually listening to what this person is telling me?”
Sometimes, you become defensive precisely because being a good partner—or friend or employee—matters so much to you. “It's a sign that they care so much that they're terrified of getting it wrong,” Harrison says.
Trade certainty for curiosity
Defensiveness has a way of making you feel absolutely certain: You’re right, they’re wrong, and if you could just explain yourself clearly enough, they would finally see it. But the harder you work to prove your point, the less attention you’re paying to theirs.
Katzman, who has spent decades in improvisational theater alongside his clinical work, suggests doing the opposite. “The way out is not to think faster,” he says. “It's really to become curious sooner.”
Improv offers a surprisingly useful model. Onstage, “blocking” means rejecting the premise your scene partner has introduced. If they announce that it’s raining and you insist that it isn’t, the scene has nowhere to go. “When we block each other, that's what defensiveness really does,” Katzman says. “I'm negating your reality, you're negating mine.”
The alternative is the improv principle of “yes, and.” In an argument, that might mean acknowledging the other person’s experience before adding your own perspective. Another improv rule applies, too: “Make your partner look good,” Katzman says.
That doesn’t mean agreeing with everything the other person says. It means remembering that you’re on the same team. “We're after understanding, not winning,” Katzman says. “The goal is to move from being certain to being curious.”
Look for the 2% truth
Even criticism that feels unfair, exaggerated, or badly timed often contains a sliver of truth. Kraiem calls it the “2% truth.” Finding that 2% can be difficult—especially when you’re busy cataloging the other 98% the person got wrong—but acknowledging it can quickly lower the temperature.
Before you point out everything the other person has misunderstood, acknowledge the small part they got right. Say, for example, your partner accuses you of never listening. Your instinct might be to list all the times you did listen. Instead, try saying: “You’re right that I was distracted when you told me about your meeting tonight.” You’re not agreeing that you never listen; you’re acknowledging the part of the complaint that’s true. That can make the other person more receptive to what you say next.
The challenge is resisting the urge to debate whether the criticism is technically accurate and focusing instead on the feelings behind it. “We focus more on the intellectual perspective,” Kraiem says, “as opposed to: How can I connect to this person and understand where they're coming from, even if it doesn't make 100% sense to me?”
Retire "never" and "always"
Certain words carry tiny invitations to fight. Two are especially potent: “never” and “always.”
"When you default to these absolute words like ‘never’ and ‘always,’ you invite defensiveness in the other person," Katzman says. "They're just going to come up and try to prove you wrong." Tell someone they never do the dishes, and you’ve handed them a debate they can win on a technicality: They did the dishes last Thursday. Now you’re arguing about Thursday. The real message—”I need more help,” or “I need you to see everything I'm doing”—never gets delivered.
The same goes for grievance-stacking. Adding a second grievance, then a third, then the thing from last month, doesn't strengthen the case; it simply creates more things for the other person to dispute. "Somebody winds up having to defend themselves on seven fronts," Katzman says, "instead of just staying with the one thing that you're trying to figure out."
Reflect back before you explain yourself
When someone tells you that you hurt them, your first instinct might be to explain what you meant—or why they misunderstood you. But to someone who has just made themselves vu

title: The Ferrari Luce has at least 500 fans
summary: Just two months after a bumpy launch earlier this year, Ferrari has reportedly already hit its 2026 sales goal for its polarizing, Jony Ive-designed Luce EV. Ahead of Ferrari announcing its quarterly earnings on Thursday, the Financial Times reports that Ferrari was aiming to sell "just under 500" Luce units this year, and reached that […]
full_text:
Just two months after a bumpy launch earlier this year, Ferrari has reportedly already hit its 2026 sales goal for its polarizing, Jony Ive-designed Luce EV. Ahead of Ferrari announcing its quarterly earnings on Thursday, the Financial Times reports that Ferrari was aiming to sell “just under 500” Luce units this year, and reached that target this month.
The Ferrari Luce has at least 500 fans
The EV, designed by Jony Ive, was reportedly particularly popular in China.
The EV, designed by Jony Ive, was reportedly particularly popular in China.
Luce sales so far were reportedly driven by “strong demand from China,” where EV sales have already taken off from makers like Geely, Lynk & Co, and Zeekr. The Financial Times says Ferrari was trying to “reach a new generation of wealthy buyers” with the Luce, particularly in China and “tech hubs like Silicon Valley,” adding that their sources say US tech entrepreneurs have had “positive” feedback on the €550,000 EV.
Long term, Ferrari is reportedly hoping to sell around 2,500 Luce units by 2030, or roughly 600 each year, making up about five percent of the company’s annual sales. It’s also auctioning off the first production model of the Luce next month, which could sell for upwards of $1.1 million.

title: Remarkable’s refurbished bundle is an awesome deal that’s over $350 off
summary: A lot of us here at The Verge are fans of Remarkable’s digital note-taking tablets, and right now one of its higher-end options is much cheaper than usual. The Remarkable Paper Pro normally sells for $629 on its own, but Woot is currently offering a refurbished bundle for $449.99 through July 31st. It includes the […]
full_text:
A lot of us here at The Verge are fans of Remarkable’s digital note-taking tablets, and right now one of its higher-end options is much cheaper than usual. The Remarkable Paper Pro normally sells for $629 on its own, but Woot is currently offering a refurbished bundle for $449.99 through July 31st. It includes the tablet, a Marker Plus stylus, and a Book Folio, saving you $368 compared to buying new. The same refurbished bundle costs $649 from Remarkable and comes with a longer one-year warranty versus Woot’s 90-day warranty.
Remarkable’s refurbished bundle is an awesome deal that’s over $350 off
Plus, Twelve South’s high-end Bluetooth adapter and Anker’s 7-in-1 charging station are each under $60.
Plus, Twelve South’s high-end Bluetooth adapter and Anker’s 7-in-1 charging station are each under $60.
The 11.8-inch Paper Pro offers a paper-like writing experience, along with a rich color display. Unlike the monochromatic Paper Pure —Remarkable’s latest tablet that retails for $399 — it features an adjustable front light, making it easier to read and keep working after the lights go down. It also supports (but does not include) the optional $229 Type Folio keyboard, allowing you to switch between handwriting and typing.
Writing feels remarkably smooth — more so than similar devices from Boox, Kobo, and even Kindle Scribe models — while Remarkable’s software lets you organize notebooks with folders and tags, write directly on PDFs, and quickly convert handwritten notes into typed text. Although it supports basic sketching features like layers and shading, an iPad Pro is a better tablet if you’re serious about drawing. The Paper Pro’s color display was made with productivity in mind, serving as a distraction-free experience for reviewing slide decks, marking up reports, editing text, and organizing color-coded notes.
A few more Verge-approved deals:
- Twelve South’s AirFly Pro 2 Deluxe has returned to its record-low price of $59.49 ($10 off) at Amazon. Unlike the standard AirFly Pro 2, the model comes with an adapter for in-flight entertainment and a travel bag. Otherwise, both are identical and let you connect up to two pairs of wireless earbuds or headphones to devices with a 3.5mm audio jack. The Pro 2 can also play music from your phone or tablet through wired speakers.
- Razer’s Kiyo V2 X webcam is down to $65 ($35 off) at Amazon, matching its best price to date. The sharp webcam records in 1440p at up to 60fps, while Razer lets you quickly tweak settings like brightness, color, and sharpness in its Synapse desktop app. Its wide-angle lens and adjustable mount also make it easy to capture more of your face or setup, and when you’re done, you can simply twist the built-in privacy shutter closed.
- Anker’s Nano Charging Station is on sale for $59.99 ($20 off) at Amazon and directly from Anker with code WS7DV2SFHWUL, which is nearly its lowest price to date. The compact 7-in-1 power strip features three AC outlets, one USB-A port, three USB-C ports, and a pair of built-in retractable USB-C cables. Each USB-C port can deliver up to 100W when used on its own (less when multiple devices are plugged in), making the hub capable enough to power everything from your laptop and tablet to your phone and desk lamp.
