title: 美國仲裁協會設立 Web3 專責仲裁員名冊，區塊鏈爭議迎專門裁判
summary:
美國最大私人爭議解決機構 AAA（美國仲裁協會）正式推出 Web3 專責仲裁員名冊，首批成員涵蓋法律專家、學者 […]

〈美國仲裁協會設立 Web3 專責仲裁員名冊，區塊鏈爭議迎專門裁判〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
美國最大私人爭議解決機構 AAA（美國仲裁協會）正式推出 Web3 專責仲裁員名冊，首批成員涵蓋法律專家、學者和科技業高層，區塊鏈爭議終於有了「專門裁判」通道。
（前情提要：幣安使用者訴訟》控訴強制平倉不公，索賠1.4億；CZ：未來數月市場波動會極高！）
（背景補充：a16z：為什麼 AI 代理需要穩定幣進行 B2B 支付？）
以私人爭議解決聞名的 美國仲裁協會（AAA） 週三宣布，正式設立 Web3 專責仲裁員名冊（Web3 Panel），專門處理區塊鏈、智慧合約和數位資產爭議。這被視為主流法律機構為加密產業打造專屬基礎設施的重要一步。
AAA 是全球最大的私人爭議解決服務提供商之一，其 Web3 名冊匯聚了來自法律、科技、學術、訴訟和數位資產產業背景的仲裁員。
Web3 爭議的技術特性
AAA 名冊關係副總裁 Eric Dill 表示，Web3 爭議本質上是「在高度技術環境中發生的熟悉商業問題」。名冊涵蓋的爭議型別包括：
- 合約解釋與治理分歧
- 資產控制與管理
- 網路安全問題
- 交易紀錄爭議
- 跨國執行
這意味著當區塊鏈智慧合約執行出錯、代幣爭議、或鏈上資產管理發生糾紛時，未來企業可以選擇具有 Web3 領域知識的仲裁員來處理。
首批名冊成員
初始入選的仲裁員涵蓋多個領域：
- 數位資產專精律師，專注於加密貨幣和科技爭議的實務經驗
- David Hoffman，賓州大學法學院教授
- Rich Widmann，Google Cloud 全球 Web3 策略主管
名冊同時涵蓋「AI 代理商務（Agentic Commerce）」和「自主交易」爭議，即由軟體或 AI 系統在人類有限參與下發起或執行協議的場景。
從 AI 代理到區塊鏈：爭議解決的下一個前沿
AAA 此前已推出「法律層」對應 AI 代理商務爭議（2026 年 5 月），Web3 名冊可視為同一方向的延伸。隨著 AI 代理和區塊鏈交易在商業場景中日益普及，傳統的爭議解決機制確實需要跟上技術步伐。
值得注意的是，Web3 名冊本身不賦予 AAA 對加密產業的監管許可權。仲裁一般需雙方的自願同意，將爭議提交給私人仲裁員。

title: CLARITY 法案延期？檢察官主動提案修法，白宮顧問：連基本共識都沒有
summary:
代表美國執法官員的組織向白宮提案，要求修改 CLARITY 法案中關於開發者的條款。白宮加密顧問 Patric […]

〈CLARITY 法案延期？檢察官主動提案修法，白宮顧問：連基本共識都沒有〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
代表美國執法官員的組織向白宮提案，要求修改 CLARITY 法案中關於開發者的條款。白宮加密顧問 Patrick Witt 回應說新規定「連基本都不沾邊」，參院 8 月休會前的表決視窗正在收窄。
（前情提要：美國參院領袖 Thune 鬆口：CLARITY 法案趕不上 8 月表決！Polymarket 市場過關機率剩 37%）
（背景補充：拆解 CLARITY 法背後的權力、利益與背叛：散戶如何避險與掘金？）
美國參議院正在審理的《CLARITY 法案》（加密市場結構法）迎來新變化。代表執法官員的組織向白宮提案，要求修改法案中關於加密開發者的條款，白宮加密顧問回應說新規定「連基本都不沾邊」。
檢察官主動提案修法
根據 Politico 週二的報導，美國助理聯邦檢察官協會（National Association of Assistant US Attorneys）和美國州檢察官協會（National District Attorneys Association）致信白宮，要求修改《CLARITY 法案》中區塊鏈監管確定性法案（BRCA）的條款。提案要求開發者的指導原則不應「建立、擴張或修改聯邦法律下的刑事責任」。
白宮顧問秒回：連基本都不沾邊
白宮加密顧問 Patrick Witt 在 X 上回應，表示提案條款「甚至不接近」川普政府的立場，暗示這並非「有效協商」的結果。參議員 Catherine Cortez Masto 據報一直在推動白宮在表決前處理 BRCA 條款。
8 月休會前的最後視窗
美國參議院將於 8 月 7 日至 9 月 14 日進入州務工作期，意味著立法者只有不到兩週的時間透過加密市場結構法案。參議院多數黨領袖 John Thune 上週已表示，參議院不太可能在今個月完成表決。
Mercury Strategies 顧問公司合夥人 Anne Kelley 在 X 上分析，即使今天啟動表決程式，包含終止討論、修正案流程、第二次終止、長達 30 小時的辯論，在沒有全體一致同意的情況下，要在休會前完成「極其困難」。
不只 CLARITY 法案的鬥爭
《CLARITY 法案》同時也面臨民主黨眾對倫理規則的挑戰，法案規定了總統川普在 2025 年靠加密投資賺進 14 億美元的收益，讓白宮多了一位競爭對手。
法案的另一個核心要點是將數位資產的監管權從美國證券交易委員會（SEC）轉移至商品期貨交易委員會（CFTC）。目前 CFTC 只有 1 位主席，SEC 也只有 3 位委員，兩個機構都處於領導層人力不足的狀態。

title: Binance.US 8 月申請 CFTC 執照，進軍預測市場挑戰 Polymarket
summary:
Binance.US 執行長 Steve Gregory 在 Rare Evo 區塊鏈會議上宣布，將於 8 月 […]

〈Binance.US 8 月申請 CFTC 執照，進軍預測市場挑戰 Polymarket〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
Binance.US 執行長 Steve Gregory 在 Rare Evo 區塊鏈會議上宣布，將於 8 月向美國 CFTC 申請指定合約市場（DCM）執照，正式進軍預測市場，挑戰 Polymarket 與 Kalshi 的領跑地位。
（前情提要：Binance.US找到CEO了！前螞蟻金服、Uber高管Brian Shroder將肩挑幣安IPO大任）
（背景補充：預測市場迎來「軍火商」時代：5(c) Capital 布局基礎設施，對抗平台壟斷與監管風險）
美國加密貨幣交易所 Binance.US 即將進軍預測市場。執行長 Steve Gregory 週三在 Rare Evo 區塊鏈會議上宣布，公司將於 8 月向美國商品期貨交易委員會（CFTC）申請指定合約市場（Designated Contract Market，DCM）執照，藉此提供預測市場服務。
DCM 執照：預測市場的「全頻段」門票
根據 CFTC 官方規定，擁有 DCM 執照的機構可以合法交易「任何基礎商品、指數或工具的期貨或選擇權合約」。這意味著 Binance.US 未來能在同一平台上提供涵蓋加密貨幣、政治事件、體育賽事甚至天氣預測的多種型別的預測市場。
申請 DCM 執照需要符合 CFTC 的 23 項核心原則，包括系統保障、紀錄儲存和利益衝突管理等要求。截至週三，CFTC 官方紀錄中尚無 Binance.US 的 DCM 申請。
預測市場戰場：Polymarket 與 Kalshi 的雙雄格局
目前美國預測市場主要由兩大平台領跑：Kalshi 和 Polymarket。Kalshi 於今年 10 月完成 3 億美元融資並獲得 CFTC 認可，正積極擴張市場份額。Polymarket 則在 4 月完成二度融資，最新估值達 150 億美元，並於 7 月向 CFTC 申請保證金交易許可，將競爭推向槓桿合約化。
Binance.US 的加入將使這場競爭更加白熱化。憑藉已有的龐大使用者基礎和交易基礎設施，Binance.US 有潛力快速在預測市場佔得一席之地。
從幣安到預測市場：重返美國市場的擴張路線
這項申請距離美國 SEC 對幣安、Binance.US 和前 CEO 趙肇駿提起訴訟已超過一年。該訴訟指控包括誤用客戶資金等，最終促使幣安以約 1.2 億美元和解。
Binance.US 目前仍由前螞蟻金服和 Uber 高經理安·施羅德（Brian Shroder）領導，正逐步擴張美國業務。除了預測市場，Binance.US 也計畫申請銀行牌照，顯示其從單純的加密貨幣交易所向綜合金融平台轉型的戰略。
與臺灣相比，預測市場在臺灣尚處於早期階段。臺灣本土的預測平台多集中於政治選戰和體育賽事，而 Binance.US 的 DCM 策略若成功，可能為亞洲市場提供新的參考模式，將預測市場從「賭博」升級為有組織的期貨交易市場。

title: 比特幣下探6.3萬、以太坊失守1900美元！全網爆倉3.9億鎂、恐慌指數續回落
summary:
比特幣今（30）日延續弱勢，報63,691美元，24小時微跌0.36%；以太坊失守1,900美元，跌幅近1%。 […]

〈比特幣下探6.3萬、以太坊失守1900美元！全網爆倉3.9億鎂、恐慌指數續回落〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
比特幣今（30）日延續弱勢，報63,691美元，24小時微跌0.36%；以太坊失守1,900美元，跌幅近1%。全網爆倉3.91億美元，聯準會鷹派按兵不動拖累風險資產。
（前情提要：比特幣回檔6.3萬、以太坊跌破1880!全網爆倉6.1億鎂，恐慌指數續走低）
（背景補充：以太坊甦醒？ETH/BTC 匯率創 3 個月新高，Arkham：歷經四年 80% 跌幅後強勢回歸）
加密貨幣市場今（30）日延續弱勢格局，比特幣在 24 小時內最低下探至 63,267 美元，截稿前報 63,691 美元，微跌 0.36%；以太坊同步走跌，失守 1,900 美元關卡，報 1,897 美元，跌幅近 1%。過去 24 小時全網爆倉金額達 3.91 億美元，其中多頭佔比逾七成，市場情緒持續低迷，恐懼與貪婪指數回落至 28，仍處於「恐懼」區間。
聯準會昨日以 9 比 3 的投票結果維持利率不變，但三位官員投下升息票，主席 Warsh 鷹派談話拖累美股全面重挫，道瓊工業指數暴跌逾 1,150 點、跌幅 2.2%，標普 500 與那斯達克分別下跌 1.5% 與 1.7%，為 15 個月來最大單日跌幅。同時伊朗傳出襲擊事件推升油價，避險情緒升溫進一步壓抑加密貨幣買盤。
比特幣震盪走低，14 天高點仍遠
比特幣昨日一度反彈至 64,744 美元，但隨後賣壓出籠，最低觸及 63,267 美元，最終收跌 0.36%。從近 14 天走勢來看，比特幣於 7 月 21 日曾攀上 66,803 美元的波段高點，此後一路震盪向下，目前價格距離高峰仍有約 4.7% 的回撥空間。
以太坊失守 1,900 美元，近一週高點在 7/27
以太坊表現更為疲弱，24 小時跌幅 0.95%，最低觸及 1,872 美元，截稿前報 1,897 美元。近 14 天以太坊高點出現在 7 月 27 日的 1,967 美元，當時 ETH/BTC 匯率一度創三個月新高，但隨後買盤未能延續，價格連兩日回檔。
全網爆倉 3.91 億美元，多頭淪為重災區
過去 24 小時全網合約爆倉金額達 3.91 億美元，其中多頭爆倉 2.91 億美元、空頭僅 1.01 億美元，多頭佔比逾 74%，共計 110,313 名交易者遭清算。最大單筆爆倉單發生在幣安 BTCUSDT 合約，價值 293 萬美元。
SOL、XRP 同步承壓
主流幣種普遍走跌。SOL 報 73.28 美元，24 小時跌 0.6%，近一週持續在 72–78 美元區間徘徊，7 月 21 日曾觸及 78.57 美元的波段高點。XRP 報 1.07 美元，跌幅 0.82%，技術面仍受制於 1.05–1.15 美元的整理區間。
恐慌指數續回落，市場情緒低迷
Alternative.me 資料顯示，今日恐懼與貪婪指數報 28，較前一日回落 1 點，連續 8 日處於「恐懼」（0–49）區間，近 8 日數值介於 26 至 31 之間。市場缺乏明確利多催化劑，聯準會鷹派立場持續壓抑風險資產表現，短線加密貨幣可能延續整理格局。

title: ARK分析師：加密正進入史上最強整合期，交易所關門潮才剛開始
summary:
ARK Invest 研究員 Lorenzo Valente 指出，加密貨幣正進入史上最大規模的產業整合期，前 […]

〈ARK分析師：加密正進入史上最強整合期，交易所關門潮才剛開始〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
ARK Invest 研究員 Lorenzo Valente 指出，加密貨幣正進入史上最大規模的產業整合期，前三大協議佔據近八成收入，交易所關門潮才剛剛起步。
（前情提要：評論》加密逐漸成熟，對你倉位最煎熬的時刻來了）
（背景補充：交易所 BitMart 宣布收攤：8/26 停止交易、2027 年初關站）
方舟資本 ARK Invest 研究員 Lorenzo Valente 週三在 X 平台上 指出，加密貨幣產業正進入有記錄以來最大規模的整合期，投資者變得越來越挑剔，沒有產品市場契合度的專案與交易所逐漸失去資金吸引力。
Valente 引用資料顯示，永續合約交易所 Hyperliquid 與迷因幣發行平台 Pump.fun 佔據了加密應用總收入約 67%。若加上合成美元協議 Ethena，前三大協議合計佔比接近 80%，呈現創新的收入集中水準。
收入集中：前三大協議吃掉八成
這三檔協議背後反映的是市場的結構變化。Hyperliquid 以低費用和高效率吸引合約交易量，Pump.fun 透過迷因幣發行機制讓零散資金快速流動，Ethena 則以合成美元掛單策略收割穩定收益。三者在不同賽道同時佔據主導地位，顯示加密貨幣的收入邏輯正在從「廣撒網」轉向「少數贏家通吃」。
Valente 預期這種趨勢在未來數月會加速，帶來更多合併、收購、破產清算和專案關閉。他將這波洗牌形容為「非常看漲」，弱者退出，資源集中到效率更高的協議上。
交易所關門潮：BitMEX 與 BitMart 相繼收攤
整合的證據已經在眼前。上週，永續合約先驅 BitMEX 宣布將於 9 月關閉交易平台，結束了 5 年多的營運。幾天後，BitMart 也宣布 8 月 26 日停止交易服務，預計 2027 年 1 月全面關站。
兩家交易所的關閉都指向同一個原因：市場競爭加劇導致交易量分散到新興平台。BitMEX 加速下架交易對，BitMart 重新檢視營運條件，都是「沒有產品市場契合度」的具體表現。
不只是收攤：併購也在加速
整合不僅體現在關閉，也體現在收購。本月初，Bybit 透過收購印尼當地數位資產公司 NOBI，在亞洲最大加密市場之一建立了本土化交易所，擴張腳步明顯加速。
從臺灣市場角度看，加密產業的整合期也意味著投資者的選擇正在收斂。早期「什麼都試一遍」的策略，已逐漸被「聚焦核心協議」取代。ARK Invest 的觀察提醒投資人，加密市場的下一階段不是爆發式增長，而是效率與集中的重新定價。

title: PS 前總裁揭開 3A 遊戲金錢陷阱，稱中型 AA 遊戲才是打破「續作迷思」的解藥
summary: PlayStation Studios 前總裁肖恩·雷頓（Shawn Layden）近日接受歐洲媒體《Euro […]
full_text:
PlayStation Studios 前總裁肖恩·雷頓（Shawn Layden）近日接受歐洲媒體《Eurogamer》訪問，直言如今 3A（AAA）遊戲開發模式已難以為繼，呼籲業界重拾 PS2 時代 AA 遊戲路線。他透露正籌備一個專注 AA 遊戲市場的發行機構，期望能為中型規模作品提供更多發展空間。
開發成本急升 迫使發行商依賴續作
Shawn Layden 指出，PS4 時代一款 3A 遊戲預算約 1.5 億美元，如今已飆升至 3 至 4 億美元。他形容現今遊戲發行的基本模式自 1990 年代初起從未改變，「壞習慣很難改掉」。Shawn Layden 表示，現在要爭取資金開發新項目，「幾乎必然」要是續作、依附知名 IP（如《魔戒》），或是「類似 GTA 但……」的模仿之作，讓 PS1 及 PS2 時代那類風格獨特的作品越來越罕見。
Shawn Layden 提出，理想 AA 遊戲流程應為 12 至 15 小時，預算約 1,000 萬至 3,000 萬美元，開發週期約 2 至 3 年。他強調這類作品應以出色玩法及令人難忘的角色為核心，而非一味追求擬真畫面或超大型開放世界。Shawn Layden 期望填補獨立遊戲與 3A 大作之間的空隙，建立一個「發行機構」，讓開發團隊可以放膽嘗試風格獨特的項目，不必背負做續作或締造大熱作的壓力。他也特別提到目標受眾的轉變：年輕玩家「時間多但錢少」，年長上班族則「錢或許不多但更缺時間」，呼籲業界重新思考應為誰而設計遊戲。
業界早有共鳴
事實上 Shawn Layden 早於 2024 年已於 Gamescom Asia 上台演講，形容業界出現「創意崩塌」現象，指單靠押注大熱作是「死亡判決」，並直言「AA 已經消失」是對整個生態系統的威脅。
這次最新訪問呼應近年不少業界人士的看法，認為不斷膨脹的製作預算及過度追求擬真效果，正成為遊戲開發面對的重要挑戰。彭博社記者 Jason Schreier 今年 3 月透露，美加地區 3A 遊戲開發成本現在普遍達 3 億美元或以上，主要用於開發人員薪酬及團隊營運，與高層薪酬關係不大。以 3 億美元預算計算，若是 Sony 等無需與平台分成的第一方作品，仍需賣出約 450 萬份才能回本，反映現行 3A 模式風險極高。
（本文由 Uunwire HK 授權轉載；首圖來源：shutterstock）

title: US launches 'powerful' strikes on Iran after attempted attack on American troops
summary: The US military called the strikes "a powerful response" to Tuesday's firing by Iran on US bases in Jordan.
full_text:
US launches 'powerful' strikes on Iran after attempted attack on American troops
- Published
The US military says it has begun launching strikes against Iran in retaliation for an attempted surprise attack on American forces in the Middle East.
Centcom said on X the strikes were "a powerful response" to Tuesday's firing by Iran on US bases in Jordan and at ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
The latest hostilities came a day after the conflict expanded, with the first publicly announced joint US-Saudi strikes, which targeted Iranian proxies in Iraq.
When the US and Israel launched military strikes on Iran in February, US President Donald Trump said the war would last only a few weeks, but it has now gone on for five months with no end in sight.
On Wednesday, Axios reported, citing an unnamed US official, that Trump had met with Saudi defence minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, who had conveyed that Saudi Arabia wants to de-escalate tensions. The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.
The conflict has reignited after several days of relative calm.
For days, both sides halted strikes as talks apparently restarted in hopes of some type of diplomatic solution. Trump called them "very friendly negotiations", though Tehran denied any discussions were happening.
Hours before the announced strikes on Wednesday, Trump vowed to retaliate against Iran for their attempted attack on US troops a day earlier.
The US president told reporters at the White House: "We're going to be hitting them very hard because it's our turn to hit them.
"They know it's coming. They asked us not to do it."
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it had targeted a US air base and a command centre in Jordan "in response to the acts of aggression of the American child-killing army".
It also said naval forces had struck three oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz after they "ignored warnings" and sailed along what it described as an "unsafe and illegal route" through the vital Gulf waterway.
Last Friday, Trump suspended an intensive bombing campaign that had lasted for 13 consecutive nights. The US said it had targeted Iranian weapons and military sites. Scores of people were reported to have died.
On Tuesday, Centcom said the joint US-Saudi strikes hit "multiple terrorist logistics and weapons sites across eastern Iraq in a strong response to over 30 IRGC-directed aerial drone attacks in the last 72 hours".
Iraq's paramilitary Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), which is dominated by Iran-backed Shia militias, said at least 20 of its members had been killed in US-Saudi strikes on its bases.
The Iraqi presidency said it denounced the bombing of the PMF bases, calling it "an unacceptable attack and a blatant violation of Iraq's sovereignty".
But Trump told Fox News the strikes had been "co-ordinated with the Iraqi government".
Saudi Arabia, which sees itself as the leading Sunni Muslim power, and Iran, the largest Shia Muslim country, have been locked in a struggle for regional dominance for decades.

title: Burnham says nuclear sub investment will protect UK and boost jobs
summary: Speaking ahead of a visit to Barrow-in-Furness, the PM seeks to stress the economic benefits of defence spending.
full_text:
Burnham says nuclear sub investment will protect UK and boost jobs
- Published
Ongoing investment in nuclear submarines will "protect Britain for decades to come" but also support 47,000 jobs and apprenticeships, Andy Burnham has said
Speaking ahead of a visit to Barrow-in-Furness, where four new Dreadnought-class submarines are being built, the prime minister said: "Security is not only about what we build, it is about who builds it, and who benefits from it."
The project to replace existing nuclear submarines will receive £8.4bn to support progress towards getting the new vessels ready for service.
Conservative shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge welcomed progress on the submarine programme but accused Burnham of "failing to commit" to fully funding defence.
Burnham has said he wants to honour the UK's commitments on defence spending - including meeting a Nato target of spending 3.5% of national income by 2035.
Both he and his new Chancellor, John Healey, face the tricky task of finding the extra money needed to fulfil the pledge.
- UK complacent about war threat, warns BAE boss - Published6 days ago
 
The Dreadnought-class submarines will replace the UK's four Vanguard-class vessels that have been in operation since 1992, carrying Trident missiles to provide a nuclear deterrent.
Those Vanguard submarines are due to be retired in the 2030s, with the Dreadnoughts entering service at the same time.
The project has taken 20 years to get to this stage and was first announced in 2006 by the then Labour Prime Minister, Tony Blair. A decade later, in 2016, MPs formally approved building the new submarines.
Thursday's announcement of £8.4bn marks the start of what has been called the fourth phase of the project.
The spending was already planned, and was included in the Defence Investment Plan, published in the final days of Sir Keir Starmer's government.
The plan set out £63.6bn over the next four years for what is called the Defence Nuclear Enterprise.
The bulk of the money (£47bn) will go on keeping the nuclear submarines in operation, continuing with the Dreadnoughts, starting work on what might replace them in 30 years' time, and constructing several other new submarines and upgrading the UK's naval docks and manufacturing facilities.
The prime minister will use his visit to Barrow-in-Furness to stress how defence spending can have economic benefits for the country.
"The submarines produced in Barrow will protect Britain for decades to come, and the 47,000 jobs and apprenticeships will change lives both in this town and in dozens of places like it," he said prior to his visit.
"British money, spent on British workers, British firms and British skills, in the places that were written off for 40 years."
The government says the spending on the UK's nuclear defence currently supports around 47,000 British jobs – and is forecast to rise to 65,000 by 2030, including 22,000 apprenticeships by 2035.
Since becoming prime minister, Burnham has said he wants to reduce the number of young people not in employment, education or training and has announced funding to help those starting apprenticeships.
In a further step, Burnham has said the public procurement process, used to decide how to spend taxpayer cash, will favour companies offering 45-day work placements.
Speaking to the Jimmy's Jobs of the Future podcast,, external he said there would be "more social value weighting in public contracts", with a particular focus on firms offering such placements.
He said the move had been inspired by his time as Greater Manchester mayor, when he oversaw a rise in the number of 45-day placements offered by private firms.
But the announcement offered little detail of the extent of the changes, how they would be implemented and how many firms he expected to roll out the placements as a result.
Liberal Democrat defence spokesperson James MacCleary called for the use of defence bonds to "raise dedicated funding to rebuild capabilities across the whole of the armed forces".
For Reform UK, Danny Kruger dismissed Burnham's announcement as a "rehashed spending plan" that did "nothing to address the crisis in the UK's nuclear programme".
"If the Prime Minister actually cared about keeping Britain safe and ensuring our Armed Forces can stand alongside our allies, he would commit to a significant increase in spending and a total overhaul of both procurement and the nuclear enterprise," Kruger said.
Green Party Westminster leader Ellie Chowns questioned the decision to spend billions of pounds on "weapons that must never be used".
"Ministers should not pretend that the best way to create employment is by funnelling ever-increasing sums into the nuclear weapons programme," she said.

title: Cooler conditions on way for parts of UK - but still no rain for drought-hit areas
summary: After another day of record-breaking temperatures for some parts of England, a cold front is moving in.
full_text:
Cooler conditions on way for parts of UK - but still no rain for drought-hit areas
- Published
Cooler conditions and some rain are on the way for parts of UK on Thursday into the weekend, as a cold front moves into the UK.
However, with more than half of England and parts of Wales officially in drought, the coming days are unlikely to bring any rain to the driest areas of the country.
The latest UK heatwave peaked on Wednesday with temperatures soaring to 35.2C at Writtle in Essex. It was the hottest day for more than two weeks, when 35.2C was also recorded in Cotton in the Elms, Derbyshire, on 10 July.
It did not reach the highs experienced last month, when a new UK June temperature record of 38C was set at Lingwood in Norfolk on the 26th, which was also the hottest day of the year so far.
Last month's record was provisionally reported as 37.7C but the Met Office announced on Wednesday a new figure of 38.0C following a verification process.
It comes after drought was declared across more than half of England on Wednesday as hot, dry weather takes its toll on the country's water supplies.
The Environment Agency (EA) announcement covered much of central, eastern and southern England, and was a public sign that further restrictions on water use might follow.
It added that the impacts are already being felt, including low river flows, early harvests and high risk of wildfires. More than 20 million people are already under hosepipe bans.
North Wales and the Upper Severn river basin entered drought conditions last week, Natural Resources Wales said.
Scotland does not declare drought but monitors "water scarcity". Some parts of eastern Scotland are in the most extreme category of "significant scarcity", according to the Scottish Environment Protection Agency.
Northern Ireland is not currently in drought.
- Pictures show scale of drought across England as rivers dry up - Published9 hours ago
 
Is the heatwave over?
Three consecutive days meeting the threshold temperature are required for it to be considered a heatwave.
The extent of this latest heatwave has been limited because Monday did not reach the threshold across most of the Midlands, East Anglia and central southern England.
Tuesday and Wednesday were both hot days, but the cold front moving in on Thursday drops the temperatures just below the threshold for many, meaning many areas narrowly miss the mark.
However, the cold front does not quite reach East Anglia and south-east England, so the heat hangs on for one more day with temperatures reaching the high 20s or possibly 30C in the hottest areas, which will therefore reach three days above the threshold.
For Friday and the weekend, temperatures in central and eastern England will still reach the mid-20s so it will still feel warm in the sunshine.
Sunday will probably turn a bit warmer again with temperatures into the high 20s. The weather will be cool in the north-west of the UK with temperatures often below average.
Boiling Point: The Week of Extreme Heat
The last week of June 2026 saw record-breaking temperatures across parts of the UK and Europe. While some enjoyed the sunshine, the heat caused trains, schools and emergency services to buckle.
Is there any rain on the way?
For the most parched areas of the UK, there is unlikely to be any rain over the next few days.
Wisley in Surrey has had 42 consecutive dry days as of Tuesday 29 July. The weakening cold front should reach Wisley but is unlikely to produce any rain there.
The wettest weather will affect the north-west of the UK, which has already seen plenty of rain this month. Aultbea in the Highlands has already had about a third more rain than its July average.
Next week there is going to be more rain in the forecast, and again the north-west will probably end up being the wettest area.
A few forecast models produce some useful rain in the south too but this is far less certain with many models producing little if any rain. It is too soon to know for sure.
The summer so far has seen temperature records tumble.
We have now had 10 days with temperatures over 34C, beating the previous record of seven set in 1976 and equalled in 2020.
There have been 31 days with temperatures over 30C, not far off the record of 34 days set in 1995 and comfortably beating 1976, which had 24 days.
There is still plenty of time left this summer to equal or beat this mark.
- Published14 hours ago

title: How the UK's extreme heat is shifting the conversation about air-con
summary: Should we embrace air conditioning despite its costs and consequences, and how much should we spend on adapting homes versus cutting carbon?
full_text:
Mandy Bourne lives with her 80‑year‑old mum in a top‑floor social housing flat in the West Midlands. Both struggle with health conditions exacerbated by the recent heatwaves.
For Mandy, temperature shifts can trigger flare-ups of her chronic lung condition. "I've got COPD and sometimes I can't breathe," she explains.
Across the UK, solid brick homes like theirs quietly absorb heat the way they have for decades. Charged‑up walls radiate warmth back into rooms that never get the chance to cool.
Mandy says she is constantly reaching for her inhaler as her flat overheats. "It's red hot in the flat. The sun is just beaming in."
That retained warmth can push night‑time temperatures in urban centres up to 7C higher than the surrounding countryside. This is the urban heat island effect and it is at its most dangerous in the early hours when bodies need cooler air and cannot find it. Modelling of a previous West Midlands heatwave by researchers from the University of Birmingham reached the bleak conclusion that the heat island impact alone accounted for roughly half the 130 heat-related deaths.
Jo Shields, head of sustainability for Mandy's housing association Walsall Housing Group, known as whg - which owns 23,000 homes across Walsall and the Midlands - hears the same complaint time and again. "The heat gain stays within the concrete or the brick," she says, "so the night-time cooling becomes harder".
Last summer, as the region baked, the residents of Ellum Pointe - a whg scheme for the over-55s - began telling their landlords they simply could not cool their flats. The response was improvised.
"We took the community room, closed all the windows and doors, and we put a mobile air-conditioning unit in there," Shields says. "And basically, we created an internal cool room." She likens it to the warm spaces opened during the pandemic for people who couldn't afford to heat their homes.
Shields' job has previously focused on decarbonising - reducing the emissions from the housing stock - but she now has to balance those pressures with the need to adapt homes to rising heat. Across the country, landlords are facing similar choices.
As Britain enters a new kind of summer, with homes built to trap warmth and heatwaves intensifying, two questions loom: should we embrace air conditioning despite its costs and consequences, and how much should we spend on adapting homes versus cutting carbon?
Historic choices
For 40 years, wealthy countries have focused heavily on cutting the carbon emissions that cause climate change, known as mitigation. Adaptation such as designing housing so it is more resilient to hotter temperatures and installing air conditioning has not always had the same focus.
Reducing emissions was seen as morally right because richer nations produced most of the gases that have warmed the planet. And with that focus came a funding imbalance.
In 2023, $1.8trn was given to mitigation, whilst adaptation did not secure even 5% of that – it scraped $65bn globally.
Spending too much on adaption was seen by many as giving up on the fight against climate change. But this mainstream view has now been challenged.
In a memo published last year, Bill Gates - a man who has poured billions into clean technology - argued that the climate movement's "doomsday" fixation on temperature targets had diverted money from the things that most improve lives in a warming world.
Climate change is serious, he wrote, but "will not lead to humanity's demise". Governments, he added, should be investing in cooling for the countries that need it.
The publication sparked backlash from climate scientists who accused Gates of making arguments based on "false dichotomies" - pitting mitigation and adaptation against each other.
Some, including US President Donald Trump, saw it as sign that the billionaire was "finally" supporting the belief that climate change was a hoax.
Gates insisted he was not arguing against cutting emissions, but rather for spending money where it saves the most suffering.
The row that followed exposed the real fault line that's coming to the surface this summer: not whether to cut carbon or adapt to the heat – but how much to spend on each.
Profit wins out
There's another reason that muddies the waters and helps explain why cutting carbon became the prime focus – it was investable. Heat pumps and EVs can be sold. Spending on shade, ventilation and cooler hospitals and homes all produce little in the way of bankable returns - even if it reduces costs of climate change long term.
Baroness Brown - also known as the engineer Julia King, who chairs the adaptation committee of the government's Climate Change Committee - argues this imbalance is written into UK law.
Under the Climate Change Act, the mitigation half of her committee recommends legally binding carbon budgets that ministers must deliver and are marked on every year.
Adaptation has no such teeth: the government writes its own risk assessment and its own plans.
"Essentially, the government writes an essay, and our job is to say, is it doing the things it said would do in its essay. It's not actually to say, are these things any good."
Her committee has spent, she says, "almost 20 years pulling our hair out" - but this year has been different. With exquisite timing it produced a report just as the first heatwave was striking Britain in May - urging lawmakers to set hard adaptation targets.
"We've actually looked at the difference that providing some sort of support with cooling for the 30% of most vulnerable homes, and cooling in our hospitals, [with] preventive care visits. The modelling we've done suggests that that would reduce 40% of the increase in heat-related deaths that are predicted for 2050."
"We're saying these are the actions that can make a big difference."
One of the most controversial ideas in the report is on air conditioning. Right now, only 5% or so of English homes have a cooling unit. The Committee recommends fitting these devices in hospitals and care homes within 10 years, and schools in 25 years.
This goes against years of government advice that passive cooling was the preferred method - using shade, ventilation and other design features to bring down temperatures, not mechanical means.
Prof Mat Santamouris from the University of New South Wales, is the world's most-cited researcher on urban overheating.
Machines, he argues, should be the last line of defence: reflective roofing alone, in one of his studies, dragged indoor temperatures from around 43C towards 30C, while a ceiling fan gives comfort for a fraction of the cost.
Putting up unshaded glass towers in cities, he says, is "crazy". "We cannot air-condition our way out of climate change."
Santamouris is scathing about who is driving the air con demand - the industry, he says, is "extremely powerful" – adding that passive cooling adds its own economic growth, as money is spent on plumbers and builders.
Against him stand those who think Britain's hostility to cooling has curdled into a type of masochism.
David Lawrence, of the Centre for British Progress think tank, puts it plainly: we don't tell people to insulate their homes in winter and then skip the radiators. So why insist shade and shutters are enough in summer?
He points out that air conditioning is standard now in offices, hotels and shops, "but we don't expect it for schools and hospitals - which is kind of odd, because those are places where millions of people are every day", and where heat measurably dents concentration, learning and health.
This dispute over the pros and cons of the technology is becoming political.
Some London councils, following a planning "cooling hierarchy", say low‑energy ways of keeping homes cool should be prioritised over air conditioning and in a small number of cases have ordered property owners to remove them; the Conservative front bench calls it "dark ages" miserabilism; other MPs and political commentators demand an "air-con revolution".

title: Interest rates expected to be held again by Bank of England
summary: It would be the fifth hold in a row, with the Bank rate standing at 3.75% - the lowest since February 2023.
full_text:
Interest rates expected to be held again by Bank of England
- Published
UK interest rates are expected to be held at 3.75% for a fifth time by Bank of England policymakers.
Uncertainty over the the global political and economic outlook, and the impact on prices, means the Bank is likely to continue its cautious approach to rates.
Its Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meets eight times a year, with its decisions heavily influencing how much borrowers are charged for loans and mortgages, as well as the returns available to savers.
The benchmark Bank rate is at its lowest level since February 2023, but few analysts predict any short-term changes.
The committee of five women and four men will announce their latest interest rate decision at 12:00 BST, with a hold the widespread expectation.
The Bank rate is the MPC's primary tool for maintaining the rate of rising prices - inflation - at a target of 2%.
The latest official figures show inflation in the UK was 2.6% in the year to June, down slightly on the previous month but still above its 2.3% target.
The inflation rate is likely to go up in July, as millions of households in Scotland, England and Wales feel the impact of a 13% rise in domestic energy prices.
The increase was the result of the impact of the Iran war on wholesale energy prices.
Conflict in the Gulf, and uncertainty over the chances of a lasting truce, hang over the MPC's meeting and decision this month and in the months ahead.
Many analysts expect interest rates to be unchanged in the foreseeable future, with the possibility of the next change being a rise.
"A new government finding its feet, and the situation in the Middle East becoming increasingly uncertain, mean that a hold on [the] base rate decision would be a welcome dose of stability," said Katie Horne, from savings platform Flagstone.
"People have had more than enough uncertainty over the past year, and even a temporary pause eases the pressure a little."
Impact on borrowers and savers
A hold would mean monthly repayments for homeowners on a tracker mortgage rate would be unchanged.
However, more than eight in 10 mortgage customers have fixed-rate deals, and the major UK lenders have been increasing rates on new deals in recent days.
The interest rate on this kind of mortgage does not change until the deal expires, usually after two or five years, and a new one is chosen to replace it.
The average rate on a new two-year fixed deal is 5.62%, according to financial information service Moneyfacts - the highest for more than a month.
Rates are going up because of lenders' funding costs rising owing to renewed volatility in the Middle East. Individual companies don't want to be inundated with applications so the sector tends to move as a pack.
"A hold is still welcome, but market expectations will need to ease back before we can hope for a return to lenders cutting rates," said David Hollingworth, from mortgage broker L&C.
Recent projections by the Bank of England suggest just over five million homeowners should expect their monthly mortgage repayments to increase by the end of 2028.
Other loans are influenced by the MPC's decision, which also has an key impact on the returns available to savers. A higher Bank rate, or the likelihood of an increase, can improve the interest rates that savers are offered.
Some of the deals available to people willing to lock-in their savings for fixed period are at their highest for nearly two years.
The guaranteed interest paid on the top one-year bond is 4.91%, the highest for new customers since October 2024.
"This rare dose of good news for savers is somewhat of a silver lining after years of poor real returns," says Rachel Springall, of Moneyfacts.

title: Inquiry finds MoD Afghan data breach was foreseeable failure
summary: The Commons' Defence Committee says in a report that the MoD used secrecy as a "shield" against proper expertise.
full_text:
Inquiry finds MoD Afghan data breach was foreseeable failure
- Published
A data breach that exposed personal details of thousands of Afghans applying to come to the UK to flee the Taliban was a "foreseeable" failure, a parliamentary inquiry has found.
In a report published on Thursday, the Commons' Defence Committee said the Ministry of Defence (MoD) had lacked the expertise to run the UK's Afghan relocation scheme after the fall of Kabul to the Taliban and had used secrecy as a "shield" against proper accountability.
The breach came to light in August 2023 but an unprecedented super-injunction prevented it from being reported on until July 2025.
A MoD spokesperson said the leak "should never have happened" and welcomed the opportunity to learn from the incident.
- Man's anger as brother left in Afghanistan after data breach - Published7 June
 
A super-injunction is a court-mandated gagging order that forbids news outlets from reporting private or sensitive information.
It also bans the media from revealing that the injunction exists.
The leak was not "an individual mistake" but a "foreseeable systemic failure" caused by "inappropriate tools, weak operating procedures, insufficient training, poor organisational continuity, and an inadequate culture of data protection and accountability", the Defence Committee said in its report.
The breach, just one of 19 reported between February 2022 and November 2023, was caused by a member of MoD personnel sharing a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet with a "trusted third party", the committee added. The BBC previously revealed the breach had originated from UK Special Forces (UKSF) headquarters.
The spreadsheet contained data of more than 18,500 applicants to the Afghan Relocations and Assistance Policy (Arap) scheme - every person who had applied to the scheme by January 2022.
Arap was set up in April 2021 to help people who feared their lives were at risk because they had worked with British armed forces in Afghanistan and to resettle eligible applicants and their family members in the UK. It was closed in July 2025.
Committee chairman Tan Dhesi said: "The Ministry of Defence should stick to defence - it should never have been left to run immigration casework schemes."
The report branded the MoD's use of Excel a "continuing cultural failure" and described the wider Afghan relocation scheme as "utterly and obviously inadequate".
Dhesi also hit out at the secrecy surrounding the breach and said the length of the super-injunction "imposed serious costs on accountability and trust".
It was originally expected to last four months, the report found, but remained in place for almost two years.
- What we know so far about Afghan data breach - Published16 July 2025
 
- How bad is Afghan data breach for MI6 and SAS? - Published17 July 2025
 
The committee also questioned the decision not to provide confidential briefing to parliamentarians, with then-Defence Secretary Grant Shapps pushing back against plans to tell then-shadow defence secretary John Healey of the breach.
Thursday's report also questioned the government's overarching policy to not comment on special forces matters, describing it as "inappropriate" in the context of the breach.
The committee added that special forces involvement "should not prevent Parliament and the public from understanding how administrative failings occurred".
Dhesi said: "Secrecy has been too easily used as a shield against proper accountability in areas far removed from sensitive operations."
The role of UKSF in the resettlement scheme was also questioned by the committee after reports the breach had been due to their involvement in deciding whether to relocate Afghan special forces.
The committee was unable to establish this connection, due to the "neither confirm nor deny" policy of the government, but it did raise concerns over the handling of these cases.
In February 2024, BBC Panorama revealed that British Special Forces had been given a de facto veto over Arap applications from their Afghan counterparts seeking to relocate to safety in the UK.
Afghan special forces served alongside UKSF on some of the conflict's most dangerous missions and are considered among those at the highest risk of reprisal since the Taliban takeover.
Last year, the BBC obtained internal MoD documents - also cited in the report - showing a British Special Forces officer personally rejected 1,585 resettlement applications from Afghans with credible links to special forces in a matter of weeks, in 2023. The UKSF officer did not approve a single application during that period.
The rejections from UKSF left many in fear for their lives and former members of the Afghan special forces told the BBC they were living in hiding.
One said he had been interrogated and beaten by the Taliban before he went on the run, while another said he had escaped first but had heard the Taliban had gone to his home looking for him.
"I'm living in a very bad situation. I am in hiding and mostly my family can't live together and we cannot go out and we cannot work," he said. "I feel I have been left alone in the midst of hell."
The government had to announce a review in 2024 and since then 884 former members of Afghan special forces, who served alongside UKSF, have since had their rejections overturned.
The defence committee report outlined that the "proportion of decisions subsequently overturned demonstrates the seriousness of that failure".
The UK government closed Arap to new applications in 2025, but the report said the government had a "special responsibility" to the Afghan special forces it had wrongly rejected. Many of them had made their applications in 2021, but were still living in fear due to "government delay or error".
The defence secretary currently faces a legal challenge at the Royal Courts of Justice from former Afghan special forces who are unable to escape to the UK.
In a hearing on Wednesday, the court heard one family had "$200 left to survive".
A MoD spokesperson said: "This incident should never have happened and we acknowledge the significant impact it has had on many people.
"Thousands of eligible Afghans have already been safely relocated to the UK, where they can rebuild their lives and we are committed to ensuring that we conclude the Afghan resettlement programme by the end of this Parliament.
"We are learning the lessons from this incident and important reforms are already in place, including improved data protection standards, strengthened case-working processes and better programme governance.
"We welcome the public and parliamentary scrutiny of our actions, so we can learn more and be held to account, and we'll continue to work closely with the committee on this issue."

title: How to do neon festival make-up - without harming your skin
summary: Neon is on trend, but some make-up products pose a serious risk to your health. Here's what to check for, and how to dazzle.
full_text:
How to do neon festival make-up - without harming your skin
- Published
Festival season's here and neon make-up is everywhere.
Bright graphic eyeliner, vampy lips and holographic highlighter are some of this year's biggest beauty trends for the main stage.
But some of these make-up products, which are being sold by third-party sellers on online marketplaces such as TikTok Shop, can contain a host of toxic chemicals, warns the Chartered Trading Standards Institute, external.
So here's what to look out for – and how to stay safe while serving festival glam.
Make eyes 'pop'
How to get the look: Dominic Skinner, make-up artist and judge on the hit BBC show Glow Up, came into the BBC's London offices to show us how to achieve the perfect festival look and make it dance and party-proof.
If you want colours to "pop", he says use a white eye pencil on the skin first and then press bright eyeshadows on top.
"It will make bold colours more intense, and last all night."
What to be aware of: Banned ingredients can cause bad rashes and allergic reactions, so check the label and avoid products that say they're "not for cosmetic use" - even if they say they're for the skin.
Also look out for banned colourants, like Solvent Yellow 172, CI 45161 (Basic Red 1:1) and CI 45174 (Basic Violet 11:1).
Be cautious of cheap products or sellers you've never heard of, says Skinner.
"There are some items that are UV reflective, glow-in-the-dark or neon that are made by cosmetics brands but are quietly labelled as a 'non-cosmetic paint'," he adds.
Go for glitter
How to get the look: Fairycore-inspired make-up is in, which means sparkles, face gems and glitter.
Don't go for subtle, says Skinner. "The 'no make-up look' is gone. Clean girl is out!"
There's a child-like quality to festival make-up, he says, so embrace it - think playful colour and crystals.
To stand out, he suggests using glitter in hair partings or your shoulders.
"Personally, I say use gems as they're bigger and more impactful, plus you can peel them off at the end of night and reuse them in the morning."
What to be aware of: Skip near the eyes to avoid nasty scratches on your cornea, says the British Skin Foundation's Dr Emma Wedgeworth, and never use craft glitter.
Use biodegradable, eco-friendly products that are better for the environment and softer on the skin. Safe adhesives, like lash glue, will keep it in place.
Give lips a vampy spin
How to get the look: Vogue says 2026 is all about juicy and blurred lips, external that play with texture more than colour. Think "your-lips-but-better", using stains and glosses.
InStyle magazine recommends dramatic, dark red vampy lips, external as a breakaway from summer-friendly pinks and peaches.
Use a liquid lip product, Skinner says, because it won't budge.
"You can do some drinking, you can do some snogging."
And he says leave that lip liner until last - it'll just "highlight how wonky your drawing skills are". Colour first, liner later.
What to be aware of: Whatever your look, don't share your balm or lipstick. That can spread nasty infections like cold sores.
Cross-contamination is real, and why make-up artists sanitise everything in between clients.
Don't forget to apply sunscreen
Use high-protection sunscreen - at least SPF 30 - as a base before the make-up and let it soak in like any primer, says Wedgeworth.
Skinner recommends matte or sweat-proof SPF to help your make-up last longer.
Reapply throughout the day, at least every two hours. Don't forget your hairline and any partings to protect your scalp.
Sprays let you layer over make-up, but can be difficult to apply thickly enough, so take shade breaks and bring a big hat for extra protection, says Wedgeworth.
Hair styles that last all night
How to get the look: Who, What, Wear, external says think about accessories - scarfs, crochet beanie caps or eye-catching hair clips, charms or cuffs.
InStyle, external suggests Mermaid waves or thin Baby Braids if your hair is long enough.
What to be aware of: If you want a colour change with a spray or dye, do a patch test first to check you are not allergic.
Put a small amount behind your ear or on your arm and wait 24 to 48 hours to check for a reaction, says Wedgeworth.
Skinner says you probably already own products that can give you a festival look.
"You just have to think creatively about how to play with it."

title: He watched the 1966 World Cup final at Wembley aged 16 - no day since has matched it
summary: Kenneth Farrington shares his memories of the 1966 World Cup Final, 60 years on.
full_text:
He watched the 1966 World Cup final at Wembley aged 16 - no day since has matched it
- Published
Ahead of the 60th anniversary, readers have been sending BBC Your Voice their memories of England's dramatic victory against West Germany at Wembley Stadium in 1966 when they won the World Cup.
Kenneth Farrington, now 76, watched from the stands as a 16-year-old and shares his account of the excitement of the final on 30 July 1966.
It was my workmate, Syd Manning, who obtained the ticket for me and arranged the transport.
When he initially asked me, I was reluctant because I thought I'd see more of the match by watching it on TV, but thankfully he was insistent saying "you may never get the chance again to attend a World Cup Final", and how right he was.
Family occasions apart, it remains the greatest, most memorable day of my life.
The cost of the ticket - in the standing area behind the goal where, as it turned out, Geoff Hurst would score his third goal and complete his hat-trick - was 25 shillings - just over a quarter of my weekly wage as a transport clerk.
I didn't bother with breakfast as Syd told me that he would be calling early. The journey down to Wembley took more than four hours.
When we parked up, I recall Wembley being besieged by ticket touts who were looking to sell.
Apparently, the fans of the more fancied teams at the time like Brazil, Hungary and Portugal had bought blocks of tickets that also included the final, so when their teams failed to make it, they sold their tickets on.
Therefore, if you wanted to turn up on the day and attend the final, it was entirely possible providing you had the money. It was harder to get tickets to the FA Cup Final that year than to the World Cup Final.
My first sight of the Wembley pitch actually took my breath away because the grass was green.
I'd been so used to viewing cup finals on our black and white TV, I fully expected the grass to be the same colour.
The match itself was enthralling - no way could it be described as a tactical battle. It was two teams attempting to win a football game.
Going into extra time was a bonus as far as I was concerned, because I was getting extra value from the outlay for my ticket.
The Geoff Hurst hat-trick goal was a great finale to a splendid occasion. And if the ball had burst the back of the net - it nearly did - I'd have caught it.
Outside the stadium, I felt like I was walking on air. My team, in the country where I was born and had never left up to that point, had won the World Cup.
An elderly England fan, probably close to the age I am now, 76, was serenading a group of supporters by singing, "Geoff Hurst scores for all the goals, hallelujah!"
I recall seeing the passion and enthusiasm in his eyes and hoping that I would always retain the same love for the game of football, thankfully I have. It probably inspired my 32-year career as a referee, officiating in over 2,500 matches.
We faced a long journey home so it was straight back in the car and there was much chatter about what we had witnessed.
When I arrived home to our small terraced house in the early hours of Sunday morning, I was so keen to share my story of the day with my mother Margaret that I left my key in the front door.
My dad had sadly died in 1960 at the age of 37, so I couldn't share my story with him, much as I would have loved to. But my mother thankfully showed an interest despite not being a fan of the game - she could sense how much it meant to me.
In 1969, I moved to Huddersfield, West Yorkshire to marry the girl of my dreams, Susan, so I lost touch with Syd.
But if he is still with us, I'd like to thank him from the bottom of my heart for providing me with a fantastic memory that will remain with me for the rest of my days.
Kenneth's story was told to BBC journalist Kris Bramwell.

title: Your burger costs more this summer, but farmers say they're not cashing in
summary: The prices of beef, bread buns and bagged salad have risen sharply over the past year, figures show.
full_text:
Your burger costs more this summer, but farmers say they're not cashing in
- Published
For many, the smell of charcoal and sizzling meat is the scent of summer.
However, soaring costs mean a backyard barbecue may no longer be an affordable meal option.
The rising cost of burgers and fast food has been labelled "burgerflation".
According to data from the Consumer Price Index (CPI), the prices of beef, bread buns and bagged salad have risen sharply since last summer.
But does this mean farmers and food producers are earning more?
We spoke to some of those whose produce could find its way from the farm to your fork.
The burger
Heather Oldfield, cattle farmer, Boston, Lincolnshire
Lincolnshire is known as the breadbasket of England due to its output of crops – and it also has a rich tradition of livestock farming.
Heather Oldfield, who farms cattle near Boston, says her family "want to feed people".
The family has 200 animals, which will be sold to Morrison's butchery. They will make many meat products, including burgers destined for barbecues.
The latest figures from the Agricultural Price Index (API), for April, show farmers like Oldfield were getting 8% less for their beef on average compared with the previous 12 months.
But shoppers were paying 9% more in May compared with a year before, according to the CPI.
"There's a lot of uncertainty," says Oldfield.
The mother-of-two says she must cover their costs to ensure the farm survives for her daughters, who want to be farmers.
Oldfield says: "How do we shore the business up into a place that's right for them to come into without saddling them with a lot of debt?"
A Defra spokesperson says the government is "backing our hard-working farmers, investing a record £11.8bn – more than any previous government".
Yet Oldfield is feeling the pressure. She also works full time for a plant breeder because the farm does not generate enough to pay the wages for both her and her husband.
The bread bun
Phil Clayton, baker, York, North Yorkshire
"I know I'm not going to be a millionaire running a bakery," says Phil Clayton.
We are speaking in the busy bakery he runs with his wife Tina. It is only 10am, but the operation has been in full swing for nine hours.
Clayton says it is "absolutely not true" that the bakery enjoys more profit due to price rises.
In May, families were paying 2% more for bread rolls than they were a year earlier, according to the CPI.
But in April, farmers were receiving 0.3% less for wheat, the main ingredient, according to API figures.
The 2% increase in prices for customers is smaller than the 3% rise seen across the whole CPI index.
Clayton says he does not regret increasing his prices by 10p to 20p.
"My responsibility is to make sure all of this lot get paid," he says, referring to his 30-strong team, which includes bakers, delivery drivers and Saturday staff employed in the cafe that adjoins the bakery.
Clayton points out the extra money shoppers pay at the tills goes towards increases in rent, wages, National Insurance, delivery fuel and the rising cost of flour – much of which originates from farms in the region.
The flour
Robert Archer, mill manager, Kirkbymoorside, North Yorkshire
Robert Archer says haulage costs have been "a big hit", forcing him to increase the price of the organic flour he mills in North Yorkshire.
"If we stayed at the same price we would be losing money and then we couldn't run the business," he says.
The mill buys more than 400 tonnes of wheat from farms in North Yorkshire and East Yorkshire each year. It generates enough flour to feed 20,000 people, he says.
The flour is sent to customers, including Phil Clayton's bakery in York.
Nelly Trevelyan, the mill's owner, says staying organic helps them to minimise percentage price rises because "we don't have nitrogen fertiliser cost increases [and] we don't use pesticides, so we haven't got those increases".
However, she says many people buy what they see as "cheap food" from "the industrial farming system" that uses more intensive methods.
The salad
Mathew Brankley, farmer, Snaith, East Yorkshire
Mathew Brankley believes food remains "relatively cheap" in the UK.
"I know that that might sound like a shock," he says. "But if you go to some places over in Europe and the States, the cost of a simple lettuce could be $2.99. In the UK, it's retailing at 80p to £1."
According to the API, vegetable growers were receiving 12.6% more for their produce in April compared to 12 months ago. But in May, shoppers were paying 8% more, according to the CPI.
Brankley insists he is no better off, explaining any extra money he is being paid for his crops is being "eaten up" by rises in the prices he pays for fuel and fertiliser.
"There's a lot of people that are taking a cut from what the customer pays in the supermarket before any of it gets back to the farmer," he says.
Despite the challenges, Brankley says he would not consider changing jobs.
"I wouldn't do anything else because I enjoy it so much."
A Defra spokesperson says: "We've already cut red diesel to its lowest rate in over 20 years [and] we are seeking views on suspending fertiliser tariffs to help farmers."

title: The Chinese robot army transforming the UK's retail industry
summary: Britain's weak productivity growth and labour shortages are creating an opportunity for China's robotics firms.
full_text:
The Chinese robot army transforming the UK's retail industry
- Published
Every time you click "buy" on an online order, the chances are that your purchase starts getting processed within minutes.
Increasingly, the journey starts with a squat silver floor robot gliding beneath a storage rack, lifting a shelf and carrying it across a warehouse to a waiting worker.
At Geek+'s factory in the eastern Chinese city of Hefei, which the BBC visited, fleets of the robots are built and tested before being shipped to warehouses around the world.
Some of Britain's biggest retailers - including Tesco, Asda and Next - now use the company's technology.
By automating these repetitive journeys, Geek+ says retailers can increase picking speeds, store more goods in spaces that are hard to reach for humans, and reduce errors.
Unlike traditional warehouse automation, which relies on fixed conveyor systems and permanent infrastructure, autonomous mobile robots can be deployed simply using QR code floor markers and safety fencing.
Geek+, which listed in Hong Kong last year in one of the biggest robotics share sales of 2025, has become the world's largest supplier of autonomous mobile robots.
The UK has struggled with weak productivity growth for more than a decade, and economists say wider adoption of robotics will be essential if businesses are to become more efficient.
In its 2026 report SME Technology Adoption in the United Kingdom, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) said technologies like robotics would be key to improving productivity.
According to the OECD, Britain's low adoption of robotics is "surprising" given its manufacturing heritage, noting that while UK firms have embraced mature digital technologies, they lag behind in robotics and automation.
That presents an opportunity for companies such as Geek+. The UK has one of Europe's largest e-commerce and logistics sectors, but many warehouses are still in the early stages of automation.
Britain has already become Geek+'s biggest European market, with UK partner MotionTech deploying more than 2,000 robots across 10 warehouse sites.
"Customers want fast deployable solutions," says Barry Pemberton, Account Director at MotionTech. "They want high volume, high storage, fast picking... ultimately on a smaller footprint with a reduced headcount."
"We seem to have a very big shortage of labour in the UK at the moment. These technologies are really important to keep businesses thriving and meet demand."
The Trades Union Congress (TUC), which represents almost 6 million UK workers, says robotics should be used to raise productivity and improve jobs, rather than simply cut labour costs.
In its response to the government's consultation on a new AI and innovation strategy, it urged ministers to ensure workers are involved in decisions about automation and that employers invest in retraining.
"Working with technologists, workers and unions can help steer the UK's research and innovation towards workers' priorities for automation... avoiding job-cutting, low-productivity automation," the TUC said in its report.
How China became a robotics leader
Robotics has become a strategic priority for Beijing under President Xi Jinping's drive to develop what he calls "new quality productive forces".
With China's working-age population shrinking, policymakers increasingly see automation as essential to boosting productivity and maintaining the country's manufacturing advantage.
"The robotics story builds directly on China's electric vehicle ecosystem," says Kyle Chan, a researcher at the Brookings Institution.
Batteries, electric motors, cameras, sensors and semiconductors developed for electric vehicles (EVs) are increasingly being used across China's robotics sector, creating what he describes as "overlapping industrial ecosystems".
One company leading that crossover is Chinese EV maker XPeng, which unveiled its humanoid robot, Iron, last year.
Founder He Xiaopeng says he no longer sees XPeng simply as a carmaker.
"We want XPeng to be a high-tech company," he told the BBC. "In the future, any car company will transform into a car and robotics company."
Analysts say China's robotics push could follow a similar path as its global EV success, with local players using manufacturing prowess, dense supplier networks and rapid product development to establish an early lead.
"China is deliberately trying to build on some of those strengths," says Chan. "As it reaches into new areas, from humanoid robots to industrial robots to delivery robots."
Tesla is pursuing a similar vision with its Optimus robot, which Elon Musk has said could eventually become a bigger business than carmaking.
But China's ambitions to dominate the global robotics industry was dealt a blow this week when the US banned the import of new foreign-made advanced robots, citing national security.
The Chinese embassy in Washington responded to the move by saying that Beijing has long opposed the US' "politicising" of trade issues and sanctions based on "groundless pretexts".
The next frontier
The Chinese-made robots now operating in British warehouses are designed to solve the problem of moving goods. Geek+ says the company's next goal is to automate everything else.
"We are working on... end-to-end unmanned warehouse solutions," says Yanyu Liu, head of communications at Geek+.
That means automating picking, handling and eventually packing goods.
Across China, companies including AgiBot and Unitree are investing billions in humanoid robots.
But the business case for humanoids is less clear than it is for today's warehouse robots. If wheeled robots move goods cheaply, reliably and efficiently or robots with just arms can do the other automated tasks, what problem does a humanoid solve?
Developers say factories, hospitals and offices have all been designed around people, and so they may eventually be able to work in different environments without the need to redesign workplaces around automation.
But experts and developers alike agree that the current technology is not yet suitable for some repetitive tasks that require more dexterity.
"I don't think [humanoids] will change the landscape of the types of technology or the automation that's going to be put into place," says Pemberton. "They're definitely going to be complementary."
Chinese companies already account for the vast majority of global humanoid deployments, but it may be years before they are commonplace in warehouses.
For Britain, where productivity pressures and labour shortages are driving demand for automation, the country's warehouses are becoming an early testing ground for China's next major technology export.
Additional reporting by Jaltson Akkanath Chummar

title: I dropped out of university and built five beauty businesses. Here's how I did it
summary: Marcia Kilgore, founder of Beauty Pie, shares her top tips on how to create a successful business.
full_text:
I dropped out of university and built five beauty businesses. Here's how I did it
- Published
The name Marcia Kilgore might not be instantly recognisable but her Beauty Pie brand is known the world over for being an industry game-changer with its online-only subscription model.
Before founding Beauty Pie in 2016, Kilgore had built other brands including luxury day spa Bliss, make-up and skincare range Soap & Glory and footwear brand FitFlop.
Here the 57-year-old serial entrepreneur shares her story and the five secrets to success she learned along the way.
1. You don't need a perfect plan
Kilgore didn't always know she wanted to be an entrepreneur but growing up she saw first-hand the stress that financial insecurity could cause.
"I remember deciding at eight-years-old that when I was my parents' age, I would never want to be stressed about my electric bill," she says.
That desire shaped her approach to work and risk. "I knew that working for other people wouldn't necessarily give me the freedom I wanted and at least when you are an entrepreneur, the risk is your own."
She didn't begin with a grand business plan - she moved from Canada to New York to study at Columbia University and her tuition plan fell through so she had to get a job to support herself.
"You can't sit around thinking: 'What am I going to do? You have to survive. I knew I had to use the skills I had to support myself and then I would figure it out."
She started working as a personal trainer and taking beauty classes in the evening.
"What ended up transpiring was that I was quite good at the beauty industry job," she says and eventually she dropped out of university to pursue a career in it.
2. Know the job inside out
Working in her salon, Kilgore says she was involved in every aspect of the business from the laundry, to performing treatments and training staff.
She says that practical experience was invaluable when she later opened Bliss Spa in London in the 1990s.
"I had trained loads of people ahead of the store opening but when we first opened it was so busy and a lot of them got afraid and quit.
"The good thing is I know how to wax and do facials so I could do all of the appointments myself."
Her advice is to start a business in an area where you have genuine knowledge.
"You want to have deep expertise, so you're not left swinging in the wind if people disappoint you or things come in from the side and surprise you," she says.
3. Challenge your own ideas
Kilgore recommends asking yourself why someone should care about your idea and be able to explain the value of an idea in one clear sentence.
"If you can't answer 'so what?' in one sentence, your idea isn't good enough yet."
That doesn't necessarily mean abandoning it but it needs to be refined more so its purpose is immediately understandable, she says.
Kilgore also warns against developing "ownership bias", believing an idea is brilliant simply because it belongs to them.
"You might think something is really great, but you're living in your own bubble," she says.
Her advice is to "test your idea with your target market before you go too far down the road of investing in something nobody cares about but you".
She adds that AI now offers significant opportunities to people starting their own business as "you don't need a huge budget for consultants".
"AI can spit your idea back and forth, challenge it and advise you on what you need to consider that you might no obviously see."
4. Expect sacrifice and be kind
When she was starting out in her career Kilgore realised she needed to be "someone that people look forward to being around".
It's important to be polite, punctual and nice as those qualities help you build loyalty, she says.
"I made sure I was the sunniest, hardest working and most diligent person to do that service."
"If you do a really great job, people will recommend you," she says and she soon opened a tiny beauty salon that became booked up months in advance.
She also explains you also need to be "willing to make some big sacrifices" to make your business successful.
"You're not going to have a lot of free time," she says as running a business requires you to be aware of changing customer behaviour, new competitors and wider market trends.
That often means reading, researching and connecting ideas outside of working hours.
Kilgore says the workload can feel easier if you have a curiosity around you as "that's what drives you".
She does have some non-negotiables and has made an effort not to miss important events while raising her children, including school plays and family holidays.
5. Do the deathbed test
A test that Kilgore has used throughout her career is the deathbed test where she asks whether a project will still feel worthwhile at the end of her life.
"Imagine you're on your deathbed, think about what you would have done differently and do that," she says.
"If it doesn't mean something, or you haven't done something good for people, are you going to feel that your life was really well spent?"
She adds that success for her isn't just about building another company but deciding which ideas are worth the time it will take to build them.

title: Major incident declared over coastal heath fire in Suffolk
summary: Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service says 17 crews are involved at the scene of the large blaze.
full_text:
Major incident declared over coastal heath fire in Suffolk
- Published
A large wildfire burning through heathland on the Suffolk coast has been declared a major incident.
Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service said about 90 firefighters were "working incredibly hard in arduous conditions" to bring under control a "large-scale, wind-driven" fire that broke out on Wednesday afternoon.
A major incident has been declared "due to the size and complexity" of the blaze, which is spreading rapidly south-west towards St James's Church, off Westleton Road, the fire service says.
Authorities have urged people to avoid the area and keep windows and doors shut.
Much of the area is a nature reserve owned by the National Trust, which said it was assisting firefighters.
The area is also close to the RSPB Minsmere nature reserve.
It asked people to avoid Westleton Heath, Mount Pleasant, Westleton Walks and the main bridleway from the entrance road towards Dunwich.
The fire service said crews were using equipment including off-road vehicles, drones and quad bikes.
"Members of the public are advised to avoid the area and keep roads clear for emergency vehicles," it said.
The fire comes as the UK Health Security Agency has issued an amber heat-health alert for the east midlands, the east, south east and London.

title: Trump considering AI controls after OpenAI hacking incidents
summary: It marks a change of tone for his administration, which has taken a more hands-off approach to the technology.
full_text:
Trump considering AI controls after OpenAI hacking incidents
- Published
US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that his administration is considering asserting more power over artificial intelligence (AI) tools after recent cybersecurity incidents.
Asked about OpenAI's tools being responsible for improperly breaching the private technology of other companies, Trump said: "We're looking at AI, we're looking at controls, we're also making sure that we lead."
It marks a change of tone for his administration, which has taken a more hands-off approach to the technology.
Trump's comments come after an escalation of not only the apparent hacking capabilities of popular AI tools, but White House threats aimed at competing Chinese tech.
Trump added that while some kind of control around AI tools was on the table, such a move would have to be done carefully.
"We don't want to restrict them where all of the sudden we come in second to China," he said.
"China has virtually no [AI] controls. It's freewheeling a little bit," Trump added.
The White House has been contacted for additional comment. The BBC has also contacted the Chinese embassy in Washington for comment.
In the last week, OpenAI has taken responsibility for at least two hacking incidents involving its AI tools acting outside of what they were designed and directed to do.
During a trip to Washington on Wednesday, OpenAI's chief executive Sam Altman was asked by a reporter if there were more systems that had been breached by the company's tools.
"I mean, there could be yeah", Altman said.
The US government intervened when Anthropic, OpenAI's main American rival, decided to release to the public a model that it had previously said was too much of a risk to be made widely available.
Meanwhile, in an internal White House memo from April, Trump's senior tech advisor Michael Kratsios accused China's AI firms of "industrial-scale" theft of US AI technology. He did so again last week, claiming that the popular Kimi 3 AI model from China's Moonshot AI was developed by stealing information from Anthropic.
The Chinese government has consistently rejected such accusations.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has also warned that Chinese AI firms could face sanctions for such activity. And the Federal Communications Commission this week banned the importation of new foreign-made humanoid robots.
Most AI models being developed in China are open source, meaning they are built and then made freely available online for anyone with the proper computer equipment to download and use.

title: Red Cross declares crisis over blood supply shortage in US for second time its history
summary: Fewer donations and higher demand has seen a supply shortage worsen, the American Red Cross tells the BBC.
full_text:
Red Cross declares crisis over blood supply shortage in US for second time its history
- Published
A blood supply shortage in the US has reached a "crisis" level, according to the American Red Cross, which says it is the second time in its 150-year history that levels have been this low.
Factors including wildfires and extreme heat have combined to create the current situation, Dr Courtney Lawrence, who works with the American Red Cross, told the BBC.
Supply levels dropped by a quarter just last month. The crisis has struck during summer, when the amount of blood needed by hospitals typically increases.
That is because of an increased number of car accidents and more people spending time outdoors, resulting in more injuries that require blood transfusions, Lawrence said.
The American Red Cross - which is the largest single blood supplier in the US, providing about 40% - is currently distributing about 3,500 more units than normal during this time of year, according to Lawrence, who added that the organisation is having to dip "very, very low into our blood inventory".
"We don't have the ability to stockpile blood super far in advance because blood does have a finite shelf life, it does expire," she said.
Donated blood has to be used within 42 days because blood cells degrade over time.
Supplies of every blood type are currently needed, but especially O positive, which is considered a universal blood type and can be given to people in an emergency when theirs is unknown.
Lawrence said hospitals they have spoken to believe the crisis could have some impact on routine operations and some have considered "whether they may need to divert patients to other trauma centres if they cannot keep enough blood on their shelves to be able to support emergencies".
She stressed that a combination of factors led to an existing shortage worsening to crisis level.
High temperatures in the US this summer have meant people are more selective about when they venture outside and some facilities that intended to have blood drives have not been able to maintain a safe and comfortable environment for them, Lawrence said.
The increased number of wildfires also diverted some resources, while there has been the unique situation of "widespread food-borne illnesses" hitting the country, according to the Red Cross - apparently referring to the explosive diarrhoea parasite, cyclosporiasis.
The first time the American Red Cross declared a blood supply crisis was in January 2022 during the Covid pandemic and a period of severe winter weather.
Meanwhile, blood supplies in Canada have also declined, by nearly 20% since the start of June, according to Canadian Blood Services.
"Over the past six weeks, appointments have fallen short by 1,500 to 2,500 each week, requiring a draw on existing inventory to meet patient needs," it said in a statement.
Unlike in the US, the reason for the drop in donations there is unknown.
"While a seasonal decline in donations is expected during the summer months and factored into planning, appointment bookings have fallen well below typical summer patterns," said Canadian Blood Services.
"There are now limited days on hand of several blood types - levels that are not sustainable for patient care should this trend not reverse itself."
