title: Drought declared across whole of Wales as conditions 'deteriorate'
summary: Wales is on course for its driest July on record in almost 190 years.
full_text:
Drought declared across whole of Wales as conditions 'deteriorate'
- Published
A drought has been extended across the whole of Wales with the country on course for its driest July on record in 190 years.
Declaring the drought, the country's environment body Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said sustained high temperatures were causing the condition of the natural environment to "deteriorate".
The decision has been made in response to record-low river levels, dry soils, widespread wildfires and mounting impacts on wildlife, farming and forestry.
NRW had already announced a drought across the north and parts of mid Wales last week.
The nationwide announcement made on Thursday will trigger more monitoring of rivers and stronger advice for the public on use of water.
The declaration of a drought does not mean there is currently a threat to water supplies for homes and businesses, with Welsh water companies saying reservoir levels are holding up after a wet start to the year.
NRW said figures had shown Wales had received 8% of its long-term average rainfall for July, with most rivers in the country "exceptionally low".
Groundwater levels are also falling in Wales, with some lower than expected for the time of year.
The environmental body said its teams were dealing with reports of "wide-reaching impacts to the environment", and that "conditions across Wales' natural environment have continued to deteriorate".
This includes drying riverbeds, fish in distress, an accumulation of algae, wildfire risk and concern from farmers about crop growth, grazing conditions and water availability for livestock.
Rhian Thomas, from NRW, said the toll from the recent dry weather had been "clear to see", and teams were closely monitoring forecasts and river flows.
"With no strong indications for notable rainfall in the forecasts, and risks of further heatwaves over the summer, it's more important than ever that we all use water wisely," she said.
"Every drop we waste is less water for our rivers and wildlife when they need it the most."
The dry weather in recent weeks has also coincided with a number of wildfires across Wales.
A fire that broke out earlier this month in the Rhinogydd mountains in Gwynedd could be seen from space, with a firefighting helicopter deployed to tackle the blaze.
Residents were evacuated from their homes following a fire close to Conwy Mountain said they had heard the blaze, which had sounded "like popcorn", coming down the mountain.
First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said he had organised a summit to look at the risks of fires from severe droughts.
Speaking to Matt Chorley on BBC Radio 5 Live, he said while there was no "immediate risk to the provision of drinking water", there needed to be "more resilience in our water supplies" across Wales and the UK.
George Tomlinson, 29, who runs Rossett Park Farming in Wrexham, said he had to sell 60 cows because the drought had killed off grazing land.
"There's nothing available for the cows to eat on the grazing platform apart from a little bit of dead grass some dry cows are eating," said Tomlinson, adding "you've got to make tough decisions in order to survive".
He said he was also worried about what the future might hold with warmer summers expected.
"If this continues a lot of farmers will be forced to close their gates and never open them again," he said, describing it as "depressing".
National Farmers Union Cymru president Abi Reader has also warned that the cost of the continuing dry and hot weather will have a financial impact on farmers.
"We're going to see costs for these farms rising, because they might be having to buy in extra feed for their livestock, or they might be spending a lot of money carting water," she said.
"We've been in this a long time now, and it's going to take a long time to recover, and absolutely everybody needs to remember that food security starts with water security," she added.
What is a drought?
A drought occurs when a prolonged lack of rainfall and high temperatures results in critically low river flows, diminished reservoir reserves and exceptionally low groundwater levels, negatively impacting wildlife, fisheries and protected habitats.
This type of drought typically develops before agricultural impacts (like failing crops) or public water shortages happen. Impacts can include:
- Shrunken rivers - a decrease in oxygen levels, an increase in water temperatures and a restriction in the migration of species like salmon 
- Habitat loss - reduced water levels cause riverbeds to dry up, leading to the loss of biodiversity and fish kills 
- Private water pressures - natural springs and private boreholes can run dry 
When drought conditions , externalare identified, NRW often triggers enhanced monitoring of waterways, restricts water abstraction licences to protect low flows and leads to the release of additional water from reservoirs into rivers.

title: Palestine Action ban to be reviewed by Supreme Court
summary: The UK's highest court gives Palestine Action permission to appeal the government's proscription of the group under anti-terrorism legislation.
full_text:
Palestine Action ban to be reviewed by Supreme Court
- Published
The controversial ban under terrorism legislation of the protest group Palestine Action will be reviewed by the Supreme Court.
In a major blow to the Home Office, the court confirmed on Thursday that it had given the group's co-founder permission to appeal the ban which came into effect in July 2025.
While the full details of the reasons for the appeal are yet to be published, the BBC understands they relate to Huda Ammori's argument that the ban breaches human rights.
Officials at the court say the appeal will be expedited - which means it will be heard after the summer break. The eventual outcome of the case could have major implications for terrorism legislation in the UK.
The decision comes weeks after the end of the first major trial of members of the group which had caused more than £1m of damage to a defence firm near Bristol with an Israeli parent company. Four members of that break-in team were jailed, with one also sentenced for causing grievous bodily harm on a police officer who was hit with a sledgehammer.
Separately, more than 2,000 people are facing potential trial for protesting against the ban by declaring their support for a proscribed terrorism group in mass demonstrations.
The battle over the banning of Palestine Action has now gone on for more than year.
Former Home Secretary Yvette Cooper banned the group on advice from the police and security officials after an escalating spate of break-ins targeting Elbit, an Israeli-owned defence firm.
The High Court initially ruled that the ban was unlawful - but five judges on the Court of Appeal then overruled it, unanimously deciding the home secretary had acted lawfully and within her powers to proscribe Palestine Action.
That decision by the Court of Appeal will now be reviewed by the Supreme Court.
During Thursday, some 117 protesters were arrested outside Westminster Magistrates' Court, with Metropolitan Police saying the majority of arrests were for expressing support for the group.
Scores of protesters had turned up there because they had expected to appear in court accused of allegedly showing support for the group at earlier public events. However, those cases had been listed in error. Many of the defendants said that they felt they had no choice but to turn up, despite the court and Metropolitan Police telling them not to do so.
Palestine Action co-founder Ammori welcomed the Supreme Court's decision to hear her appeal - and said that the latest arrests were part of a wider crackdown on Palestinian solidarity.
"We will continue to fight this proscription all the way to the Supreme Court and, if necessary, to the European Court of Human Rights to overturn what has become one of the most extreme attacks on free speech and the right to protest in modern British history."
The Home Office has repeatedly said that the ban of the group has nothing to do with protest in support of Palestinian causes - and was necessary because it was causing significant criminal damage to legitimate businesses.
Both the High Court and the Court of Appeal have ruled that Palestine Action's activities include criminal acts - although they were divided on whether those incidents justified turning to terrorism laws.
Those laws - approved by MPs in Parliament - allow the government to ban a group for either serious violence or serious criminal damage for an ideological cause - and trigger wider powers for the police to investigate and charge suspects for organising activities and fundraising.
The Home Office has been contacted for comment.

title: Burnham says he told Trump UK will be pragmatic about North Sea oil
summary: Andy Burnham says he told the US president he couldn't ignore North Sea resources when people are struggling.
full_text:
Burnham says he told Trump UK will be pragmatic about North Sea oil
- Published
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he told US President Donald Trump he would take a "pragmatic approach" to the issue of North Sea oil and gas.
Trump has long urged the UK to increase drilling and claimed that Burnham had pledged to "open up the North Sea" in their first phone call together.
Asked about the president's comments, the new prime minister said: "There is a resource there. When people are struggling - you can't ignore that and hence me indicating that to the president."
Burnham has faced pressure from some trade unions, industry figures and some of his own Labour MPs to back increased drilling in the North Sea.
In its 2024 general election manifesto, Labour promised not to issue new licences for drilling but said it would honour existing ones.
As energy secretary in Sir Keir Starmer's government, Ed Miliband was a staunch supporter of Labour's manifesto position. He has previously described the licence issued to Rosebank, Britain's largest untapped oil field, as "climate vandalism".
Miliband is now the foreign secretary in Burnham's government.
- Is Burnham promising a new dawn for North Sea oil and gas? - Published19 July
 
- The city caught in the middle of the big energy shift debate - Published30 April
 
Although the government has not made any announcements on the issue, Trump has praised what he perceives as a change of stance by the UK government.
In a social media post, published the day before Burnham became prime minister,, external Trump wrote: "The People of Aberdeen, in Scotland, are dancing in the streets because the new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has stated that he will be opening up, all the way, the invaluable North Sea Oil!"
This week, when asked about his conversation with Burnham, Trump said: "He said he's going to open up North Sea oil.
"If he does that, you're going to be a wealthy country."
He later added: "You buy a lot of your energy, as you know, from the North Sea. You buy from Norway and Norway gets it from the North Sea... Norway's got trillions of dollars in the bank."
"Scotland has a better part of the North Sea."
Asked about Trump's comments, Burnham said: "I indicated in the phone call that we had a week last Monday that I would take a pragmatic approach when it comes to the North Sea, and that is my intention as we go forward from here."
In response, Green Party leader Zack Polanski said: "Our country is burning. Crops are failing. Thousands have been killed by extreme heat.
"Allowing new oil and gas drilling in the North Sea will worsen the climate breakdown putting more lives at risk and doing untold damage to our economy.
"It's not too late for Burnham to do the right thing and commit to leaving dangerous fossil fuels in the ground."
The Conservatives and Reform have urged the government to approve more drilling in the North Sea, arguing it would reduce energy prices.
Last year, Tory Party leader Kemi Badenoch said it would be "absurd" for the UK to leave "vital resources untapped".
Some Labour MPs have expressed unease about more drilling, with Rachael Maskell urging the government to "follow the climate science because we have got a climate emergency".
Simon Francis, from the End Fuel Poverty Coalition, said: "No household struggling with their energy bills will see a penny come off by drilling more from the North Sea.
"Gas is sold at the global market prices, so whatever is pumped out is sold to the highest bidder, not handed to British billpayers at a discount."
Sir Keir's government had already made concessions, allowing "tie-backs" - production in unlicensed areas close to or connected to already licensed areas.
Currently, the debate over North Sea drilling has focused on two oil fields - Rosebank and Jackdaw, located in Scotland.
In 2022 and 2023, regulators approved drilling at the sites, but that was overturned in 2025 following a legal challenge.
The legal process is ongoing, but the government will at some point have to decide whether to permit companies to produce oil in the two areas.
Other oil and gas licences have been approved in recent years but remain largely undeveloped.
If he wanted to encourage more drilling in the North Sea, Burnham could also opt to scrap the Energy Profits Level, also known as the windfall tax.

title: Why do parts of England and Wales keep falling into drought?
summary: More than half of England and the whole of Wales has been declared to be in drought this week - the third such event over the past five years.
full_text:
Why do parts of England and Wales keep falling into drought?
- Published
More than half of England and the whole of Wales has been declared to be in drought this week - the third such event over the past five years.
Farmers have described suffering from reduced yields and being forced to harvest earlier, and field fires increasing.
The drought comes despite winter bringing above average rainfall, and reservoirs still close to expected levels for this time of year.
So why are parts of the country struggling to get hold of water?
There is no single definition of drought, according to the Environment Agency (EA), it depends on who is impacted, the availability of water and its use.
A drought can affect things including the environment, farming, or the water supply - what response the government and industry take depends on what the drought is affecting.
Possible measures include rescuing and relocating fish, increased business checks on water usage, and redistribution of water supplies.
1 of 5
The sources of our water for drinking and farming vary significantly across the country.
The three main sources of water are rivers, reservoirs and from deep underground - groundwater.
Reservoirs have seen some decline during this hot weather period due to a combination of low rainfall and higher demand from households.
There are a number of temporary use bans - or hosepipe bans - in place affecting around 20 million people.
This is seen as a precautionary measure when reservoir levels are dropping but demand remains higher.
- Drought declared across whole of Wales as conditions 'deteriorate' - Published2 hours ago
 
- More than half of England in drought, Environment Agency declares - Published1 day ago
 
- Pictures show scale of drought across England as rivers dry up - Published23 hours ago
 
But currently, nearly all water companies are at drought level 1 - Anglian is the exception at 2 - out of a possible maximum of 4.
It is rivers and groundwater levels which have been significantly impacted by a sudden drop in rainfall.
South East England relies more heavily on groundwater - where rainfall is stored beneath the surface in pore spaces and fractures in the rock.
Chalk areas across the country - from the Yorkshire Wolds to the Wessex Downs - are all reporting levels either at expected or below normal for this time of year, with the Cotswolds particularly struggling.
But these groundwater stores "respond more slowly to changes in the climate than rivers, which is why they provide a useful buffer during periods of drought", said Prof Alan MacDonald of the British Geological Survey.
Wales has received just 8% of its average rainfall so far this month. England has received 7% of its average, with that figure as low as 1% across southern England. Therefore, groundwater levels are expected to drop even further still.
The low rainfall and high temperatures, which increase evaporation rates, have hit rivers hardest.
The EA said nearly 80% of England's rivers are seeing flows below normal or lower - the River Thames at Reading has recorded its lowest level on record.
Farmers feel the brunt
Farmers source water for their crops and livestock over summer from a combination of stored winter rainfall on site, and by extracting it from natural sources - a process called abstraction.
This can be from groundwater or from surface water, like rivers and streams. So, as levels drop, this becomes a serious issue.
Eleanor Gilbert told Radio 4's Today programme that the hot weather has been "very tough" on her farm in Berkshire, which has recorded "less than 30mm of rain since the end of March".
Moisture content has to be at a specific level for harvesting different crops.
Gilbert said they have been harvesting at 03:00 BST to bring the moisture up, as at that time of day it's cooler and water condenses.
But the dry conditions caused by the hot weather have prevented the grain from swelling. It means the farm's yield is down to almost half of what it was the previous year.
The EA and Natural Resource Wales grant abstraction licences to farms, but when water levels drop they can impose what is called a "hands-off flow restriction".
This means farms are prevented from abstracting water, this is to protect the environment.
There are currently 1,353 of these restrictions in place. The EA has also warned that voluntary restrictions may be put in place next month - when farmers are asked to reduce their volumes of water use, only irrigate at night or on certain days of the week.
Ben Andrews, a mixed organic farmer in north Herefordshire, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that he has had an abstraction licence restriction since the start of the month.
"We will have paid for the plants, paid for the labour, if we don't get to pick any of them then it's investment that's lost."
Even with these measures in place there have been 61 environmental incidents due to the drought, such as reported fish deaths which, although lower than last year, are rapidly increasing and thought to be underestimated. , external
Could droughts get worse?
Climate change is raising global temperatures, which in the UK is expected to lead to drier summers and more intense and longer lasting heatwaves - both of which could contribute to lower river and groundwater levels.
On Wednesday, the National Drought Group - which includes regulators, the government, the Met Office, water companies, farmers, the Canal & River Trust, anglers and conservation experts - held a briefing with Water Minister Emma Hardy.
The Department for Environment Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said the group reviewed the impact of the drought in England, the country's preparedness and response to it.
Hardy said: "We're delivering long-term change in the water industry and driving record investments in infrastructure, including nine new reservoirs.
"We expect water companies to follow their drought plans, to go further and faster to reduce leaks, and to ensure supplies are not disrupted even in the driest of weather."
In May, the Lords Environment and Climate Change Committee called on the government to undertake a series of measures, including investing in drought data collection and sharing, and increasing water storage by ensuring large reservoirs are built.
Baroness Sheehan, the committee chair, said: "England is at risk of sleepwalking into serious water scarcity if the government does not act now to safeguard the water system."
Meanwhile, the National Farmers' Union for England and Wales (NFU) has called on the government to change the planning system for water., external
Scientists have said that climate change is likely to bring wetter and milder winters. The NFU said abstraction licences should be made more flexible to enable more water to be taken during these wetter winter months ahead of any dry summer spells.
It has also called for applications for building on site reservoirs to be sped up.
Alongside the current pressures on the system there is extra water demand expected in the coming years from new houses, data centres and other sectors which could further squeeze supplies.
Would more reservoirs make this better?
"We need to invest for the long term, in new water storage facilities, whether it's at the local level supporting farmers or at a large scale with the water companies themselves being allowed to build reservoirs," Sir John Armitt, former chairman of the National Infrastructure Commission, told Radio 4's Today programme on Thursday.
He said for a long time governments have resisted building new reservoirs on the basis other solutions could be found, but the recent weather extremes the UK has been experiencing "have really caught people out".
There has been no major reservoir completed in England since 1992. Sir Jon Cunliffe, former Bank of England deputy governor, reviewed the sector last year and concluded that there had been "underinvestment" - blaming both the water industry and regulators.

title: Dad pays tribute to son who died after sea rescue
summary: Seven-year-old Musa Ahmed is remembered as a boy who "never failed to bring happiness" to others.
full_text:
Dad pays tribute to son who died after sea rescue
- Published
A seven-year-old boy who died a week after being rescued from the sea "never failed to bring happiness" to others, his father has told the BBC.
Musa Ahmed and five relatives got into difficulty in the water in West Mersea on 22 July, having travelled to the Essex seaside from east London.
His 15-year-old cousin, Sameeha Rahman, and her mother Shelina, 41, drowned at the scene.
Shahin Ahmed said his son was "a unique and happy personality, a sphere of joy" in a tribute after his death on Tuesday evening.
"Everyone who knew him had a unique relationship with him. He made every person feel special and never failed to bring happiness," Ahmed said.
"He was everyone's favourite and he made everyone feel like his favourite."
Ahmed also referred to Islam and said Musa "embodied" traits of the Prophet Muhammad.
About 100 people attended a vigil to remember the three victims on Wednesday evening.
Police were first called to the unfolding emergency on the island, near Colchester, at 17:35 BST on 22 July.
While Musa was airlifted to London for treatment, three others were taken by ambulance to a different hospital.
Ahmed said the group - who were all related - had been swept away by a "very strong" tide and police said they made "significant efforts to help each other".
Detectives have been speaking to people who were on the beach as they try to understand how the tragedy happened.
Craig Bowe, who was renting a beach hut for his daughter's birthday at the time, managed to help Musa on to a lifeboat, but said he was "not in a good way".
Colchester City Council and West Mersea Town Council have both said warning signs are due to be installed at the beach this summer.

title: Challenging times ahead for Newcastle - Shearer
summary: MOTD pundit and Newcastle United legend Alan Shearer explains why he is worried about what will happen next at his old club after the departure of manager Eddie Howe.
full_text:
Challenging times ahead for Newcastle - Shearer
- Published
Thank you, Eddie Howe. You gave me the best day of my life as a Newcastle fan.
Whatever the reasons are for him leaving the club, I think every supporter of my age or younger - and I am 55 - would say the same.
Eddie will always be a legend in the eyes of the Geordie public for ending our long wait for a major trophy with that epic day he gave us at Wembley when we won the Carabao Cup in 2025.
I had craved that moment for my entire life. I had been to Wembley before as a Toon player and I had been there before as a Toon fan, and we'd all had the same feeling of walking away empty-handed.
He will be remembered for changing that, and we have to say a massive thank you for everything else he has done since he took charge in November 2021, when the club were 19th in the Premier League, five points adrift of safety after 11 games.
Eddie kept us up that year, then finished fourth, seventh and fifth in the next three seasons, with some amazing nights in the Champions League along the way. He did a brilliant job.
The best way of showing how far we have come under him is that we finished 12th last season and it was a disappointment, but I would not blame him for that, either.
What happened last summer massively hindered Newcastle, with Alexander Isak leaving and the club missing out on their main transfer targets.
Unfortunately, that trend has continued this year. I would not be surprised if it influenced Eddie's thinking about whether to stay or go, and it also makes me worry about what will happen next.
Speaking purely as a fan, I think we have to get ready for a tough season and some very challenging times ahead.
'You cannot keep selling your best players'
The timing of Eddie's exit is the biggest surprise for me - three weeks into pre-season, and with only three weeks to go until the Premier League starts again.
I don't know exactly what has gone on behind the scenes for this to happen now but I guess, from his point of view, he was seeing his best players being sold - first Isak, then Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali this summer - and with speculation over captain Bruno Guimaraes' future too.
He has probably thought it was a tough enough job anyway, but it is just getting tougher.
You cannot keep on selling your best players and then hope to be in contention at the top of the table - I hope I'm wrong but it is probably inevitable that Bruno will be next to leave.
Whatever Bruno's intentions were before, when Eddie was in charge, then he must look now and think well, we are selling our stars and now the manager, who he clearly had a great rapport with, has gone too.
It's not just the players leaving that is a bad look, it is seeing a series of attempted signings fail to get over the line as well.
Hugo Ekitike, Johan Manzambi and Victor Munoz all went to Liverpool or Aston Villa ahead of Newcastle in the past 12 months and now it also looks like James Trafford has chosen Leeds instead.
That's something else that Eddie has maybe looked at, because there has to be a reason why Newcastle are not getting so many of their targets.
Losing the manager on top of all this is a huge blow, especially a high-calibre one like Eddie who is going to get some huge job offers from home and abroad off the back of his achievements at St James' Park.
I think even someone really experienced would find the situation a difficult one and Matthias Jaissle, who is expected to get the job, is only 38.
While he has been successful with Al-Ahli in Saudi Arabia, you cannot really compare that to working in the Premier League, which is a completely different beast.
'Newcastle is a changing football club'
Take a step back and, whether we like it or not, we can all see what is happening with all the ins and outs at Newcastle. Whatever statements come out of the club, it is clear the landscape has changed.
It is a changing football club - in terms of its owners' aims and ambitions and their transfer strategy, which all seem massively different to the way they were even three years ago.
Back then the sky seemed to be the limit, and the talk was about competing with the very best.
Now, the approach seems to be to sell their best players and replace them with younger, hungry and up-and-coming prospects. If it was that easy to do it successfully and still compete at the top of the table, then everyone would do it - but it isn't.
The club's spending always had to comply with the Premier League's profitability and sustainability rules but it still felt like the plan was to battle it out for silverware every season.
Go back to the summer of 2023, when Newcastle had just finished fourth and added Tonali, Harvey Barnes and Tino Livramento to a squad already containing Isak, Gordon and Bruno.
It felt like they were ready to challenge for everything, and capable of beating everyone. Howe had made them a horrible team to play against, in the nicest possible way.
Three years on, much of that team has gone and now the manager has too, but it is the whole model which feels the most different.
The goalposts have moved massively from where the club said they wanted to get to, compared to where they are now.
When we won the Carabao Cup, I was hoping it was just the start of something very special, but it seems a lot has changed since then.
Alan Shearer was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

title: US GDP growth dips as inflation and trade deficits pressure economy
summary: GDP grew by 1.5 percent in the second quarter following a 2.1 percent increase in the first quarter.
full_text:
US GDP growth dips as inflation and trade deficits pressure economy
GDP grew by 1.5 percent in the second quarter following a 2.1 percent increase in first quarter.
Economic growth in the United States slowed in the second quarter amid a growing trade deficit and tensions between the US and Iran which weighed on global fuel prices.
The US Gross Domestic Product (GDP), a measure of goods and services, grew by 1.5 percent between April and June, marking a slowdown from 2.1 percent growth in the first quarter of 2026, according to the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis report released on Thursday.

- list 2 of 4US Fed holds interest rates steady, citing ‘elevated’ inflation
- list 3 of 4Sam Altman meets lawmakers on back of OpenAI agents hacking companies

Consumer spending saw a bump of 3.2 percent for the quarter, both on the back of generous tax refunds from US President Donald Trump’s ‘One Big Beautiful Bill Act’ as well as heightened petrol prices that cost consumers.
Fuel prices are on the upswing after a brief reprieve. The average price for a gallon of petrol (3.78 litres) is $4.09, up from $3.84 this time last month, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily petrol prices. By comparison, the average price was $2.98 when the US and Israel first struck Iran on February 28 .
Analysts also point to the artificial intelligence spending boom as a reason for the surge, even as those are heavily import reliant and contributing to trade deficits.
“Overall, the economy continues to rely on technology investment,” Rachel Ziemba, adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, told Al Jazeera.
That will likely continue into third-quarter reports, which will take into account the month of July. On Monday, it was reported that Nvidia is in talks to make a $250m investment in OpenAI.
However, there are concerns about how long such investments will last amid questions over circular financing propping up the sector.
“Data centres continue to drive investment and economic growth, increasing the sector’s role in the economy while raising questions about its sustainability,” Ziemba said.
Meanwhile, the Personal Consumption Expenditure Price (PCE) Index report, one of the US Federal Reserve’s key metrics for gauging the rate of inflation, increased 3.7 percent on an annual basis for the month of June after a 4.1 percent surge in May.
The slowdown was marked by a brief retreat in petrol prices last month before they climbed higher again over the past month.
“Today’s report is a snapshot of an economy under a ceasefire that no longer exists. Even with last month’s temporary inflation relief, prices are still elevated and families are saving less as they try to keep up,” Alex Jacquez, a member of the National Economic Council under former US President Joe Biden, said in a note provided to Al Jazeera.
On Wednesday, the US Federal Reserve opted to maintain interest rates at 3.5-3.75 percent.
US markets are on the upswing in midday trading, largely driven by an increase in Microsoft stock amid better-than-expected sales and growth in cloud services. Markets have also risen following the PCE and GDP reports.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq is up 2.6 percent, with the S&P 500 following at 1.2 percent and the Dow Jones Industrial Average up 0.5 percent.
Gold prices, which are typically considered a safe investment during economic uncertainty, extended their gains by 1.9 percent to $4,108.30 per ounce after rising 2 percent on Wednesday.

title: Spain’s enclave Ceuta raises alarm as thousands cross border from Morocco
summary: Estimates suggest up to 2,000 have entered the Spanish territory in recent days in an attempt to reach Europe.
full_text:
Spain’s enclave Ceuta raises alarm as thousands cross border from Morocco
Estimates of up to 2,000 migrants have entered Spain’s territory of Ceuta in recent days in attempts to reach Europe.
Authorities in Ceuta have raised the alarm after thousands of migrants breached the border to the North African Spanish enclave from neighbouring Morocco in recent days.
The government of Ceuta said on Thursday that between 1,500 and 2,000 people had entered in the last 10 days. Hundreds more were estimated to have arrived on Thursday, prompting regional President Jesus Vivas to declare an “absolute humanitarian and social emergency” and call on Madrid to send troops to reassert control of the border.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items- list 1 of 4Hundreds protest in Libya outside UN agency against undocumented migrants
- list 2 of 4‘Dignity has no passport’: Pope makes appeal for migrants in Canary Islands
- list 3 of 4Pope Leo urges migrant protection, integration on visit to Lampedusa
- list 4 of 4France’s Morocco reset: What French PM Lecornu’s visit to Rabat signals
Spain’s Interior Ministry rejected calls to declare a national emergency, saying such a measure does not cover migration crises, but promised additional resources.
Footage showed some of the migrants shouting “Viva Espana!” as they entered the territory, many of them having travelled by water from the Moroccan side on inflatable devices.
Crowds were shown walking around the breakwaters onto local roads, reported The Associated Press news agency. State news agency EFE said others had crossed by the border by land, scaling fences.
Migrant rights activist Zakaria Zarroqui told the Reuters news agency that the surge in migrant numbers was similar to one that occurred in May 2021, when some 10,000 Moroccan and sub-Saharan youths entered the enclave within days.
“The situation remains out of control as we speak,” Zarroqui said, adding that people were still flocking to the Moroccan city of Fnideq in an attempt to cross the border.
Ceuta, together with Melilla — another autonomous Spanish city in North Africa — represents the European Union’s only land border with Africa. Both cities often experience surges in attempted crossings by people seeking to migrate to Europe.
Earlier this month, Spain’s Supreme Court ruled that migrants intercepted at sea while attempting to reach Ceuta or Melilla cannot be returned to Morocco.
“It has been a slow trickle since the Supreme Court’s ruling, but today has been an explosion,” a Guardia Civil spokesperson told Reuters.
Spain’s Interior Ministry said it was working closely with Morocco to address the surge in irregular arrivals, blaming people-smuggling networks for exploiting the Supreme Court’s ruling and encouraging undocumented migration.
Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska is expected to visit Ceuta on Friday to evaluate the situation.

title: Republicans delay vote on Trump’s US attorney general pick amid concerns
summary: Senate committee postpones vote as key Republican says he has not received information on 'anti-weaponisation' fund.
full_text:
Republicans delay vote on Trump’s US attorney general pick amid concerns
Senate committee postpones vote as key Republican says he has not received information on ‘anti-weaponisation’ fund.
Key Republicans have delayed a Senate committee vote on United States President Donald Trump’s pick to become attorney general.
The delay of the Judiciary Committee vote, which was originally set for Thursday, represents a major stumbling block in the nomination of Todd Blanche, who is currently leading the Department of Justice (DOJ) in an acting capacity.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3Trump halts $1.8bn ‘anti-weaponisation’ fund amid bipartisan backlash
- list 2 of 3Trump nominates Todd Blanche as US attorney general, teeing up Senate fight
- list 3 of 3California Governor Newsom says US Department of Justice investigating him
The decision came amid concerns from two key Republicans over Blanche’s proximity to Trump and, particularly, a controversial legal settlement in the president’s lawsuit against the top federal tax agency, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). Blanche had served as Trump’s personal criminal defence lawyer before being tapped for the DOJ.
A spokesperson for the committee said late on Wednesday the vote would be postponed “as work continues to secure sufficient support” for Blanche.
All Republicans on the committee would need to vote in favour of Blanche to bring his nomination to a full vote in the chamber.
Republican Senators John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, who are leaving Congress, have been vocal in their scepticism over Blanche.
Their concerns have focused on Trump’s settlement with the IRS, following a lawsuit relating to an agency leak of Trump’s tax returns. The deal included a provision that shielded Trump and his family from future tax investigations. It also created a so-called $1.8bn “anti-weaponisation fund” under which individuals who alleged political prosecution by the federal government could seek compensation.
Both Republicans and Democrats vehemently opposed the fund, which they characterised as a scheme to use taxpayer funds to reward Trump’s allies.
During previous Senate hearings, Blanche has maintained that the plan was discontinued. A federal judge has also ruled the settlement illegal. Still, critics have said they have not received sufficient guarantees that the plan could not be resurrected, and have requested that Blanche and officials put their intention to abandon the settlement in writing.
Cornyn on Wednesday accused the DOJ of “stonewalling” further requests for information. He told reporters “the ball is in Blanche’s court”.
Trump, meanwhile, weighed in on the situation on Wednesday, suggesting Cornyn was holding up proceedings out of discontent with the president.
In May, Trump made the unexpected move of endorsing Cornyn’s Republican primary challenger, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. That came despite polls indicating that Cornyn, who has served in the Senate for more than two decades, would fare far better in the November race against Democratic candidate James Talarico.
Paxton went on to defeat Cornyn in the primary race.
“Maybe John Cornyn’s upset with me because I didn’t endorse him,” Trump told reporters on Wednesday.
On Thursday, Trump posted on Truth Social that he may withdraw Blanche’s nomination “temporarily”. He also criticised Cornyn and Tillis.
Trump wrote:”[Blanche] has the potential to go down as one of the Greatest Attorney Generals of All Time. However, John Cornyn, of Texas, and Thom Tillis, of North Carolina, both of whom I refused to Endorse, and whose political careers have been ended by my action, are refusing to vote for this Great Nominee, who will remain, in any event, as Acting. Remember, both Cornyn and Tillis voted for Merrick Garland, and others, too numerous to mention. I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd’s name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office.”
At the DOJ, Blanche has overseen many of Trump’s top priorities, including investigations and prosecutions into the president’s political enemies.
Still, under questioning from Senators this month, Blanche repeatedly maintained he oversaw the DOJ independently from the White House.
Blanche has also faced questioning over the DOJ’s handling of investigation files related to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein. The department was legally compelled by Congress to release those files earlier this year.

title: UEFA members vote to boycott FIFA if Infantino’s World Cup plans pursued
summary: European nations agree in virtual meeting to boycott FIFA competitions in protest at the private equity plan for World Cup.
full_text:
UEFA members vote to boycott FIFA if Infantino’s World Cup plans pursued
European nations agree in virtual meeting to boycott FIFA competitions in protest at private equity plan for World Cup.
European football’s governing body, UEFA, has voted to boycott FIFA events – including the World Cup – if the proposed sale of the event to private investors goes ahead.
The unanimous vote by UEFA member federations agreed on Thursday to boycott all FIFA competitions in protest against Gianni Infantino’s plan to sell stakes in the World Cup.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items- list 1 of 4What has FIFA charged Argentina with, and what could the punishment be?
- list 2 of 4Storm apologize after co-owner berates teen girls for support of Cunningham
- list 3 of 4South Africa’s le Clos breaks Commonwealth Games medal record
- list 4 of 4Viral finger-clicker suspended as cricket storm remains in global spotlight
“UEFA and its national associations will not participate in FIFA competitions,” the European football body said after an urgent online meeting of its 55 members.
The strategy meeting was called to counter FIFA President Infantino’s offer of $20m to each of its 211 global members, which must be accepted by mid-September.
Infantino’s secret proposal was revealed on Tuesday to spin off its commercial operations in a $20bn operation, with 20 percent owned by private investors.
The core investor would be a New York venture capital investment firm created by Joshua Kushner, the brother of US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.
What did UEFA’s statement say after FIFA boycott vote?
“No UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership,” UEFA said in a statement.
“The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product. It is one of football’s greatest sporting legacies. It has been built over generations by players, national teams and supporters across every continent.
“No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale.”
The next FIFA competition is in Europe, the Women’s Under-20 World Cup hosted by Poland from September 5 .
What has been said elsewhere about FIFA’s World Cup plan?
Earlier on Thursday, Infantino called the plan to sell stakes in the World Cup a proposal but “not an obligation” after the idea provoked a furious response from football authorities around the globe.
Asian Football Confederation (AFC) President Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa branded FIFA’s lack of consultation over its plan as “totally unacceptable”, saying the move undermined the sport’s existing continental structure.
Former FIFA President Sepp Blatter slammed the football governing body’s plans, saying the tournament was not a commercial asset that belonged to a few executives.
“Football belongs to no individual and to no institution. It belongs to the people,” Blatter told the news agency Reuters on Wednesday.
FIFA have been contacted by Al Jazeera for a response to UEFA’s vote.

title: Police arrest dozens at London rally supporting Palestine Action
summary: The protest is the first in support of the proscribed group since Andy Burnham became prime minister.
full_text:
Police arrest dozens at London rally supporting Palestine Action
The protest is the first in support of the proscribed group since Andy Burnham became prime minister.
British police have arrested 77 people as crowds gathered outside a London court to declare support for Palestine Action, which is proscribed as a “terrorist” organisation in the United Kingdom.
The rally outside Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Thursday was organised by the Defend Our Juries activist group to picket the start of hearings against the first of thousands of people charged with voicing support for Palestine Action.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3Israel’s illegal settlements are Europe’s credibility test
- list 2 of 3Israel arrests dozens of Palestinians in West Bank amid settler attacks
- list 3 of 3House of Hope: New film follows a Waldorf-inspired school in the West Bank
Defend Our Juries says it is seeking to safeguard the legal process in the UK. Critics accuse the government of undermining civil liberties in an attempt to shield Israel from the consequences of the genocidal war it launched in Gaza almost three years ago.
“Expressing support for Palestine Action is an offence under the Terrorism Act. Officers have begun making arrests,” London’s Metropolitan Police said in a post on X.
In pictures posted online, dozens of people could be seen outside the court in central London.
In a post on X, Defend Our Juries said “hundreds are outside Westminster Magistrates today to say this is not terrorism”. The number of attendees has not been confirmed.
Several protesters waved Palestinian flags in support of those in the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank, which is also experiencing a surge in violence by Israelis from illegal settlements under the army’s protection.
Rights groups say the rapid increase in settler violence there is a direct result of the Israeli government’s policy.
The demonstration in London is the first in support of Palestine Action since Andy Burnham became prime minister earlier this month.
Israel’s assault on Gaza was not a priority for the government during Keir Starmer’s tenure, and critics have accused his administration of being complicit.
Since launching his campaign to become prime minister, Burnham has attempted to reframe the Labour Party’s foreign policy. Before taking office, he conceded that his party “didn’t get it right” on Gaza and said he was “sorry”.
However, rights groups say his apology is meaningless unless it is backed by action.
Burnham has already granted the United States permission to use some UK military bases to carry out “defensive” strikes against Iran, a conflict that began on February 28 and which several legal experts have described as illegal.
The leader of the UK Green Party, Zack Polanski, has meanwhile demanded that Burnham reverse Palestine Action’s proscription.
It is within the prime minister’s power “to scrap this proscription and end these dystopian scenes for good”, Polanski said in a post on X. “There is simply no excuse in a democracy for a crackdown in support for protest groups like this.”
Polanski is the Greens’ first Jewish leader and has accused the right-wing press of erasing his religious identity because of his support for Palestine and opposition to Israel’s genocide.
In a post on X, Defend Our Juries sarcastically criticised the UK’s terrorism laws, which outlaw expressing support for Palestine Action.
“Britain today: An elderly woman in a wheelchair is escorted away by the police and risks up to 14 years in prison for supporting terrorism since the Home Secretary proscribed a protest group in 2025. Her crime? She said: ‘I support Palestine Action and I encourage you to join’,” it said.
New appeal given green light
Later on Thursday, it was reported that the UK’s Supreme Court has said it will hear another appeal against the “terrorist” designation imposed on Palestine Action.
A lower court ruling in June found that the government’s decision to ban the group was lawful, citing its “support for violence”. The High Court had ruled in February that the ban unlawfully interfered with freedom of expression.
Huda Ammori, who cofounded Palestine Action in 2020 and brought the legal challenge against proscription, was granted permission to appeal against that decision on Wednesday, the Supreme Court’s website showed.
She said in a statement: “We will continue to fight this proscription all the way to the Supreme Court and, if necessary, to the European Court of Human Rights to overturn what has become one of the most extreme attacks on free speech and the right to protest in modern British history.”

title: The economy slowed a bit -- but Americans continued to spend
summary: The U.S. economy grew at an annual rate of 1.5% in the spring, according to the Commerce Department. That's a modest slowdown from the previous quarter — but consumer spending picked up steam.
full_text:
The economy slowed a bit — but Americans continued to spend
The U.S. economy grew more slowly this spring than it did earlier in the year, but consumers continue to spend freely.
Gross domestic product — the broadest measure of economic activity — grew at an annual rate of 1.5% in April, May and June, according to a report Thursday from the Commerce Department. That's a modest slowdown from the first three months of the year when GDP grew at a 2.1% pace. A decline in government spending and a jump in imports, which count against the domestic tally, account for much of the change.
Consumer spending continues to power the economy, growing at a solid 2.1% pace during the second quarter. It's not clear how long shoppers can keep that up, however, in the face of rising prices.
Loading...
A separate report from the Commerce Department shows prices in June were up 3.7% from a year earlier. Inflation has been outpacing wage gains in recent months, forcing shoppers to dip into savings or borrow money to support their spending. The personal savings rate fell to 2.7% in June — a three year low.
The Commerce Department's inflation yardstick is closely watched by the Federal Reserve. Prices have been climbing faster than the central bank would like. But the Fed opted not to raise its benchmark interest rate on Wednesday.
Trade swings weighed on GDP during the quarter. Exports rose during the quarter, but imports rose faster.
"Trade has gone up and down and all around and clearly the tariffs are swinging things around," said Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics. "One quarter it might add to growth. The next quarter it might subtract from growth. Net over time, it's kind of sort of a wash."

BreakingChina voices ‘serious concern’ over new US curbs in senior trade talks
Beijing raises objections during a high-level call while both sides seek to build momentum ahead of an expected Xi-Trump summit
China on Thursday voiced “serious concern” over recent US economic restrictions during a video call between Vice-Premier He Lifeng, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.
The exchange took place as both sides sought to finalise economic deliverables ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s expected visit to the United States in September.
“The Chinese side expressed serious concern over the recent economic and trade restrictions imposed by the United States on China,” according to a readout by Chinese state news agency Xinhua.
The readout added that the two sides engaged in “candid, in-depth and constructive” exchanges, centred on implementing the “important consensus” reached at the Beijing meeting between US President Donald Trump and the Chinese leader.
Despite months of escalating trade tensions – including additional US tariffs, export controls and tit-for-tat restrictions targeting each other’s companies – both sides have continued engaging in an effort to secure outcomes ahead of the leaders’ summit.
On Tuesday, the Trump administration announced bans on imports of new Chinese robots and power inverters, citing threats to US national security and supply chain vulnerabilities.

full_text:
Top US science journals more likely to reject paper by Chinese authors: study
Even among American-based scientists, those with Chinese surnames had lower publication rates than those without, team finds
Researchers based in China or having a Chinese surname were far less likely than their US and Canadian counterparts to have papers published in the world’s most prestigious journals, according to a new study.
Just 2.5 per cent of submissions from China-based researchers were accepted, compared with 8.3 per cent overall for those from North America, a team found after analysing a rare dataset of more than 110,000 manuscripts submitted to Science and Science Advances between 2015 and 2020.
Even among US-based scientists, those with Chinese surnames had lower publication rates than those without Chinese surnames, they reported in Science Advances on July 15.
Sam Zhang, the study’s lead author and a computational social scientist at the University of Vermont, said one reason might be that China’s research system offered career and financial incentives for scientists to submit to elite journals such as Science.
That could encourage submissions even when some studies were not the best fit for the journals’ broad scientific scope.

Sam Mostyn says there is a widespread ‘failure to understand and engage with and feel proud of the very civic underpinnings of our democracy’

Australia faces a “growing catastrophe” from poor understanding of the country’s constitutional foundation, the governor general, Sam Mostyn, has warned as attacks on institutions and threats against elected officials undermine democratic participation.
Two years after her appointment as King Charles’s representative in Canberra, and as she brings a modern touch to the role of vice regal, Mostyn said that knowledge of how the country’s system of government operates was in steady decline and better civics education was needed.
“Where I see the most woeful lack of understanding … the basic understanding of the tenets of our democracy, is in the adult population,” Mostyn said.
“It’s mostly people who attack our system, who say we shouldn’t have a governor general, or who ask the governor general to do things that are not within my powers, or criticise me for signing the bills that I must sign, because they think I should have a view that clearly I do not have as governor general. Certain things I must do under my constitutional requirements.
“We’ve got a growing catastrophe, I think, in a failure to understand and engage with and feel proud of the very civic underpinnings of our democracy.”
In an interview for Guardian’s Australian Politics podcast, released on Friday, Mostyn said schoolchildren and newly sworn Australian citizens had the best understanding of how government and institutions worked.
The comments come as parliaments, the courts, the Australian Electoral Commission, and officeholders around the country face mounting criticism and abuse. Since the Covid pandemic, social media and online commentary has been identified as hotbed of corrosive sentiment, coinciding with rising threats against officials.
“It starts with understanding why we have a constitution, how it came to be,” Mostyn said of a potential solution.
“It’s 125 years old this year. It was built in a particular way, to bring the states and territories together, in order to build a sense of unity around the country, and it sets up everything that then builds the strength of our democracy.”
Mostyn said part of the problem was an absence of “a shared set of facts”, including in online discourse.
“I think this is a moment where it’s important for everyone, particularly people like me, in these offices, to keep up the project of why it matters that we show respect for each other, we learn to understand each other.
“There is a big risk that if we don’t, this is the beginning of the unraveling of social cohesion.”
The former businesswoman, AFL commissioner, political adviser and community leader has prioritised civics engagement and education in the role, bringing a less formal and more down-to-earth approach to the office of governor general. When she was appointed to the role – traditionally filled by former politicians, judges and military leaders – Mostyn promised an unstinting focus on kindness, on care and on respect.
Earlier this month, she hosted a roundtable on social cohesion and civics education with the Constitution Education Fund at her official residence in Canberra, Government House, attended by educators, public service leaders and thinktanks. Former high court chief justice Robert French is the fund’s chair.
Mostyn warned the types of people considering seeking political office in Australia is changing, because of sustained abuse and threats against elected representatives at all levels.
She said local councillors and mayors had told her public life was becoming difficult and increasingly unappealing.
“They [have] shared with me that lack of civility in their own communities, as directed to them as elected representatives, has become very very challenging, making it very difficult to seek office.
“If you know that you’re putting yourself into very dangerous traffic with people who now don’t feel the need to be respectful, who make direct threats … we’ve seen this all around the world with elected representatives at all levels.
“This desire to be hateful, to attack, to not enter into good, peaceful, robust but respectful discussions on things where we might not agree, and so that’s happening certainly in local government.”
Mostyn is the Crown’s representative in Australia, presides over the executive council, gives royal assent to legislation from parliament, appoints ministers and officials, dissolves parliament for elections and is the commander-in-chief of the Australian Defence Force.
She holds the reserve powers of the constitution, and attends and hosts hundreds of events every year, including for the Order of Australia.
In the past two years, Mostyn has used a growing social media presence to educate the public about the function of the governor general, and has conducted dozens of interviews, including with local media outlets when visiting far-flung communities.
In the wake of the Bondi beach terror attack in December last year, Mostyn immediately flew to Sydney to comfort victims and members of Australia’s Jewish community. At the height of the Socceroos World Cup campaign last month, she attended a Canberra pub to watch Australia play Paraguay in the middle of the day.
Speaking at Admiralty House, the governor general’s residence on Sydney Harbour, Mostyn revealed she had followed precedent from recent governors general and asked the Electoral Commissioner for an exemption from compulsory voting, preferring to be as removed as possible from political matters.
Her appointment to the role was not without controversy.
The Greens voted against legislation put to parliament to ensure Mostyn was paid the same amount as her predecessor. Gen David Hurley took a lower base salary due to his military pension.
Commentators criticised Mostyn’s qualifications, and said her high-profile positions on several issues including the voice to parliament referendum should have disqualified her from being appointed. One newspaper column called her “a governor-general from the Chairman’s Lounge.”
But Mostyn has confounded some critics in her first two years on the job.
In May, Chris Kenny, a columnist with the Australian newspaper lamented that too few commentators were ever prepared to admit when they were wrong about matters in public debate, acknowledging he had been mistaken in editorialising against Mostyn’s appointment on Sky News.
Kenny had argued her record could be “too political for Yarralumla”. But instead, Mostyn, he said, “has been diligent, dignified, hard-working and apolitical”.
The chief executive of the Constitution Education Fund, Kerry Jones, said Mostyn’s involvement could not be under stated.
“Probably the most important issue facing our country, our constitutional arrangements, our democracy, is that the people of Australia, the voters of Australia, seem to have lost a sense of trust in the institutions of government and the people in those institutions,” she said.
“If we survive – and when we look back on this period, which is being called a lack of social cohesion, or polarisation, or the rise of populism in politics and that is resulting in racism increasing again, and resulting in antisemitism and Islamophobia – the fact that the governor general is saying it is a crisis and we need to do something about it, could be seen as one of the most significant acts ever taken, I believe, by an Australian governor general for the good of Australia.”
Jones praised Mostyn’s energy and wisdom.
“She cares for every single Australian citizen in every community across Australia, and that radiates from everything she says.”
Mostyn said one of her guiding principles comes from the memoir of one of her predecessors, the academic and writer Sir Zelman Cowen.
Cowen served as governor general from 1977 until 1982, having replaced the controversial Sir John Kerr.
