The new high-water mark is 10,981.83 this morning. We shall see if the index can reach the “psychologically important” (i.e., meaningless) 11,000 mark today.
Up there among the winners this morning is NatWest Group. The bank is up 3.6% after upgrading its financial outlook and share buyback plans after revealing a jump in profits. The Polar Capital investment trust, which has exposure to AI companies, is the top gainer, up 4.3%.
Those chemical leak costs and paused share buyback have put Melrose Industries at the bottom of the index this morning.
Melrose shares are down 6.3%, making it the biggest faller on London’s blue-chip index. Spreadbetting platform IG Group is down 5% after publishing financial results and revealing a plan to buy US fantasy sports business Underdog.
Aerospace company Melrose Industries has paused its share buybacks as it waits for potential legal and regulatory action over a leaking chemical tank in California.
The company’s GKN Aerospace business said the tank at its Garden Grove facility was leaking methyl methacrylate, a flammable chemical used in the acrylic for windows for the F-35 fighter jet and passenger cabin windows on commercial aircraft, because it was overheating. The local area had to be evacuated in case the tank exploded (which it did not).
Melrose on Friday said the was “back to partial production” after the chemical tank incident at the end of May, and that it was “working closely with relevant authorities and customers to safely resume full production”.
However, the company paused its £175m share buyback, “pending clarification of financial impact of the Garden Grove incident, including from ongoing regulatory and legal processes”.
Peter Dilnot, chief executive of Melrose Industries, said:
We are managing the situation at our Garden Grove transparencies site following the incident in May. Partial production has since resumed, and we will continue to work closely with customers, regulators and other authorities to safely restore the site to full production in the second half.
The incident has already cost the company £16m in lost revenues, plus another £13m in exceptional costs. It will have another £25m to £30m in costs in the second half of the year.
UK house prices edge up in July amid interest rate caution
Joanna Partridge
Economic uncertainty dampened UK house price growth in July as prospective house buyers remained cautious about interest rates amid the ongoing US war with Iran in what should be peak housebuying season.
House prices rose by just 0.1% in July from a month earlier, according to lender Nationwide, while annual price growth slowed to 1.8% this month, down from 2.2% in June.
The UK’s biggest building society said the price of an average home edged slightly higher in July to £277,542, up from £277,484 the previous month. However, this is still lower than the average price recorded in May, when it rose above £278,000.
Robert Gardner, chief economist at Nationwide, said:
Market activity and house prices have remained soft in recent months, in part reflecting the uncertain economic backdrop. Geopolitical tensions remain high, with the conflict between Iran and the US again exerting upward pressure on energy prices and market interest rates in recent weeks.
Financial market expectations for the future path of Bank Rate have been volatile, reflecting shifting views about the inflationary implications of events at home and abroad.
British Airways owner's profits fall as Iran war pushes up fuel costs
The owner of British Airways has reported a steep fall in profits and said it expects no growth in passenger capacity this year as the US-Israeli war in Iran takes its toll.
International Airlines Group (IAG) said it expected demand to stay strong, but added that its “disciplined cost control” could only partly mitigate the impact of “a significant fuel price increase” caused by the attacks on Iran. Iran closed the strait of Hormuz in response to the attacks, a key export route for oil from the Gulf.
The company, which also owns Iberia and Aer Lingus, among others, said that it was a “resilient revenue performance despite lower capacity than planned”.
Revenue increased in the first half of 2026 by 1% to €16bn, while profit after tax fell 21% to €1bn.
Luis Gallego, IAG’s chief executive, said:
With these results IAG has again demonstrated that its excellent fundamentals are supporting continued value creation for our shareholders, despite the impact of the crisis in the Middle East and wider geopolitical events.
BP to sell North Sea business; Korea's stock market rises a record 18%
Good morning, and welcome to our live coverage of business, economics and financial markets.
BP has put its North Sea oil business up for sale, saying it will try to find a buyer amid a political dispute over whether the UK government should allow more drilling.
Prime minister Andy Burnham on Thursday signalled that he would be open to more extraction in the North Sea, although he did not make clear if that would mean new licences or allowing expanded use of existing wells.
BP, one of the biggest companies on the FTSE 100, said it was selling the North Sea business as part of an ongoing portfolio review under American chief executive Meg O’Neill. The American was appointed in December with a remit to refocus the company after a tumultuous period of three chief executives in three years.
The company said it wanted to direct the spending required on the North Sea to other places which could offer higher financial returns.
O’Neill said:
The UK has been our home for more than 100 years and will continue to play an important role in our future. We’re proud of the jobs we create, the contribution we make to the UK economy, and the work we do to keep energy flowing every day.
The North Sea remains integral to the UK’s energy system. However, as we focus our portfolio and direct capital to our highest-value opportunities, we believe our North Sea business will be better positioned as part of another company. It has world-class people, resilient assets and a proud heritage, and it is precisely these qualities that can attract an owner ready to back its next chapter. We are seeking an outcome that recognises that value.
The question of whether to allow more North Sea drilling has become politically contentious in recent months. Environmental campaigners are aghast that Labour is considering allowing more drilling for planet-heating fossil fuels, but Burnham appears to have decided it would be more useful to drill at a time of high energy prices.
Donald Trump revealed Burnham’s plans after a first phone call between the US president and the new prime minister. Burnham later told reporters:
I indicated in the phone call that we had, a week last Monday, that I would take a pragmatic approach when it comes to the North Sea, and that is my intention as we go forward from here.
There is a resource there. When people are struggling, we can’t ignore that. Hence, me indicating that to the president.
Record day for Korea’s stock market
South Korea’s stock market has been going through a period of turbulence for the ages thanks to the AI boom – and fears it will bust. It continued on Friday, with the largest single-day increase in the benchmark Kospi index’s history.
Korea’s Kospi is up an astonishing 17.91% today. It fell 11% on Tuesday – just shy of the record 12.06% decline hit in early March in the first days of the Iran war – and 6% on Wednesday.
Global stock markets have been dominated in recent months by artificial intelligence companies. But Korea’s stock market does not have the depth of the US, meaning its AI-exposed chip companies are even more dominant. The share price of chipmaker SK Hynix soared 30% on Friday, while Samsung Electronics was up 28%.

title: ‘Rob has the bucks cash’: NSW Liberals used Reformers funds to pay for ‘personal expenditure’, Icac hears
summary:
Robert Assaf separately tells anti-corruption inquiry money funnelled through lobbying firm to create ‘maximum benefit from a tax perspective’

  • Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A group of young conservative Liberal power brokers accused of soliciting illegal donations used some of the funds to pay for a bucks night, one of its members has told a corruption inquiry.

The Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Friday heard again from Robert Assaf, who this week was the first witness from the conservative right Liberal factional group the Reformers to give evidence.

Continue reading...
full_text:
A group of young conservative Liberal power brokers accused of soliciting illegal donations used some of the funds to pay for a bucks night, one of its members has told a corruption inquiry.
The Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Friday heard again from Robert Assaf, who this week was the first witness from the conservative right Liberal factional group the Reformers to give evidence.
The inquiry is investigating allegations that the Reformers solicited or accepted illegal donations to recruit or renew members to the party – a practice known as “branch stacking”. The group wanted more conservative policies on same-sex marriage, abortion and euthanasia.
The counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC asked Assaf about a decision to move alleged payments from prohibited donor Michael O’Hara from a bank account in the Reformers’ name to Beckington, a registered lobbying firm set up by the group and run by member Christian Ellis.
O’Hara earlier this week admitted to a fake arrangement in which he paid Beckington for “strategic wealth strategy investment advice”. He disputed whether the payments to the Reformers were to the NSW Liberals or should be considered political donations.
On Friday, Assaf said funnelling money through Beckington rather than the Reformers account was to create “the maximum benefit from a tax perspective”.
Dwyer replied: “That’s an explanation that you thought of overnight. Is that right?”
Asked if he was aware that it was illegal to minimise tax by creating fake invoices, Assaf said he knew that now, but not at the time. Asked if he thought the arrangement was “dishonest”, he said: “I would have thought it was tricky.”
Assaf admitted to temporarily using funds from the Reformers account to pay for a bucks night.
In a WhatsApp message to the group in August 2020, Reformer Jean-Claude Perrottet, the brother of former premier Dominic Perrottet, wrote: “Rob has the bucks cash coming back.”
Asked what this meant, Assaf said: “I think you recall I referred to us being immature and young, using the account as an advance on our personal expenditure.”
“This was one of those moments where we, I think, we had booked a venue for either my bucks or Christian [Ellis’s] bucks. It required an upfront payment.”
“I think it was cancelled, maybe because of Covid, one of them, so it was waiting for it to get reimbursed.”
He also said he had make fake invoices to Beckington in the name of his wife, Carmel Assaf, but did not agree that this was to reimburse him for Reformers work. He said he had done so to claim a 10% fee promised to him for finding new clients for Ellis.
The commission heard Assaf was employed in communications at Catholic Schools NSW, the governing body for 600 schools in the state, in 2019, alongside Reformers associate Dylan Whitelaw, who gave evidence earlier in the week.
The Catholic Schools NSW chief executive, Dallas McInerney, is alleged to have arranged and approved payments to the group to support branch stacking efforts through Beckington, where Whitelaw later came to be employed.
Assaf disputed an earlier claim made by Whitelaw that he spent 60% of his time at Catholic Schools NSW on factional work, saying it was more like 10 to 20%. But he said he would sometimes “chuck a sickie” to do Reformers work.
Under questioning from Dwyer, Assaf admitted that he knew that money being paid to Beckington was to fund work that Whitelaw was doing for the Reformers. “I knew that, yes,” Assaf told the hearing.
The inquiry heard that Assaf’s friendship with Ellis later broke down.
The inquiry heard that when McInerney allegedly wanted to end the relationship with Beckington in 2021, Assaf provided the former with advice about it on “multiple” occasions.
“[That advice] would have been something like: ‘Christian’s a liar. He’s greedy. I don’t trust him, and I’m not sure he’s doing much for you at the moment,” he said.
The inquiry on Friday returned to whether the federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, had knowledge of and supported the Reformers.
Assaf said he recalled sending a screenshot of a message from McInerney in which he said he wanted to “shake down Angus for 10K”, and reading a message sent by Whitelaw in which he claimed McInerney had received “the commitment from Angus, the 15k injection plus a 3k monthly donation”, but denied any donation had taken place.
“I don’t think Angus worked out,” Assaf said. Taylor, who is not accused of wrongdoing, on Friday again denied making payments to the group.
The Icac presiding commissioner, Fabian Gleeson, intervened on multiple occasions during Assaf’s evidence. Before the lunch break, Gleeson told Assaf he had become “a bit argumentative in your response”.
“I believe they call that hangry commissioner,” Assaf said.
Gleeson said: “I’m not aware of what young people’s speak is these days, Mr Assaf. What I’d like you to do is to sit there, concentrate, and answer a further question which council assisting has, and then we’ll adjourn. Understand?”
Assaf was expected to appear again on Monday, before the commission is scheduled to hear from the NSW shadow attorney general and Liberal leader in the upper house, Damien Tudehope.
Many of the Reformers worked as staffers in Tudehope’s office, and Tudehope gave frequent talks at Reformers recruitment events. O’Hara is his former business partner.
Tudehope, who has stood aside from his shadow cabinet roles during the inquiry, is not accused of wrongdoing.
The inquiry will also hear from Jean-Claude Perrottet and Jeremy Greenwood, both named in Icac’s allegations. The watchdog heard on Thursday that Jean-Claude Perrottet allegedly paid for memberships as part of branch-stacking efforts, forbidden under Liberal party rules.
He has previously denied any wrongdoing, while Dominic Perrottet is not accused of wrongdoing.
Icac’s hearings continue.

title: Gina Rinehart threatens ABC with legal action over Race Around the World program

Hancock Prospecting says chair Kim Williams among those ‘on notice’ for failing to remove program that joked about turning Rinehart’s insides into a sausage roll

Gina Rinehart has threatened the ABC with legal action over crude comments aired on the national broadcaster, including a joke about mixing her guts into a sausage roll.

The four-minute film, titled A Very Relaxing Video, aired on the Race Around the World program on 12 July and concluded with the film-maker, Kate McGuinness, making crude and offensive comments about Rinehart.

full_text:
Gina Rinehart has threatened the ABC with legal action over crude comments aired on the national broadcaster, including a joke about mixing her guts into a sausage roll.
The four-minute film, titled A Very Relaxing Video, aired on the Race Around the World program on 12 July and concluded with the film-maker, Kate McGuinness, making crude and offensive comments about Rinehart.
“When the revolution comes will you hide under the bed or will you know exactly how to shove a stick right up Gina Rinehart’s butthole, stirring it round, mixing her guts up nice and smooth, to make one big sausage roll to make something out of nothing?” she said.
On Friday, Hancock Prospecting released a statement detailing that it first wrote to the ABC board on 23 July. The company said the ABC was asked to “immediately remove” the segment from all of its platforms; publicly apologise to Rinehart; and “undertake a comprehensive investigation” into how it was approved and published.
“One week has now elapsed,” the statement said.
“The ABC’s Board and senior management have provided no substantive public response, nor any substantive response to Hancock or Mrs Rinehart, and have taken no steps to remove the material from ABC platforms, despite widespread public condemnation and the serious risks its publication and continued publication pose to Mrs Rinehart.”
According to Hancock, it has sent legal letters to the ABC’s chair, Kim Williams; deputy chair, Lisa Caffery; and its managing director, Hugh Marks.
It said the letter informed them they have been formally placed on notice over “detailed allegations of serious contraventions of multiple Australian criminal and civil laws arising from the ABC’s publication and continued publication of the material”.
News24 first reported that the mining magnate had “launched legal action” against the ABC and several senior executives.
On Friday, the ABC on Friday confirmed it had received the legal letters.
“The ABC has received correspondence from lawyers acting for Ms Rinehart and will respond to it in due course,” a spokesperson said. “The ABC Ombudsman is independently reviewing audience complaints in relation to the 12 July Race Around the World episode in accordance with the ABC’s complaints handling process.”
The episode, which was rated M for “coarse language” and “sexual references”, was still available to stream on iView on Friday afternoon.
On Thursday, McGuinness issued an apology and said it wasn’t her intention to promote violence.
“My writing is cartoonish and always satirical. Unfortunately, jokes do not land with everyone. Its purpose was never to be taken literally,” she said in a statement uploaded to the ABC’s website.
Pressure had been mounting on the ABC to respond amid wide outrage in sectors of the media and from the Western Australian premier, Roger Cook, who said the skit was “unacceptable” and used “confronting” language.
The media regulator said it would wait until the results of the ABC’s processes before making a decision on any next steps.
“Under Australia’s co-regulatory broadcasting system set out in the Broadcasting Services Act … national broadcasters are given the first opportunity to respond to complaints about alleged breaches of their respective codes of practice,” a spokesperson for the Australian Communications and Media Authority (Acma) said.
“If complainants are dissatisfied with the broadcaster’s response or do not receive a response within the statutory timeframe, complainants may make their complaint to the Acma.”

title: Labour hire firm paid Mick Gatto more than $1m to secure work on Big Build, CFMEU inquiry told
summary:
M Group’s lawyer tells inquiry while the firm’s directors ‘may have done business with Gatto’ they were not ‘frontmen’ for him

  • Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A labour hire company accused of being a front for underworld figure Mick Gatto paid him more than $1m over nine years, with its lawyer telling an inquiry it did so to secure work on Victorian government Big Build sites where the construction union had influence.

Integrity expert Geoffrey Watson SC appeared before the Queensland inquiry into the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU) on Friday, defending his Rotting from the Top report, which alleged Gatto controlled several M Group companies through “dummy directors” Michael Portia and Tony Paragalli.

Continue reading...
full_text:
A labour hire company accused of being a front for underworld figure Mick Gatto paid him more than $1m over nine years, with its lawyer telling an inquiry it did so to secure work on Victorian government Big Build sites where the construction union had influence.
Integrity expert Geoffrey Watson SC appeared before the Queensland inquiry into the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU) on Friday, defending his Rotting from the Top report, which alleged Gatto controlled several M Group companies through “dummy directors” Michael Portia and Tony Paragalli.
Watson alleged the companies received “favourable treatment from the CFMEU” on Victorian government Big Build projects and “showered with benefits” due to their connection to Gatto. Gatto, Paragalli and Portia have previously denied the allegation.
On Friday, Watson said he “probably shouldn’t have said Mick Gatto owned them [the companies]” and “should have acknowledged that it’s probable that Paragalli and Portia also own part of it”.
But he stood by his central allegation that Gatto “controls” the companies.
“More than ever, it is my view that all the evidence points to Mick Gatto controlling the M Group companies,” Watson said.
Watson said since his report was completed, he has seen bank accounts that showed M Group companies paid Gatto $1.04m between 2016 and 2025, with payments becoming “larger and more regular” over time.
This included $65,000 in payments over six weeks in April 2020 and a single payment of $77,000 in July 2022.
Watson said M Group paid Gatto $200,000 in the first half of 2025, while M Group Trades and Labour entered administration in May owing $13.7m in tax.
“While a company is running up a tax debt of $13m, it is paying Mick Gatto $200,000,” he said. “It was paying Gatto in preference to its employees. It was paying Gatto in preference to its tax debt.”
M Group’s barrister, Simon Wilson KC, said while Portia and Paragalli “may have done business with Gatto”, they were not “frontmen” for him.
He said M Group did not dispute it “paid Gatto a substantial amount of money over a substantial number of years” but argued it did so “to protect its income sources”.
Wilson said the company had won tenders but was then blocked from starting work by a larger CFMEU-aligned group.
“They’d win a tender, start to put people on the site, and they’d be blocked out by bigger groups,” he said. “They had to get Gatto to come in and say, ‘Come on, these people can be in.’”
Watson responded that the payments amounted to paying Gatto to “fix contracts”.
Wilson also argued that if M Group was genuinely Gatto’s company, it would not have needed to make the payments.
The pair clashed frequently during Watson’s cross-examination, prompting Commissioner Stuart Wood KC to repeatedly intervene.
Watson’s third and final appearance at the inquiry comes after Jacinta Allan was forced to step down as premier this week after she lost the support of Labor caucus, due in part to her failure to act on the corruption scandal.
Her successor Ben Carroll’s first act as premier on Tuesday was to commit to a royal commission into the construction industry.
The newly appointed administrator of the CFMEU, Michael Crosby, told ABC’s 7.30 on Thursday night though he was “sceptical about royal commissions”, it was “encouraging” that Carroll’s proposal would examine the entire construction industry rather than focusing solely on the union.
“We will fix this union up. It’ll be back in the fold of the union movement as a powerful, strong, ethical union. That’s not going to last if it’s sitting in an industry riddled with corruption,” he said.
He said he believed there was “still criminality” in the sector as a result of “fixers” who are “holding themselves out as able to have some influence about who gets contracts and who doesn’t.”
Watson on Friday also revealed that “nobody” from the Victorian Labor government has contacted him despite criticising his estimate that corruption in the construction union cost taxpayers up to $15bn.
“They made [statements] to the press without asking me anything about how I arrived at the report or what I did to achieve it,” he said.
“They were bitterly critical remarks. It’s hard to interpret them as anything less than suggesting I made it up.”
The shadow attorney general, James Newbury, said “Labor may have a new leader, but under Ben Carroll, underworld linked labour hire firms are still profiting off the corrupted Big Build”.
The Victorian government has been contacted for comment.

title: Forced out of Australia’s military due to his sexuality, David says an apology is ‘long overdue’ for veterans like him
summary:
Exclusive: ADF personnel who were discriminated against for being LGBTQ+ are owed a national apology, federal government told

  • Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A national apology should be issued to LGBTQ+ veterans and service personnel who experienced discrimination at the hands of the Australian Defence Force, according to recommendations to the federal government.

David Gibson, who was discharged from the military in 1989 because he was bisexual and chair of GLBTI Rights in Ageing, said it was time for the prime minister to issue an apology.

Continue reading...
full_text:
A national apology should be issued to LGBTQ+ veterans and service personnel who experienced discrimination at the hands of the Australian Defence Force, according to recommendations to the federal government.
David Gibson, who was discharged from the military in 1989 because he was bisexual and chair of GLBTI Rights in Ageing, said it was time for the prime minister to issue an apology.
Gibson entered the military after high school in the 1980s and was posted to Townsville where he said the defence force conducted “witch hunts” to out homosexual members who under policy were prohibited from serving.
He still doesn’t know how the ADF found out about his sexuality, but described extensive interrogation by military police and said he felt “abandoned” by the whole system.
“I was thinking I just want this interrogation to end, and I foolishly thought … if I just admitted who I was, my true self, that this would be the end,” Gibson said.
“But the interrogation just flipped, and this is why I call it a witch hunt, because then they flipped into, give us names, who have you slept with? … And in the end I was so bullied by that process, I made up a situation … because again I just wanted it to end.”
Gibson was then sent to another military base in Victoria where he wasn’t allowed to speak with officers, and was told to work in an isolated office. In 1989, he was discharged.
He said while homosexuality was criminalised at the time, the military in the 1970s and 80s more often put personnel through an administrative instead of a criminal process because “they didn’t want the negative publicity [and] they didn’t want [to grant] the rights that you are afforded when you go through the military justice system”.
Gibson, who made a submission to the royal commission into defence and veteran suicides, said he felt decades of shame during and after his time in the military and the “traumatic” process led him into a deep depression.
“It’s disgraceful the way in which we treated people, and that’s my personal story but it’s not an isolated story,” Gibson said.
“An apology is long overdue … we need an apology from the prime minister.”
The Senate’s foreign affairs and defence committee has considered new legislation introduced after the royal commission into defence and veteran suicide, designed to modernise treatment of mental health problems and improve fairness in the military discipline system.
The bill would also create a new power to extinguish historical service offences. Until as late as 1990, the ADF maintained a policy prohibiting homosexual members from serving, resulting in discharge and conviction because of consensual same‑sex activity.
But the committee’s report, released on Friday, said other forms of discrimination against LGBTQ+ people needed to be addressed as well, recommending the Albanese government go further than the draft bill to provide long-overdue recognition.
The report calls for “restorative outcomes” for the victims of historical discriminatory administrative policies within defence, including those targeted because of their sexual orientation or gender identity.
The policies included administrative discharge, forced resignation, security clearance revocation and other personnel actions.
Among the recommendations are a call for affected veterans or service people to be able to have their defence records annotated to show official actions against them were driven by discrimination, and that the conduct would not constitute an offence under current Australian law or breach contemporary defence policies.
The report says the defence department should offer a certificate of honourable service to personnel and veterans who suffered because of discriminatory policies, and that the federal government should issue a formal apology.
Like landmark apologies to the Stolen Generations of Indigenous Australians and victims of child sexual abuse, the statement would recognise harm experienced by LGBTQ+ personnel and veterans during their military service.
The inquiry heard evidence from organisations including GLBTI Rights in Ageing, which advocates for the rights, wellbeing, visibility and inclusion of older LGBTQ+ Australians. Its members proposed a national apology to the inquiry.
Witnesses appearing before the inquiry said the new powers to extinguish convictions were appropriate recognition that laws were discriminatory, inconsistent with contemporary Australian values, and caused enduring harm to veterans and their families.
Air Vice-Marshal Lara Gunn, defence’s head of joint support services division, told the inquiry additional measures relevant to historical administrative were being considered. 
 Committee chair and Labor senator Raff Ciccone said a modern ADF “must learn from the mistakes of the past”.
“Many LGBTIQA+ personnel served Australia with distinction while facing discrimination because of their sexual orientation or gender identity,” he said.
“Everyone who serves our country should be judged on their service and ability, not on who they are. The Committee’s recommendations include further measures to address the harm caused by past discrimination against LGBTIQA+ personnel and veterans.”

title: BP puts North Sea oil and gas business up for sale
summary:
Move, which will end six decades of production in area, comes as new CEO tries to simplify firm and cut debt

  • Business live – latest updates

BP has put its North Sea oil and gas business up for sale, as it looks to end six decades of production from the region.

The oil major announced on Friday morning that it had launched a formal process to market its North Sea business for a potential sale. The move comes as BP’s new chief executive, Meg O’Neill, tries to simplify the company and cut its debt levels.

Continue reading...
full_text:
BP has put its North Sea oil and gas business up for sale, as it looks to end six decades of production from the region.
The oil major announced on Friday morning that it had launched a formal process to market its North Sea business for a potential sale. The move comes as BP’s new chief executive, Meg O’Neill, tries to simplify the company and cut its debt levels.
“The North Sea remains integral to the UK’s energy system. However, as we focus our portfolio and direct capital to our highest-value opportunities, we believe our North Sea business will be better positioned as part of another company,” O’Neill said in a statement.
O’Neill also said the UK would “continue to play an important role” in BP’s future.
“We’re proud of the jobs we create, the contribution we make to the UK economy, and the work we do to keep energy flowing every day,” she said.
BP’s involvement in the North Sea dates back to 1964, when it was granted its first UK North Sea licence. The company discovered the West Sole gasfield in the winter of 1965, followed by its largest discovery in the area, the giant Forties field, in 1970.
The sale announcement comes a day after Andy Burnham said he would take a “pragmatic” approach to oil and gas drilling in the North Sea, saying the government could not ignore the potential energy resources it holds.
BP’s North Sea sale is “a watershed moment”, said Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG.
“It says a lot when BP isn’t prepared to stick around to see if the new government can re-energise the UK’s energy policy. Clearly BP thinks it will take too long at a time when the need to exploit new energy fields is pressing, and waiting around for Whitehall to move is not a prudent use of resources.”
The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said she was in close contact with BP over its plans.
“The North Sea is a vital national asset and we will take a pragmatic approach, recognising that oil and gas will be part of our energy mix for years to come,” she said.
“I’m in close contact with BP and have made clear that my priority is ensuring that the workers and local community are protected during this sale process.”
O’Neill took over as BP’s CEO on 1 April. Less than two months later the company removed its chair, Albert Manifold, citing serious concerns about “important governance standards, oversight and conduct”.

title: ‘Extremely scary findings’ show climate crisis is supercharging Europe’s wildfire weather
summary:
Latest study says global heating has made hot, dry and windy conditions in Spain at least 20 times more likely

The extreme heat and drought stoking huge wildfires in Spain and France were made far more likely by the climate crisis, a scientific analysis has found.

Global heating made hot, dry and windy weather at least 20 times more likely in Spain and twice as likely in France, experts from the World Weather Attribution (WWA) consortium calculated. The finding is the latest to pin the blame for the continent’s sweltering and deadly summer firmly on the heating caused by the burning of oil, gas and coal.

Continue reading...
full_text:
The extreme heat and drought stoking huge wildfires in Spain and France were made far more likely by the climate crisis, a scientific analysis has found.
Global heating made hot, dry and windy weather at least 20 times more likely in Spain and twice as likely in France, experts from the World Weather Attribution (WWA) consortium calculated. The finding is the latest to pin the blame for the continent’s sweltering and deadly summer firmly on the heating caused by the burning of oil, gas and coal.
The intense heatwave at the end of June, which is estimated to have killed 20,000 people, could not have happened without the extra heat trapped by carbon pollution, a previous WWA study showed. Another found that the climate crisis-driven heat was “sucking soils dry” as extreme drought spread across Europe.
Searing heat and parched land led to very high “daily severity ratings”, the metric that was used in the new analysis and which measures how severe a wildfire will be if ignited. Studies of the 2025 wildfires also found they were supercharged by the climate crisis.
This year’s wildfires in western Europe have been made worse by a wet winter and spring, which boosted the growth of vegetation, which then dried out and provided fuel for the fires – so-called whiplash conditions. Global heating is making winters wetter and summers drier and hotter in Europe.
Dr Clair Barnes, a research associate at Imperial College London and part of the WWA study team, said: “We’ve seen repeatedly how climate change increases hot, dry, flammable conditions that are extremely conducive to wildfires.
“What’s unique about [the July fires in Spain and France] is that it’s still early in the season – and with another heatwave looming, these findings are extremely scary. What we’re seeing is a clear sign of the escalating impacts of [human-caused] warming.”
Julie Arrighi, the director of programmes at Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, said: “What we are seeing now in Spain and France goes well beyond what we would expect from past events.”
The wildfires have released huge plumes of toxic smoke. Dr Augustin Colette, at the French National Institute for Industrial Environment and Risks, said: “The smoke increased particulate [pollution] peak levels up to 20 times above what is considered ‘fair air quality’, and extremely poor air quality was felt up to 400 km away from the fires.” About 1.5 million people a year are estimated to have their lives shortened by wildfire smoke.
Severe wildfires have burned across Spain and France since early July, killing people, destroying thousands of homes, and forcing more than 300,000 people to flee. The WWA analysis assessed the seven-day period with the highest daily severity ratings (DSR) for each country. The scientists used weather records and established statistical methods to estimate how much more likely a week of extremely high DSR is in today’s heated world compared with in the world before mass fossil-fuel burning raised the global temperature by 1.4C (2.5F).
Big wildfires have also broken out in the UK and Greece, where three firefighters lost their lives.
The UN’s climate chief, Simon Stiell, said: “These European megafires show how fast climate-driven extreme heat and dry landscapes can turn wildfires into devastating national disasters.
“Humanity continuing to burn colossal amounts of coal, oil and gas is making these conditions more dangerous, and these megafires more deadly and destructive,” he said. “But the solutions are equally clear: all countries must move faster from fossil fuels to renewables and protect people from worsening climate impacts, from wildfires, to megastorms and floods, to droughts hitting food production.”
-

title: Calls grow ‘to flunk’ Portugal’s education minister amid exam marking fiasco
summary:
Fernando Alexandre’s push to digitise marking process deemed a failure with some students and parents contemplating legal action

Pressure is growing on Portugal’s education minister to resign amid student and teacher protests over his handling of this year’s national school exams.

Fernando Alexandre is accused of failing to take responsibility for what critics say is an unprecedented and chaotic school exam season affecting children aged 14 to 18, prompting student protesters to call for him “to be flunked”.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Pressure is growing on Portugal’s education minister to resign amid student and teacher protests over his handling of this year’s national school exams.
Fernando Alexandre is accused of failing to take responsibility for what critics say is an unprecedented and chaotic school exam season affecting children aged 14 to 18, prompting student protesters to call for him “to be flunked”.
At the centre of the controversy, which has plunged the Portuguese education sector into its worst crisis in decades, is Alexandre’s push to fully digitise the process for marking exams.
The centre-right government said the shift was necessary to modernise Portugal’s public administration and make school evaluations “more rigorous and objective” for the more than 260,000 students taking exams in primary and secondary schools.
But many parents, teachers and students have graded the change a failure and some people are contemplating pursuing legal action against the state. About 19,000 people have signed a petition calling for the annulment of all of this year’s results.
The principal of one of the largest school groups in Portugal, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said: “I struggle to trust in the process after everything that happened.”
In the weekly newspaper Expresso, the journalist and political commenter Daniel Oliveira decried the “inexplicable chaos” of the process, attacked Alexandre’s “unspeakable display of incompetence”, and said the credibility of the entire examination system had been “mortally wounded”.
It didn’t take long for the cracks to show in the new system, in which digitised, anonymous questions were distributed randomly to teachers and the grading professors’ remit was changed.
From the start of the exam season in mid-June, schools reported errors in the allocation of papers, with retired teachers and at least one dead teacher being called to mark them. Some educators were told to mark subjects out of their areas of expertise.
While grading the exams, several teachers reported difficulty accessing the marking platform, missing continuation pages, incomplete student answers, illegible scanned images and students’ answers disappearing from the online system.
André Azinheira, 32, a secondary school maths teacher, said he had received clear instructions to grade answers despite uncertainty over whether he was assessing a student’s full submission or whether pages were missing.
He said: “I knew someone could be wrong, but I had no way of knowing if pages were indeed missing, so I had to do my part. I may have hurt students or not, I have no idea. But I predicted there would be several errors in the grades.”
The Guardian heard of other cases in which teachers expressed similar dilemmas.
Reacting to growing unease from schools and students, Alexandre blamed staff for failing to “remove staples from the tests”, supposedly complicating the digitisation process. He dismissed teachers’ complaints about errors in the digital marking platform as insignificant or “false”.
After the results were released, three days late in mid-July, thousands of students complained about extreme discrepancies between their predicted grades and the posted exam grades, with some realising their grades were still missing.
Upon requesting access to a copy of the exam, several students reported finding missing pages, unknown handwriting and answers due to switched tests, and, in some cases, lost exams. Some students with special educational needs have complained that during the digitisation of the tests, the tags identifying those additional needs were left out, potentially affecting the grading.
An education watchdog later said that 26,000 exams had been affected by software or “parameterisation” errors, and that more than 18,000 grades were being changed.
Requests for re-evaluation of national high school exams have already exceeded 20,000, three times more than last year, according to data revealed by the minister of education this week. Every re-evaluation process has a cost of €25 (£21) a test, and the payment has to be made by the student.
After witnessing his friends and colleagues’ stress over switched and missing papers and exam grades, Raul Noetzold, 18, created a students’ movement called Chumbado.pt to call for Alexandre’s resignation. Last Friday, hundreds of students, parents, teachers and members of several opposition parties protested outside the education ministry.
Luciana Almeida, 18, would have attended the protest but she lives and studies in Penafiel, a three-and-a-half-hour drive from Lisbon. Almeida said she had not received a grade for the Portuguese exam she took in June. After her classmates received theirs, she discovered her paper had got lost in a pile of undigitised exams and she had been forced to repeat the test.
“I worked hard and I feel cheated because they lost my test,” said Almeida. “I feel at a disadvantage compared with others. And it will be hard for me to trust the new results … These college applications won’t be fair. It’s our future that’s at stake and the ministry of education is ruining it.”
Last week, an embattled Alexandre announced that students affected by software errors would not be awarded less than the minimum pass mark. But some teachers are not happy about that decision, saying in some cases it will unfairly affect students’ college applications.
And many parents remain furious. Rita Reino, 53, president of the parents’ association of Camões high school in Lisbon, said: “At this stage there is no fair solution. The state has violated the principles of equality and fairness. We want to hold the state accountable; we want to sue the state.”
The fiasco is proving politically damaging for the government, although the prime minister, Luís Montenegro, has so far resisted calls to fire Alexandre. A recent survey found that seven out of 10 Portuguese are deeply unhappy with the government and cite the exam debacle as one of the leading causes of dissatisfaction.
In a statement, the education ministry acknowledged that the “disruptions in implementation” had caused “instability in the education system and anxiety among students and families”, which it said it regretted.
It added: “Despite the constraints of the first phase, the process is now proceeding in the second phase without significant problems, and on the third day of grading more than 65% of the tests had already been graded.”
Asked about the calls for Alexandre to resign, the ministry said: “Calls for resignation are part of the public, political and democratic debate. However, given the situation, the priority of the ministry of education was to identify the problems, correct them quickly, and ensure that no student is harmed in their school career or access to higher education.”

title: Friday briefing: Why attacks on hospitals from Ukraine to Lebanon now happen with impunity
summary:
In today’s newsletter: ​The legal protections once considered foundational ​in conflict are now routinely bypassed​,​ with healthcare personnel treated as legitimate targets

Good morning. While you were asleep, Donald Trump claimed a deal had been reached for the “complete disarmament of Hamas” in Gaza. His announcement, characteristically, does not seem watertight, with briefings from both sides revealing points of contention, and as such is being treated with caution by some world leaders.

That label now feels almost obsolete on the global stage, as laws are ignored, norms tossed aside, and multinational institutions degraded.

full_text:
Good morning. While you were asleep, Donald Trump claimed a deal had been reached for the “complete disarmament of Hamas” in Gaza. His announcement, characteristically, does not seem watertight, with briefings from both sides revealing points of contention, and as such is being treated with caution by some world leaders.
As anyone paying attention knows, the conflict has seen Israel and Hamas accused of war crimes, and two years ago, the international criminal court issued an arrest warrant for Benjamin Netanyahu. Elsewhere in the region, the Israel-US military operation in Iran has been repeatedly declared as “illegal”. That label now feels almost obsolete on the global stage, as laws are ignored, norms tossed aside, and multinational institutions degraded.
Cynics might suggest nothing new here; that the international rules-based order has always been illusory, wielded by the powerful to be followed (and disregarded) at will, to suit self-serving whims and ambitions. But even the mirage appears to have faded. And nowhere is this more acutely felt than in conflict zones, by those who are unwell or injured – and the healthcare workers treating them, in particular.
For today’s First Edition, we ask how this deathly reality came to be. Beirut-based Guardian reporter William Christou reflects on Israel’s ongoing campaign of attacks on Lebanese healthcare workers, and we ask Natasha Sax – a legal expert with Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), who has worked in Gaza, Iraq and Lebanon – why international law is failing. Before that, today’s top stories.
Five big stories
- 
  England news | Hundreds of people have been evacuated and a major incident declared after a wildfire spread over more than 80 hectares (200 acres) on the coast of Suffolk, just a few miles from the Sizewell B nuclear power station. 
- 
  UK politics | Labour has accused Reform UK of being “up to its neck in sleaze” as it called on the Electoral Commission to urgently investigate substantial donations made to the party by the mother of a convicted fraudster. 
- 
  Middle East | Donald Trump has said a deal has been reached for Hamas to disarm and for Israel to withdraw its forces from Gaza, however briefings from both sides exposed disputes over its implementation that could prove difficult to overcome. 
- 
  Europe | The Spanish government is deploying extra troops and police officers to its north African enclave of Ceuta after thousands of people swam and waded into the tiny territory from neighbouring Morocco in a matter of hours. 
- 
  UK news | The co-founder of Palestine Action has won permission to challenge the ban against the group at the UK’s highest court. 
In depth: ‘When international agencies withdraw, local medics remain’
Palestine tops the list of countries with the most healthcare workers killed in the past five years. There, Israel’s relentless attacks on Gaza’s medical infrastructure are well documented. Lebanon ranks second, with 569. It’s a subject William has covered extensively, his latest report turning to the psychological impact on medics and their families.
Countries with the most healthcare workers killed since 2021
During the last two wars in Lebanon, William tells me, Israel’s targeting of healthcare workers has been “consistent”. Since fighting escalated again this March, at least 135 Lebanese medics have been killed, with nearly 400 others injured. Including the last war in 2024, the death toll is close to 400.
Particularly common are “double-taps”: Israel striking a target, waiting for paramedics to arrive, then striking again. “In April there was a quadruple tap,” William says. In Mayfadoun, southern Lebanon, paramedics responded to the injured after an Israeli airstrike. “That team was hit,” says William. “Another team went out. They were also hit. Another crew went: hit, again.” Four medics were killed, and six wounded.
Southern Lebanon has borne the brunt, where Israel has been conducting what UN-appointed human rights experts describe as forced displacement. “The way healthcare officials put it to me,” William says, “is that it’s an attempt to degrade the ability to sustain life in these areas, similar to what’s been seen in Gaza, so the population leaves for ever.”
When international agencies withdraw, local medics remain long after.
“They stay, knowing the risk of death,” says William. “Some die, others watch their colleagues be killed.” A group of medics he met attempted to figure out the criteria Israel uses to target them. “It was impossible, so they gave up eventually.”
Many of them are unpaid. “One man I spoke to recently said that after the 2024 war, he promised he’d never do it again. But this time, he couldn’t stop himself from volunteering. There’s a sense of duty to their communities.”
William remembers many of their stories. There’s Hafez Yahya, a civil defence medic killed by an Israeli drone strike in May. He’d been a volunteer for 25 years. “I also met Mohammed Suleiman,” says William, “whose 16-year-old son Joud was one of three paramedics killed by an Israeli drone strike in March while bringing food to people in Nabatieh.”
They were wearing paramedic uniforms. It’s inconceivable.
Countries with most attacks on healthcare
Just 10 years ago, the United Nations security council condemned the “prevailing impunity” for attacks on medics, hospitals and other healthcare facilities in conflicts, urging they not “remain unpunished”. A decade on, the situation has deteriorated. Hospitals and medics are under attack; in Ukraine, in Sudan, in Gaza, in Lebanon, in Myanmar and far beyond in unprecedented numbers.
I ask Natasha Sax if these attacks are the result of gaps in international law. “Not at all,” she tells me. Healthcare in conflict zones is governed by international humanitarian law (IHL), “one of the most comprehensive and densely codified bodies of law anywhere”.
The legal framework for protecting hospitals, medical workers and ambulances is set out in the Geneva conventions, signed in 1949 by every internationally recognised state in the wake of the second world war. “Such universal agreement is basically unheard of in international law,” says Natasha. “The issue is a lack of will to implement it.”
Enshrined in law
IHL is clear: medical units such as hospitals and pharmacies – their patients, too – have special legal status. Parties have a duty to respect (not attack or actively harm) and protect: a positive obligation to ensure they can function. On the ground, Natasha says, this simply isn’t happening. “Mass displacement orders stopping access, local water and sewage systems destroyed, besieging, raiding and turning hospitals to rubble? We see all of this today – clear violations.”
There are narrow exceptions to these rules. Even then, harm to civilians and infrastructure must be proportional to military advantage gained; the impact on patients (present and future) must be considered. Evacuation warnings are a must, weapons and methods that minimise harm … the list continues.
All of this, Natasha says, is ignored today with alarming regularity. She points to Gaza. Here, half of hospitals are totally non-functional, the remaining 18 only operating partially. The consequences for the civilian population are both present and future.
Medical personnel are covered by IHL too: entitled to work, protected from acting against medical ethics, or punishment for providing assistance. The law dictates everyone is entitled to healthcare in conflict zones, whether civilian or previously fighting: in a medic’s care, all are patients. “IHL guarantees the workers who treat them are protected. Except, in many conflicts, we are seeing them killed, arrested, detained and persecuted.”
This is no accident
In the last 10 years, MSF recorded 255 security incidents, of which 107 took place in medical facilities. These increases are reflected in wider WHO data. Globally, incidents have more than doubled since 2021.

title: Middle East crisis live: Trump claims Gaza deal reached; Iran targets US bases in Kuwait
summary:
Response from Hamas and Israeli officials suggest Gaza deal still faces obstacles; Tehran launches drone strikes at Kuwait in retaliation for recent US attacks

  • Trump claims agreement for ‘complete disarmament’ of Hamas in Gaza but support uncertain

  • Saudi Arabia prepares sea and possible land offensive against Houthis

We are getting some of the first international reactions of the supposed Gaza deal announced by Donald Trump.

In the UK, Louise Haigh, who runs the new office of the prime minister, said any progress in peace negotiations is “extremely welcome” while the government awaits Israel’s response.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Middle East crisis live: Trump claims Gaza deal reached; Iran targets US bases in Kuwait
Response from Hamas and Israeli officials suggest Gaza deal still faces obstacles; Tehran launches drone strikes at Kuwait in retaliation for recent US attacks
Donald Trump claims a deal has been reached for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its forces from Gaza, but many hurdles and conditions remained in the Palestinian territory.
“The agreement will be carried out in carefully structured phases,” the US president said on social media. “As disarmament is completed, Israeli forces will withdraw, and the International Stabilization Force will work with a new Palestinian police force to take responsibility for Gaza being safe for its residents and its neighbors.”
Senior Hamas officials have reportedly agreed to the plan, but the question of whether the group disarms before or after Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza has already emerged as a point of contention. “We will not take any action regarding disarmament prior to Israel’s withdrawal from the Strip,” Ghazi Hamad, a member of the Hamas negotiating team, told Al Jazeera.
Earlier an Israeli official told the Reuters news agency that the proposed terms were not satisfactory.
“Israel demands the complete disarmament of Hamas, including the removal of weapons from Gaza and the complete demilitarisation of the Strip as a precondition for any process,” the official said, adding that the plan under discussion did not “provide a satisfactory response to these demands and Israel conveyed its objections”.
The announcement comes nine months after a US-brokered ceasefire was signed. Negotiations between Israel and Hamas had largely deadlocked over the implementation of its second phase, including the disarmament of Hamas and the reconstruction of Gaza.
In the US-Israeli war on Iran, which is showing signs of escalating across the region, Iran’s army on Friday launched drone strikes at US military facilities at the Ahmad Al Jaber airbase in Kuwait. The strikes were in response to recent US attacks on Iran including a strike on a home in Qeshm, Iran’s state media reported.
And Saudi Arabia is preparing for a major military offensive against the Houthis by sea and possibly by land in central Yemen, Yemeni sources believe, in a move to break the chokehold on its oil exports through the southern Red Sea.
In other developments:
Twenty-five commodities vessels passed through the Bab el-Mandeb strait on Thursday, while traffic through the strait of Hormuz remained low with only two tankers transiting, according to Kpler shipping data.
Analysts are expecting major oil companies to report large profits while fighting between Iran and the US impeded petroleum shipments. Six of Europe’s largest oil companies have posted first-quarter profits of $22bn altogether, a total 43% higher than the same time last year, according to Global Witness.
Saudi Arabia on Thursday said it had set up a maritime defence alliance of 14 regional countries to secure navigation around the Bab al-Mandab strait.
An Iranian strike hit a Chinese firm’s building in Kuwait on Thursday, severely damaging the structure and killing a worker, Kuwait’s military said, hours after Jordan’s air defences shot down five missiles launched from Iran.
Egypt’s government said on Thursday authorities were analysing drone fragments from an unprecedented strike on one of its ports, after President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi warned of regional escalation. His government had earlier confirmed that a fire on two gas vessels in the Damietta port – one of which was US-owned – was a result of a drone strike, the first to target the country since the outbreak of the Middle East war.
Reuters has issued some news alerts after speaking to a Hamas official about the next phase of the Gaza ceasefire, including disarmament.
The news agency reported the official saying Israel must withdraw its forces from Gaza, and that if it does not approve the accord then Hamas will not implement it.Israel has yet to publicly say anything about the deal.
Hamas disarmament news 'extremely welcome,' says Louise Haigh
We are getting some of the first international reactions of the supposed Gaza deal announced by Donald Trump.
In the UK, Louise Haigh, who runs the new office of the prime minister, said any progress in peace negotiations is “extremely welcome” while the government awaits Israel’s response.
“It’s extremely welcome news if there has been any progress in the peace negotiations and any step forward to disarming Hamas,” she told BBC Breakfast.
“Obviously, we will need to await the Israeli government’s response and its commitment to the ceasefire and a way forward and a withdrawal from Gaza, and to cease its activities of settler violence and taking action against such settler violence in the West Bank.
“But if progress has been made, then it’s extremely welcome news, because the suffering in Gaza and the wider region has been too extreme for far too long, and the human cost of the war has been absolutely obscene and intolerable.”
She added: “We’re awaiting the response from the Israeli government, so we’ll set out the details in due course of our wider government response.”
'Massive' blasts reported in southern Lebanon as IDF bombs 'Hezbollah tunnels' near Beaufort Castle
Meanwhile, in Lebanon, local media reported “massive explosions” overnight in the southern parts of the country, where Israeli forces say they have blasted an underground tunnel network belonging to Hezbollah.
Lebanon’s official National News Agency (NNA) reported explosions in Yahmar al-Shaqif, Arnoun and Kfar Tebnit, all areas close to the Beaufort Ridge that is occupied by the Israeli military.
The explosions began at about midnight and “reverberated with tremendous and unprecedented force throughout the entire south”, NNA reported.
A correspondent for the news agency said the blasts near Beaufort Castle, the 900-year-old castle and strategic ridge captured by Israeli troops in May, had “caused the windows of a number of houses in the town of al-Qlailah to shatter, due to the force of the blasts and the tremors felt by residents across the region”.
The report added: “The explosions caused damage to some homes, while residents reported that the sound of the blasts was intense, accompanied by a powerful shock wave that shook the town, as well as the smell of gunpowder in the air.”
In a post on X, the Israel Defense Force (IDF) said it “destroyed several key features in the underground tunnel network” in the Beaufort Ridge area. It claimed that the tunnel network, located about 6km (just under 4 miles) from the Israeli town of Metula across the border, was built over 20 years and consisted of several levels, serving as a “central terror headquarters for [Hezbollah’s] “Badir” unit in southern Lebanon, which was funded and planned by the Iranian terror regime”.
“The existence of the infrastructure posed a threat to the residents of the north [of Israel] and to our forces,” the IDF said.
“Over the past weeks, IDF forces have completed their hold on the Beaufort Ridge area, while controlling and clearing the underground infrastructures and preparing them for destruction.”
More now on Iran’s military saying it launched drone strikes targeting US military facilities in Kuwait on Friday, as fighting between Washington and Tehran resumed after a nearly week-long lull.
The army said it targeted “fighter aircraft shelters, satellite communications systems and equipment storage facilities at Ahmad al-Jaber air base in Kuwait”.
There was no immediate comment from the US military’s Central Command.
The Iranian army said in a statement the strikes came in response to US military’s recent aggression and “brutal attack” on a residential home on Qeshm Island, Agence France-Presse reports.
Local media reported on Thursday that three members of a family were killed in US strikes on the island in the strait of Hormuz.

title: New York sues Kalshi, alleges it offers a gambling platform 'plain and simple'
full_text:
New York sues Kalshi, alleges it offers a gambling platform 'plain and simple'
The suit wants to bar the company from operating what it says is an unlicensed gambling business and seeks financial redress.
- New York State sued prediction-market platform Kalshi, accusing it of running an unlicensed gambling business and seeking to bar it from operating in the state.
- Attorney General Letitia James said Kalshi’s event contracts are illegal bets, including on sports, elections and culture, and alleges the platform allows underage wagering.
- The lawsuit, filed in the New York Supreme Court, seeks triple Kalshi’s gains, $100,000 per unauthorized or attempted wager offer and a full accounting of customer bets, losses and company profits.
New York sued prediction-market Kalshi, alleging it offers sports and event wagers in the state without a gaming license.
The petition, filed in the New York Supreme Court on Friday, asks a judge to bar the company from operating an unlicensed gambling business and seeks an accounting of customer bets, losses and company gains, plus restitution, damages and civil penalties.
The state is seeking a penalty equal to three times Kalshi’s gains from the activity, plus $100,000 for each unauthorized or attempted offer of sports or mobile sports wagering, according to a statement published by Governor Kathy Hochul and Attorney General Letitia James.
Kalshi, which targeted a $40 billion valuation during a June funding round, and the prediction markets sector are facing legal challenges across the U.S. In Minnesota, Kalshi and rival Polymarket scored a temporary win when the U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota ruled the state’s law banning prediction markets likely runs afoul of the Commodity Exchange Act, and granted a preliminary injunction against the law to the two companies and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.
James’ office described Kalshi’s event contracts as bets and said the platform takes wagers on professional and college sports, elections and culture. The lawsuit alleges Kalshi allows users aged 18 to 20 to wager and lists markets involving New York college teams, both prohibited for licensed sportsbooks in the state.
“New York’s gambling laws protect children from underage betting and help combat gambling addiction,” James said in the statement. "No matter what they call themselves, prediction markets like Kalshi are gambling platforms, plain and simple."
The World Cup helped boost Kalshi's numbers, adding 3 million during the course of the tournament, according to CNBC. That's more than double the 2 million the firm said it had at the start of May.
According to the attorney general’s statement, the lawsuit follows an October cease-and-desist order from the New York State Gaming Commission.
A federal judge denied Kalshi’s bid to block state regulators on July 7 and rejected an injunction pending appeal on July 27.
CoinDesk approached Kalshi for comment outside of regular U.S. office hours, and had not heard back by publication time.

title: Quantum Solutions, Hyperscale Data tap crypto treasuries to fund AI data centers
full_text:
Quantum Solutions, Hyperscale Data tap crypto treasuries to fund AI data centers
The firm’s board raised the sale cap to 4,375 ETH through Oct. 30, nearly 66% of June holdings, although 3,050 of its remaining ETH is pledged.
- Tokyo-listed Quantum Solutions sold 1,000 ETH for $1.9M, taking its sales since June to 1,904 ETH, or 29% of its starting balance.
- The firm’0s board raised the sale cap to 4,375 ETH through Oct. 30, nearly 66% of June holdings, although 3,050 of its remaining ETH is pledged.
- Another crypto treasury firm Hyperscale Data monetized about 100 BTC and opened a bitcoin-backed credit facility at a 4.5%-5% rate to fund its Michigan AI campus.
Tokyo-listed Quantum Solutions (2338) sold 1,000 ETH for $1.9 million and more than doubled its disposal ceiling to fund an AI data center business.
The move came as another crypto treasury firm, Hyperscale Data (GPUS), monetized about 100 BTC and opened a bitcoin-backed credit line for a Michigan AI data center..
Quantum sold the ETH on July 30 at $1,903 per token, generating $1.903 million after fees, according to a company filing. It expects to recognize a $100,970 loss against the position’s May 31 carrying value of $2,003.97 per ETH, the filing adds.
The sale price was 47% below the $3,595.02 average acquisition cost Quantum reported in June.
The firm sold 904 ETH for $1.61 million on June 16 at an average price of $1,777 per token. The two disposals raised about $3.51 million and reduced its holdings by 29% to 4,764.8 ETH from 6,668.8 ETH.
Quantum’s board raised the cumulative sale limit to 4,375 ETH from 1,875 ETH through Oct. 30, leaving it authorized to sell another 2,471 ETH. Using the full limit would mean disposing of nearly 66% of the holdings it reported in June.
Of its remaining ETH, 3,050 tokens are pledged as collateral to an unnamed Singapore financial-services firm, while 1,714.8 ETH remain in a trading account. +
Based on the companies’ latest disclosures, the sale also cost Quantum its position as Japan’s largest listed ETH holder. Def Consulting reported holding 4,976 ETH as of June 30.
Quantum plans to use the proceeds for data center deposits, GPU servers, networking equipment and working capital. It signed a nonbinding agreement with Hong Kong-based Integrated Capital in June to explore a Japanese data center, though no investment amount, financing terms or timetable has been set.
Separately, NYSE American-listed Hyperscale Data said it monetized about 100 BTC and established a bitcoin-backed credit facility carrying an expected variable interest rate of 4.5% to 5%.

title: Bitcoin’s calm is back and so is the setup for a volatility explosion
full_text:
Bitcoin’s calm is back and so is the setup for a volatility explosion
Bitcoin’s daily price swings have tightened to their narrowest since January, making clean trades harder to find. Here's what could happen next.
- Bitcoin trading has entered one of its quietest stretches since January, with prices largely stuck between $62,000 and $65,000.
- Bollinger bandwidth on bitcoin’s daily price chart has tightened to the narrowest since the start of the year, signaling a significant squeeze in volatility.
- Such prolonged periods of tight trading ranges have historically preceded sharp moves in bitcoin’s price, though the direction of the next big move is uncertain.
Trading bitcoin 
The price of the largest cryptocurrency is stuck in a tight range, with volatility at six-month lows, and traders are struggling to identify a break to bet on. Not surprisingly, transaction volume has slumped and is on track for the lowest since November 2023.
Back in January, the bitcoin price had been stuck in a narrow band, $86,000-$90,000, since the second half of December. Trading volume had dropped to an average of $5.1 billion a day, and has fallen to $2.2 billion this month, according to research from K33.
What happened next is interesting. Volatility picked up in the following weeks, the price rose to nearly $98,000 by mid-January and then slid down to around $60,000 by early February. Trading volume rose.
And that’s precisely the point. Volatility is cyclical: long stretches of quiet price action often precede a sharp move in one direction or the other. Like a coiled spring, the tighter the market compresses, the more forcefully it can unwind.
To see what that looks like, consider bitcoin’s Bollinger bands on the chart above. These are lines drawn at two standard deviations above and below the cryptocurrency’s price. They measure the extent of the price’s daily swing, its volatility, and the gap between them is now at the narrowest since January.
When Bollinger bands get this tight, momentum trades dry up and range traders have to settle for tiny price moves. For anyone who thrives on bigger swings, the market is simply refusing to cooperate. The Bollinger bandwidth indicator in the lower pane has dropped to 5.66 points.
BTC’s price action has largely mirrored this cyclical volatility pattern since at least 2018.
While the timing can’t be assured, the current squeeze is likely to be followed by a decisive move. Direction is never guaranteed, meaning the break could go either way, but the calm itself tends to be temporary. The longer the lull persists, the more forceful the eventual breakout could be.

title: New York sues Kalshi over alleged illegal gambling operation
summary: The lawsuit adds to a growing clash between New York and the CFTC over whether federally regulated prediction markets are subject to state gambling laws.
full_text:
New York sues Kalshi over alleged illegal gambling operation
The lawsuit adds to a growing clash between New York and the CFTC over whether federally regulated prediction markets are subject to state gambling laws.
New York has sued prediction market platform Kalshi, alleging it operates an illegal, unlicensed gambling business by offering event contracts on sports, elections and other outcomes.
The lawsuit seeks to stop Kalshi’s alleged illegal gambling operation in the state, require the company to forfeit illegal gains, pay restitution to users and pay civil penalties equal to three times those gains.
“No matter what they call themselves, prediction markets like Kalshi are gambling platforms, plain and simple,” Attorney General Letitia James said in Friday’s statement. “We are taking them to court to uphold our laws and protect New Yorkers.”
The lawsuit comes after the New York State Gaming Commission issued Kalshi a cease-and-desist order in October 2025, prompting the company to sue the regulator in federal court.
A judge denied Kalshi’s request for a preliminary injunction in July, and an appeals court later rejected its bid to block enforcement while the appeal proceeds.
Kalshi did not immediately respond to Cointelegraph’s request for comment.
CFTC defends federal oversight of prediction markets
The lawsuit adds to an escalating jurisdictional dispute over whether event contracts offered by federally regulated prediction markets are subject to state gambling laws.
Just before New York filed its case, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) filed an emergency motion seeking to block New York’s enforcement efforts, arguing that the state’s actions interfere with the agency’s exclusive authority under the Commodity Exchange Act to regulate designated contract markets like Kalshi.
Related: CFTC issues second warning to prediction markets on cookie-cutter self-certifications
The CFTC has taken similar positions in disputes involving at least nine states, arguing that allowing states to prohibit event contracts listed by federally regulated exchanges would create conflicting state rules and undermine federal commodities regulation.
Prediction markets continue to gain mainstream traction
Prediction markets allow users to buy and sell contracts tied to the outcome of future events, with prices reflecting the market’s estimate of the probability that an event will occur.
Kalshi’s rival, Polymarket, has also faced regulatory scrutiny, with several countries restricting or investigating its operations over gambling and licensing concerns.
Kalshi began expanding into blockchain-based infrastructure in December 2025, launching tokenized prediction markets on Solana and later adding support for multiple blockchain networks.
The broader prediction market sector has also grown alongside major sporting events.
According to analytics firm Chainalysis, blockchain-based prediction markets processed about $20 billion in trading tied to the 2026 FIFA World Cup, with more than 400,000 wallets participating.

title: Aave weighs closing 6 V3 blockchain markets, offboarding 50 low-use reserves
summary: DeFi risk management service LlamaRisk recommended that Aave wind down every reserve on Sonic, Scroll, zkSync, Metis, Soneium and Aptos, but action against most of those instances was already taken.
full_text:
Aave weighs closing 6 V3 blockchain markets, offboarding 50 low-use reserves
DeFi risk management service LlamaRisk recommended that Aave wind down every reserve on Sonic, Scroll, zkSync, Metis, Soneium and Aptos, but action against most of those instances was already taken.
An Aave governance proposal would wind down the lending protocol’s V3 markets on six blockchains and retire dozens of low-use token listings, a cleanup covering $98.1 million in supplied assets and $15.6 million in debt.
Risk service provider LlamaRisk, working with other Aave service providers, recommended offboarding 50 low-use reserves and 21 matured Pendle principal token listings across 11 deployments. It also proposed retiring all 25 reserves on Sonic, Scroll, zkSync, Metis, Soneium and Aptos. The balances were measured on July 28.
An ARFC is a detailed proposal and precursor to an Aave Improvement Proposal; it is not, by itself, proof of a completed final onchain vote or execution.
Aptos exit follows recent launch
The proposed Aptos exit comes just 11 months after Aave launched its V3 market there, with available liquidity down 94% over six months and quarterly revenue below $1,000, according to LlamaRisk.
Every reserve on Scroll, zkSync, Metis and Soneium was already frozen, whereas Sonic and Aptos remained active and are recommended for freezing. The temp check on Aave’s multichain strategy concluded on Dec. 5, 2025, with 923,400 votes in favor and under 1% against increasing the reserve factor on underperforming instances, shutting down the instances on zkSync, Metis and Soneium, and establishing a $2 million annual revenue floor for new instance deployment.
Related: Aave positioned to capture tokenized asset growth in DeFi: Standard Chartered
Scroll was then added to the affected protocols through an accelerated process in April, as LlamaRisk filed a direct-to-AIP proposal to freeze every Scroll reserve and raise selected reserve factors, describing the measure as completing Scroll’s deprecation after a rapid deterioration in network liquidity and Aave market activity. Aave also published an updated risk framework on June 9, covering asset, bridge, monitoring and chain risk and criteria for winding down reserves or deployments, and this month’s announcement indicated de facto adoption of those rules by the protocol.
Source: Stani Kulechov
Aave founder Stani Kulechov said in a Thursday post that this will also “reduce Aave’s economic and technical risk surface as part of the new Aave Risk Framework and Technical Asset Listing Framework.”
Related: Aave brings V3 lending and GHO stablecoin to Monad
Still, this is not a reversal of Aave’s multichain expansion strategy, rather a strategic refocusing on select protocols. “Aave will continue applying continuous risk assessment for all assets across all deployments,” Kulechov said. The comments also follow Aave launching on Avalanche earlier this month.
