title: US Senate’s Fauci hearing renews COVID origin debate but reveals little
summary: Hearing underscores years-long partisan divide on lightning-rod issue fuelled by misleading White House claims.
full_text:
US Senate’s Fauci hearing renews COVID origin debate but reveals little
Hearing underscores years-long partisan divide on lightning-rod issue fuelled by misleading White House claims.
Washington, DC – A Senate committee hearing this week has once again shone a spotlight on the political divisions over the United States government’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic.
Wednesday’s hearing, held by the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, continued years of criticism, mainly from Republicans, against immunologist Anthony Fauci, who led the government’s response to the pandemic.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3An AIDS-free generation is within reach, but not guaranteed
- list 2 of 3Todd Blanche’s loyalty to Trump questioned in Senate confirmation hearing
- list 3 of 3Hakeem Jeffries puts affordability at centre of Democrats’ midterm campaign
Spearheaded by committee chair Rand Paul, several Republicans rehashed claims that the virus that causes COVID-19, SARS-CoV-2, emerged from an infectious disease lab in Wuhan, China, and did not naturally transfer from animals to humans.
Stephen Morrison, the director of the Global Health Policy Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said the hearing was a reflection of the deep, enduring partisan divides over the issue.
But he added that the meeting with Fauci did little to shed new light on the pandemic after years of investigation, hearings and political posturing.
“There’s no space for any civil discussion around any of these issues. There’s no desire really,” Morrison told Al Jazeera.
“So, what’s the lasting impact of this? I mean, it continues to impose unconscionable pain and suffering on [Fauci] and his family. It doesn’t advance the debate one inch on the whole question of COVID origins and what was past US policy and what should US policy be going forward.”
Wuhan lab leak theory
Wednesday’s hearing was based largely on a previous 520-page report from 2024, created by the Republican-led Select Subcommittee on the Coronavirus Pandemic.
That report claimed it was likely that SARS-CoV-2 emerged from the Wuhan Institute of Virology, a Chinese research facility. Senator Paul has embraced this viewpoint, as has President Donald Trump.
In April of last year, shortly after Trump took office for his second term, the White House launched a webpage purporting to reveal “the true origins of COVID-19”, largely based on the report.
The site highlighted several claims that experts say pave over the nuanced scientific debate about the origins of the virus.
Drawing on the 2024 report, the White House asserts that SARS-CoV-2 “possesses a biological characteristic that is not found in nature” and that “data shows that all COVID-19 cases stem from a single introduction into humans”, setting it apart from previous natural pandemics.
Joel Wertheim, a professor of medicine at the University of California San Diego, told Factcheck.org that both claims were false.
While COVID does contain a characteristic to enter cells that is not found in its closest coronavirus relatives, that quality does exist in other coronaviruses more broadly. As Wertheim put it, “It is most certainly found in nature.”
Meanwhile, a pair of studies released in 2022 found at least two unique paths through which initial human infection occurred, contradicting the White House’s claim that the pandemic arose from a “single introduction into humans”.
The White House webpage also focuses on Fauci, who led the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) until 2022 and served as the chief medical adviser to former US President Joe Biden, Trump’s election rival.
Biden pre-emptively pardoned him in January 2025, fearing the physician might be arrested under the second Trump administration.
Ahead of Wednesday’s hearing, Trump took the opportunity to renew his derision of Fauci, writing on Truth Social that the medical expert’s “ideas were CRAZY”.
Trump also accused Fauci, without evidence, of orchestrating a cover-up for China, where COVID was first documented. The Republican leader was serving his first term as president when the pandemic began.
Ongoing debate
To be sure, there has been criticism from within the international scientific community that the lab leak theory was discounted too swiftly in the early days of the pandemic, as it became seen as political.
Trump and other world leaders had been quick to use anti-China rhetoric when discussing the virus.
There currently remains no conclusive evidence proving either the lab leak theory or that the virus had a natural origin. The vast majority of infectious disease scientists, including Fauci, have said neither possibility can be ruled out.
Still, a preponderance of experts say evidence indicates that the virus was most likely transferred from an animal, likely a bat, to humans, in a process called zoonotic spillover.
A 2024 survey of virologists and other scientists, conducted by the Global Catastrophic Risk Institute (GCRI), found most respondents believed natural transmission was considerably more likely than a lab leak, although most acknowledged it was impossible to definitively dismiss the theory.
Following three years of research, a World Health Organization (WHO) advisory board released a report in 2025 that also concluded “the weight of available evidence … suggests zoonotic spillover”.
Still, WHO director Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus cautioned, “As things stand, all hypotheses must remain on the table, including zoonotic spillover and lab leak.”
Inside Fauci’s diary
Fauci has long argued the scientific evidence indicates that the virus emerged from natural animal transmission, but he has repeatedly rejected the notion that he has outright dismissed the lab leak theory.
In a 2024 letter to the House Subcommittee on the Coronavirus Pandemic, his lawyers maintained (PDF) it was “completely wrong” to say that Fauci had ever called the possibility a “conspiracy theory”.
Instead, they said Fauci and his allies rejected an array of conspiracy theories that have been tied to the lab leak theory, including the idea that he had “sneaked unnoticed into the CIA headquarters to try to convince CIA officials to debunk the lab leak theory”.
Wednesday’s hearing was preceded by the release of entries from Fauci’s private diary, stored on a government computer drive.
They were obtained through Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, a vaccine sceptic and Fauci critic, who passed them along to Senator Paul.
In one entry, Fauci described a claim that he “deliberately” worked with the Chinese to create the virus as a “way-out conspiracy theory”.
He and his legal team have also repeatedly rejected Republican claims that he leveraged millions in grant money to compel scientists to change their views about COVID’s origins.
The White House website, for instance, asserts that Fauci “prompted” an early study on COVID origins to downplay the lab leak theory. No evidence has been presented to support those claims, which have also been rejected by the scientists involved.
Did Fauci mislead?
On Wednesday, several Senate Republicans charged that Fauci’s diary entries showed he had intentionally misled the public by downplaying the possibility the virus had emerged from the Wuhan lab.
Fauci’s supporters, however, have said the diary fails to prove any deliberate attempt to mislead. They argue his public and private statements were consistent in the early days of the pandemic, when scientists’ understanding of the virus was shifting daily.
Fauci’s diary entries indicated he met with a group of experts in February 2020, noting “there was not total agreement” on the likelihood the virus had been created via human manipulation. Senator Paul and others said Fauci did not adequately reflect that view in his public statements.

title: Pathirage beats Chopra and Nadeem to win Commonwealth gold in javelin
summary: Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage wins gold, while Neeraj Chopra takes silver, but Arshad Nadeem makes early exit.
full_text:
Pathirage beats Chopra and Nadeem to win Commonwealth gold in javelin
Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage wins gold, while Neeraj Chopra takes silver, but Arshad Nadeem ,makes early exit.
Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage made history with Sri Lanka’s first gold medal in athletics when he saw off a strong field to win the 2026 Commonwealth Games javelin final.
The 23-year-old faced the daunting prospect in Glasgow of battling the great Pakistan and India pairing of Arshad Nadeem and Neeraj Chopra, so long the top two in the discipline.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Why is UEFA threatening FIFA boycott? Infantino’s World Cup plan explained
- list 2 of 4FIFA COO Lamour says staff deceived over Infantino’s World Cup plan
- list 3 of 4FIFA studying impact of expanding World Cup to 64 teams for 2030 edition
- list 4 of 4Infantino’s plan to sell stakes in the FIFA World Cup: All to know
Nadeem, the defending champion who also won Olympic gold at Paris 2024, made a shock early exit after three throws on a blustery evening at Scotstoun Stadium.
The going wasn’t much easier for Pathirage, who only registered one legitimate throw in his first five efforts.
That, however, was enough to seal the gold with a throw of 89.75 metres.
Chopra put an injury-plagued year behind him to secure silver with a season best of 85.83, while his compatriot, Yash Vir Singh, threw a personal best of 85.41 to claim bronze.
Five of the finalists had thrown more than 90 metres in their career, including world champion Keshorn Walcott. The Trinidad and Tobago star struggled with his first five throws and only managed 82.55 metres with his last to place sixth.
Pathirage started off as a fast bowler in cricket, where he was clocked – as a teenager – at a speed of 134 kilometres per hour (83 miles per hour).
The record speed registered in cricket was 161.3km/h (100.2mph), bowled by Pakistan great Shoaib Akhtar, who held the nickname ‘The Rawalpindi Express’.
Sri Lankan cricket’s loss has clearly been the gain of the rest of the nation.

title: Children face higher threat of US deportation as legal support deal expires
summary: Advocates warn expiring contract could leave 24,000 children without legal representation, increasing risk of expulsion.
full_text:
Children face higher threat of US deportation as legal support deal expires
Advocates warn expiring contract could leave 24,000 children without legal representation, increasing risk of expulsion.
Immigration advocates have warned that children who entered the United States without documentation or a legal guardian could soon lose their legal representation.
That could lead to higher rates of deportation as a federal contract providing the service expired on Friday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Nine deaths tied to Trump’s immigration enforcement operations in US
- list 2 of 3ICE kills 26-year-old in Maine: What happened, and who else has ICE killed?
- list 3 of 3Trump urges ICE to keep using traffic stops after deadly incidents
“We have no understanding of what’s going to happen to those children come next week,” Melissa Lopez, the executive director of Estrella El Paso, said during a news conference earlier this week.
“We don’t know if they’re going to have legal representation. The government as of yet has not identified who will take over this representation,” Lopez said.
The expiring contract paid about 100 legal groups across the country to provide legal services to about 24,000 unaccompanied minors.
The contract allowed the groups to enter government-funded shelters as part of their representation. It was unclear what would happen after the contract expires, or if they would still be allowed to access their young clients.
The administration of US President Donald Trump has not said why it was allowing the contract to expire. The Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the care of unaccompanied children, did not reply to a request for comment from The Associated Press on what their policy would be going forward.
The change comes as the Trump administration has pursued a mass deportation campaign, predicated, in part, on speeding up court processes to increase expulsions.
The organisations that spoke at the news conference this week also charged that the Trump administration has been withholding payments even before the contract’s expiration, while simultaneously demanding detailed information about their clients. The providers said they cannot ethically provide the information.
“They are clearly trying to destroy the program by grinding down the financial health of nonprofits. We’ve seen layoffs and furloughs, and we will see a lot more of that if these invoices aren’t paid,” said Michael Lukens, the executive director of the Amica Center.
Several laws seek to protect unaccompanied children, including the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008, which says the government should facilitate legal representation for children put into deportation proceedings.
Beyond asylum, unaccompanied children can also apply for a special protected status if they cannot return to their home country due to abuse or neglect.
Two Democratic members of the House of Representatives from Pennsylvania, Chris Deluzio and Summer Lee, sent a letter to the US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr and Acting Director of the Office of Refugee Resettlement Angie Salazar earlier this week asking for further details on the contract expiration.
In particular, the letter asked how the government will “ensure its compliance with statutory language and court order requiring that unaccompanied children receive legal services”.
In a statement, Lee said that “children, many of which have fled violence and exploitation, should not be forced to appear in court alone without representation”.

title: Will US or China win the next war? That’s the wrong question to ask
summary:
Who will win the next war? That is the question posed on the cover of the latest Foreign Affairs magazine which explores, among other things, the US-China military and technological rivalry. At its core is a clash of strategic philosophies between the US-led order and China’s world view, which has propelled the latter’s rise to the world’s second great power.
The magazine’s contributors reflect a deeply ingrained Western strategic tradition, rooted in liberal realism, that says that the United...
full_text:
Will US or China win the next war? That’s the wrong question to ask
We should be asking how we can avoid conflict and work towards ending mutual threats, such as climate change and human injustice
The magazine’s contributors reflect a deeply ingrained Western strategic tradition, rooted in liberal realism, that says that the United States must maintain its primacy to underwrite global stability, defend democracy and retain its financial, technological and military power. Any challenger is inherently revisionist.
Lead essayist Paul Scharre argues that new technologies in drones, artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics challenge not only America’s traditional air and naval power but also allow states such as Iran to conduct asymmetric warfare, which erodes US hard and soft power.
Former US Pacific commander Admiral Dennis Blair reinforces this view, arguing that China’s military build-up is not defensive but designed to overturn the status quo in East Asia. He advocates deterrence, using US alliances, forward deployments and technological leadership to guarantee regional stability.
Academics Michael Beckley and Hal Brands apply the Anglo-American strategic views of land-based “heartland” (introduced by British geographer Halford Mackinder) and coast-based “rimland” (developed by Dutch-American political scientist Nicholas Spykman) in framing the US-China contest as an age-old struggle between incumbent maritime powers consolidating their positions against land-based revisionists.
They correctly argue that the “autocratic axis” is united less by ideology than by a shared resentment of US dominance, while the democratic coalition is fractured by competing interests and sometimes opposite views on how to engage Beijing.

title: Missing Australian hiker found dead in Wyoming, officials say
summary:
Body of William Standish discovered in Teton mountains as investigators say fatal fall likely cause of death

A 28-year-old Australian hiker who lost contact with his family while hiking the Continental Divide Trail between Yellowstone and Grand Teton national parks in Wyoming has been found dead, according to authorities.

The man, identified as William Standish, was discovered by rescuers on Wednesday morning in the Wigwams, a series of rocky peaks on the west slope of the Teton mountain range, the Teton county coroner said. Investigators say it was likely he suffered a fatal fall.

Continue reading...
full_text:
A 28-year-old Australian hiker who lost contact with his family while hiking the Continental Divide Trail between Yellowstone and Grand Teton national parks in Wyoming has been found dead, according to authorities.
The man, identified as William Standish, was discovered by rescuers on Wednesday morning in the Wigwams, a series of rocky peaks on the west slope of the Teton mountain range, the Teton county coroner said. Investigators say it was likely he suffered a fatal fall.
Standish had been attempting a thru-hike of the Continental Divide Trail between the Yellowstone and Grand Teton national parks when he disappeared after contacting his family on 23 July, according to a statement from Teton county rescuers.
Evidence suggests Standish may have fallen from a steep ridgeline that separates Grand Teton and the Jedediah Smith wilderness, officials said.
Standish was discovered by a helicopter team after it spotted an orange backpack – and then saw his remains below the ridge.
His family said it had stopped receiving updates from him via a Garmin GPS device and Facebook Messenger on 23 July, leading to a search being mounted by Teton county rescue crews.
On 19 July, Standish gave an update from a location near Old Faithful, and described his planned route in the Tetons, Gros Ventre wilderness, the Wind River range, and the Divide Basin.
Four days later, the family received a Garmin check-in without coordinates or a message. There was also a Facebook Messenger video that they believe placed him in the Wigwams.
The Teton county search and rescue team said it “sends its sincere condolences to the family and friends of the deceased”. It also expressed gratitude to federal agencies who assisted in searching for Standish.
Standish had reportedly been following a popular thru-hike, or end-to-end through-hike, starting in Canada, the most northern point of the 3,100-mile Continental Divide Trail – which passes down through Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado, and New Mexico.
There have been other hiking-related deaths in North America recently.
The Colorado Sun reported that a 15-year-old boy died after being struck by lightning on the state’s Mount Blue Sky on Monday. Sheriff’s officials identified the boy as Levi Strobel. Four other people were seriously injured, including Levi’s younger brother.
In Arizona, a man died during a hike on Phoenix’s South Mountain. Richard Fletcher, 61, left his home early on Saturday morning. Investigators later said his death was consistent with a heat-related or medical event, authorities told local media.
A 62-year-old man died in New Hampshire when he suffered a medical emergency in the state’s Welch-Dickey trail in the White Mountains. He was evacuated by national guard helicopter and later pronounced dead, according to New Hampshire Public Radio.
Two hikers also died in Canada’s Banff national park. One was a woman in her 20s after falling from a mountain near Marvel Peak on Tuesday. Three days earlier, a 65-year-old from Calgary fell from Mount Temple, also in Banff, the CBC reported.

title: Trump Administration Amps Up Pressure On Senate To Confirm Todd Blanche As Attorney General
summary: Trump officials are urging the Senate to confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general as Republican holdouts threaten to derail his nomination.
full_text:
With just a week left before the Senate leaves for its August recess, the Trump Administration is increasing pressure on lawmakers to confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general.
The White House said in a press release on Friday that Blanche “should be confirmed by the U.S. Senate without delay.” The White House included statements from law enforcement organizations, state attorneys general, former Justice Department officials, and other groups that it said were “united in demanding [Blanche’s] expeditious confirmation.”
That same day, Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged the upper chamber to confirm Blanche before leaving Washington, D.C., to go on recess at the end of next week.
“Todd Blanche has been an invaluable partner in advancing President Trump’s agenda and as a result of his leadership at the Department of Justice, Americans are safer today,” Rubio said in a post on X. “The Senate should not leave for recess without confirming him as Attorney General.”
Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins also on Friday called on lawmakers to confirm Blanche.
“President Trump chose the right leader for @TheJusticeDept,” Rollins said in a post on X. “It’s time for the Senate to confirm Todd Blanche as Attorney General.”
Two senators in the President’s own party have threatened to pull their support of Blanche, saying that they want confirmation from the DOJ that the proposed $1.8 billion “Anti-Weaponization Fund,” which was part of a settlement agreement for Trump’s $10 billion lawsuit against the I.R.S. over the leak of his tax returns, has been eliminated.
Trump and Blanche have said that the fund, which would have provided compensation to people who claim that they were unfairly targeted by the government, is “dead.” But Sen. John Cornyn, a Republican from Texas who was one of the two holdout votes, said this week that he has not received written confirmation of that.
“This is about making sure that even if you’re the President of the United States, you don’t get favorable terms from the government in a settlement of a lawsuit that ordinary citizens would not get,” Cornyn said on Thursday. Cornyn lost his re-election run in his state’s Republican primary in May, to the President-backed challenger, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.
The Trump Administration’s renewed pressure on the Senate to push through Blanche’s confirmation comes a day after the President indicated he might pull the nomination.
“I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd’s name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office,” Trump said in a Truth Social post on Thursday, referring to the two Republican holdouts.
During his Cabinet meeting at Camp David on Friday, Trump said of Cornyn threatening to pull his support of Blanche: “I don’t really blame him, to be honest with you.”
“I endorsed his opponent,” Trump said. “The man that lost, the man that I didn’t endorse, has become very angry, and that’s ok.”
“I mean, I understand that,” he continued. “I probably would do the same thing.”

title: The Strait of Hormuz Is Exposing a Blind Spot in the Energy Transition
summary: Alternative fuels like jet fuel can help address the energy price volatility that has resulted from the Iran war.
full_text:
Every week brings more twists and turns to the war in Iran and the crisis that has kept the Strait of Hormuz, a key lane for fuel shipments, mostly closed. As the crisis has continued, electrification and non-fossil fuel power has received more and more attention. In the long run, electric vehicles can displace the oil that is refined into fuel for the internal combustion engine. And renewables can displace natural gas in the power sector. Largely missing from the public discussion is the opportunity to catalyze a broader shift to alternative fuels across sectors that can’t be electrified easily.
The closure of the Strait of Hormuz hasn’t just stopped the flow of natural gas and crude oil but has also simultaneously made it more difficult to get refined products—everything from jet fuel to cooking fuel—to market. In theory, both the rapid price increases and the present volatility should provide a strong incentive to invest in alternative fuels. The reality is more complicated. The same forces that make the case for alternative fuels also make it hard to invest right now.
There’s perhaps no better example to illustrate the challenge than jet fuel. Hundreds of thousands of barrels of jet fuel left the Strait of Hormuz every day before the crisis. In some places, including Europe, that supply had been central to keeping planes in the air. More than 40% of the continent’s jet fuel imports originated from the Persian Gulf last year, according to data from S&P Global.
Alternatives are already on the market. Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), an umbrella term for a wide range of fuel sources including everything from recycled cooking fuel to plant-based fuels, is blended with jet fuel in many parts of the world, bringing down carbon emissions from flying. But in recent years SAF has been anywhere from 3 to 5 times more expensive than conventional jet fuel. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has closed some of that gap leaving SAF prices closer to 1.5 to 2 times as expensive.
But, with higher fuel prices eating into airline profits, companies are now poorly positioned to take advantage of the moment. To facilitate SAF production, airlines typically agree to long-term agreements to purchase the fuel. With high levels of geopolitical uncertainty, this is not the moment for executives to commit to a price premium without a regulatory mandate. SAF may sound nice, but it remains unaffordable.
The refiners who make SAF, on the other hand, are enjoying record profit margins. But they, too, see too much uncertainty as prices fluctuate wildly. On earnings calls this summer they say they are more focused on improving operations and executing existing plans than investing in new projects.
At a national level, the thinking should be different. SAF is more expensive, but a government can now clearly see the differential as an energy security premium as well as a sustainability advantage. It’s well worth paying to protect the country’s economy in the event of a Hormuz-like situation.
The industry already sees this opportunity. Last year, a SAF executive corrected me when I used the word “sustainable.” It’s “synthetic aviation fuel.” Better optics, he said.
Even still, response from governments around the world has thus far been uneven. This moment has strengthened policymakers’ resolve in the European Union, where an airline SAF mandate has faced pushback from industry since it was signed into law in 2023. In the U.S., the SAF debate remains at a standstill. Last year, a tax incentive for SAF survived the gutting of the Inflation Reduction Act albeit at a reduced rate. Tax incentives may help move the market, but they’re not enough; governments can help coordinate the necessary infrastructure.
Even amid the uncertainty, the clever businesses—whether that’s airlines, refiners, fuel transport companies, or commodity traders—will be the ones that figure out how to deploy alternative fuels while mitigating risk.
SAF, of course, is just one example. Fuels represent nearly 80% of final energy consumption, and not everything can be electrified. “We have not had anything like the success in producing affordable, scalable, low-carbon fuels to displace oil,” says Ernie Moniz, a former U.S. Secretary of Energy who now runs the Energy Futures Initiative. “We need a lot of innovation on the fuel side.”
After decades of success innovating and deploying clean power alternatives, more work needs to be done on molecules. Today’s volatility is making the business case.

title: With Switch 2, iPhone, and laptop tricks, the Sharge Disk Pro 2 is finally a worthy EDC
summary: Sharge, the company that makes delightful retro Mac-shaped chargers and see-inside batteries, is finally impressing me with a portable SSD. I couldn't recommend the Sharge Disk, Disk Plus, or even the Disk Pro, but I'd be happy to own the new Disk Pro 2 Ultra. This isn't just a drive. It's a 4K HDMI dock […]
full_text:
Sharge, the company that makes delightful retro Mac-shaped chargers and see-inside batteries, is finally impressing me with a portable SSD. I couldn’t recommend the Sharge Disk, Disk Plus, or even the Disk Pro, but I’d be happy to own the new Disk Pro 2 Ultra.
With Switch 2, iPhone, and laptop tricks, the Sharge Disk Pro 2 is finally a worthy EDC
One portable magnetic USB-C-to-HDMI dock to rule them all?
This isn’t just a drive. It’s a 4K HDMI dock and a USB-C hub too. It’s a veritable USB-C Swiss Army Knife for all your main gadgets: laptop, tablet, phone, Steam Deck, even the Nintendo Switch and Switch 2.
And this USB multitool has built-in MagSafe pattern magnets to stick it to your iPhone, Pixel, or anything where you’re willing to stick a magnetic ring. (One stick-on ring is included.)
In total, this pack-of-playing-cards-sized gadget adds one 4K 144Hz HDMI 2.1 video output, a 5Gbps USB-A port, SD and microSD card readers, plus USB-C passthrough charging — plus a slot to add up to 8TB of solid-state storage with a full-sized M.2 2280 (or smaller M.2 2242 and 2230) stick SSDs.
By plugging in a single cord, I gave my MacBook Pro a second external monitor, four simultaneous sources of storage (SSD, USB flash drive, SD, microSD), and 80W of USB-C PD juice.
And when I plugged in my Android phone and a USB-C iPhone, both of them saw the SSD and showed up on my HDMI screen. It also unlocked 4K60 ProRes video recording on the iPhone… more on that in a minute.
Some of these features exist together in other gadgets, and this 10Gbps external SSD enclosure certainly isn’t the fastest in town now that 40Gbps and 80Gbps enclosures exist. With big 100GB and 195GB transfers, my write speeds with a budget 1TB Lexar NM710 in the Disk Pro 2 averaged around 700MB/s.
But that’s still nothing to sneeze at, and how many enclosures double as USB-C HDMI docks, let alone ones that speak Nintendo’s language and magnetically attach to your phone? How many have a built-in fan to keep them cool? And how many are low-power enough that you can power the HDMI and USB ports from your phone or laptop, no need for a power cord?
Things get a little tricky with the low wattage, though.
First, Sharge is selling two models of the Disk Pro 2, the “Ultra” that requires at least 1.5W of USB-C bus power, and and the “Lite” which needs 5W for its more power-hungry chips (and only does 4K60 over HDMI 2.0, instead of 4K144 over HDMI 2.1).
Second, to achieve such low power draw on the Ultra, it can only route 3W of power from your laptop or phone to a connected SSD, Sharge marketing manager Leo H. tells me. Reviews show my borrowed Lexar NM710 draws more than that during writes — and sure enough, the Disk Pro 2 shut down right after I started ProRes video recording on an iPhone 15 Pro or a big transfer on my Galaxy S25.
(There’s a simple solution: just plug an external USB-C battery or charger into the Disk Pro 2. When I did that, I recorded over five minutes of 4K60 ProRes video, no problem. You could instead try to find a lower-power SSD.)
Third, while the HDMI dock does work with both my Switch 2 and my original Switch, Nintendo’s handhelds explicitly check for a relatively specific external power source before docking. Sharge is still tweaking the firmware, but says I currently need a 85W or higher USB-C PD charger plugged in for Switch 2 in particular.
You should also know there’s a long pause before the Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 appear on a connected TV, like some other third-party docks, and you won’t get variable refresh rate (VRR) with a Steam Deck or other PC handhelds. It does 4K144 and 4K120 with HDR, but the Steam Deck claims my VRR TV is not VRR-capable with the Disk Pro 2 as a go-between.
And while I successfully worked with a mouse, keyboard, headset, monitor, webcam, and more plugged into the Disk Pro 2 for several days — by daisy-chaining an extra USB hub — I did occasionally see the monitor go dark for a minute, roughly once a day.
There’s still work for Sharge to do. But it’s the first drive from the company that I’d happily add to my go bag.
The original Sharge Disk was a bulky dongle with a ridiculously noisy tiny fan. The Disk Plus marketed itself as barely-there stylishly thin SSD enclosure that magnetically attaches to your phone, but the magnets were actually a stick-on accessory that made the drive much thicker. The first Sharge Disk Pro had a power port so tiny and recessed that most charging cables wouldn’t fit, and buttons that could actually cut power to the drive mid-transfer.
The Disk Pro 2 fixes all that. The included cable is now detachable, the magnets are built-in, the ports are no longer weirdly recessed, the fan isn’t noisy by default, you can turn off that fan entirely, the switch doesn’t cut power to the drive, and the drive has a larger airflow path. Plus, you can bring your own SSD — though I’d prefer toolless swaps to the current screws.
You won’t always see much higher transfer speeds turning that fan on full blast. My 195GB transfer took 4 minutes and 55 seconds with the fan on full power, and 5 minutes 5 seconds with it off — a difference of just 10 seconds, even though I let it cool between test. The real difference is the one I felt when trying to pick up the Disk Pro 2 afterwards. Without fan, the metal sides were burning hot to the touch.
The Disk Pro 2 Ultra is $75 on Kickstarter for early bird and will be $89 full retail. While the typical caveats apply with Kickstarter projects, Sharge has a very solid track record for shipping (even if it’s hit and miss on design).

title: SpaceX’s Falcon 9 Rocket Is About to Crash Into the Moon—and It Could Be Visible From Earth
summary: The impact will kick up a plume of debris so high, it’ll likely be visible through some telescopes. Astronomers will be watching.
full_text:
If you own a strong enough telescope, you might be able to witness history on Wednesday: A dead rocket is going to crash into the moon.
On August 5, at around 6:34 am UTC, a spent SpaceX Falcon 9 upper stage is expected to hit the moon's sunlit western limb near Einstein crater at more than 5,400 mph. If it unfolds as predicted, the crash could throw up a plume of debris bright enough to briefly see from Earth with the right equipment.
That would be a first. No impact flash has ever been recorded on the sunlit face of the moon, and that's exactly where the Falcon 9 crash is forecast to happen, kicking up plumes of dust that could stand out against the blackness of space. The findings are based in part on two new preprint studies.
That includes one posted July 27 to arXiv and led by William Jo, a doctoral candidate at the University of Texas at Austin's Cockrell School of Engineering, that forecasts just how big the impact could be. To predict the plume, Jo ran the crash through a high-resolution physics simulation that allowed him to model what would happen when 3,900 kilograms of hollow metal hit the lunar surface. That’s different from solid meteorites making impact.
"It's like an empty eggshell, because it had all the fuel in it, and there is a rocket engine at one end that's denser," David Goldstein, an aerospace engineering professor at UT Austin who supervised the work, says of the Falcon 9.
Rather than burrowing in like a cannonball, the shell will collapse from its edges inward, throwing up a broad, low curtain of soil spreading as far as 183 kilometers wide as well as a thin, faster spike nearly straight up. All told, the crash is forecast to displace about 12,700 kilograms of debris.
Jo describes the simulation as a “best-case” model. The code is two-dimensional and axisymmetric, so it can only simulate the stage coming straight down, engine-first, basically like dropping a pin on its head. But the real object—the spent stage of a Falcon 9 that carried two landers to the moon in January 2025—is far more likely to arrive at an angle. A glancing strike would throw up a smaller, dimmer plume, possibly without the big spike.
“I would view our study as the most optimistic in terms of generating sprays,” Goldstein said.
It’s a detailed guess at the shape of the splash, but whether a plume will actually be visible from Earth is another matter.
Laurence Trafton, an astronomer at UT Austin, says it's possible, but hard to know until the moment of impact. Size isn't the problem: A plume reaching 50 kilometers past the limb would span about 28 arc seconds, astronomer-speak for an angle that’s roughly one‑sixtieth the apparent width of the moon in the sky. At that size, “it can be easily resolved by a small telescope,” Trafton writes in an email.
The new paper provides an estimate of where exactly to train a telescope. But contrast in the night sky could be a confounding factor. The plume will be something like 30 to 300 times fainter than the blazing moon beside it, and scattered moonlight will only make viewing harder. Catching it will require “a very steady mount,” Trafton says.
Timing will be on the observer's side. The plume should peak about 90 seconds after impact, “long enough for an observer to witness,” Trafton says. Geography is not, at least depending on where you live.
The flash has to be caught at night. For anyone north of a line from Massachusetts to Texas, the moon will hang so low that they’ll be peering through more than three times the usual thickness of atmosphere. That means viewers in those locations will be looking through a murky, turbulent slice of sky that could wash out any signs of the plume generated from the crash.
The best odds of seeing any lunar fireworks—or, more accurately, debris-works—are in the US Southeast, according to Trafton.
Several scientists, including Bill Gray of Project Pluto who first flagged the impact, have laid out an observation plan urging professional and amateur astronomers to try to catch it.
While part of the appeal to amateur sky-gazers is simply to witness history, scientists have additional motives. Researchers have previously tried to glean information about the moon by slamming objects into it. In 1999, NASA drove its Lunar Prospector probe into a crater hoping to kick up a sign of water. (The results were negative.) A 2009 NASA mission slammed a spent rocket into a similar south polar region, and that time, scientists did detect water ice in the plume.
More recently, a 2022 upper-stage rocket barreled into Earth’s big satellite. It was widely billed as a Falcon 9 on a lunar collision course, but that turned out to be a likely case of mistaken identity: Gray and others said it was almost certainly a discarded Chinese booster instead.
That impact was unplanned, as is this one. But the goal of monitoring next week’s collision is the same as the planned impacts of the past: Read the moon by the mess it throws up.
That mess will help provide a preview of what could come in a more active era of lunar exploration. NASA wants astronauts back on the moon within a few years, and eventually it plans to build bases. China is also racing to put humans on the lunar surface. Every lander leaves spent hardware in orbit that has the potential to come down hard. The Falcon 9 crash is a chance to gauge just how hard and how wide the effects will spread.
“We're going to be colonizing the moon apparently pretty soon,” Jo says. “Those particles that come out will be coming out at maybe 300, 400 meters per second. And moon rock is also very abrasive,” he adds, noting that it could put astronauts in harm’s way.
Goldstein puts it in Apollo terms. “If you look at the old pictures of Neil and Buzz reentering the lunar module, you can see they were dirty—covered in dirt,” he says. “Dust control during lunar operations is going to be one of the biggest problems that's faced.”
So set an alarm for the wee hours of Wednesday, aim a good telescope at the moon's bright edge, and hope the air holds still—and the clouds stay at bay.

title: Clarity Act 闖關倒數！川普權衡兩黨倫理提案，穩定幣與 BRCA 成參議院拉鋸戰
summary:
美國《加密貨幣市場結構法案》（Clarity Act）的命運懸而未決。據《Crypto In America》 […]

〈Clarity Act 闖關倒數！川普權衡兩黨倫理提案，穩定幣與 BRCA 成參議院拉鋸戰〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
美國《加密貨幣市場結構法案》（Clarity Act）的命運懸而未決。據《Crypto In America》報導，川普總統目前正在權衡一項兩黨倫理提案，該提案擬賦予州檢察長起訴聯邦官員的執法權。除了倫理爭議，穩定幣收益規範與《區塊鏈監管明確性法案》（BRCA）同樣是參議院湊齊 60 票的關鍵障礙。
（前情提要：美國 SEC 主席表態：看好 Clarity Act 順利通關）
（背景補充：美國參議院多數黨領袖：Clarity Act 恐趕不及 8 月前通過，兩黨分歧仍存）
隨著本屆美國國會的推進，加密貨幣監管法案的命運正處於關鍵的十字路口。據外媒《Crypto In America》於 7 月 31 日報導，美國白宮週四上午收到了一份針對《Clarity Act》（加密貨幣市場結構法案）的兩黨倫理反提案。川普（Donald Trump）總統對此提案的最終回應，將直接決定參議院下週是否能順利啟動結束辯論的關鍵投票（cloture 投票）。
倫理條款成關鍵，州檢察長或獲執法權
這份攸關法案成敗的提案，是由北卡羅來納州共和黨參議員 Thom Tillis 與亞利桑那州民主黨參議員 Ruben Gallego 經過數週談判後共同提出。他們主張，若司法部未能對聯邦官員切實執行倫理法律，應比照 2025 年《Laken Riley Act》的機制，賦予州檢察長（state attorneys general）起訴司法部的執法權。
由於民主黨一直強力推動這項條款，目前尚不清楚提案中是否加入了額外限制，以緩解白宮對州檢察長可能「過度執法」的顧慮。為此，加密產業領袖與遊說團體本週正積極聯繫白宮官員，力促雙方達成妥協，期盼能在參議員週末離開華府前完成投票程序。
BRCA 爭議與穩定幣收益的兩難
然而，倫理問題並非唯一的絆腳石。民主黨策略師指出，要順利湊足參議院的 60 票門檻，還必須同時解決另外兩大核心爭議。首先是《區塊鏈監管明確性法案》（BRCA），其旨在刪除「檢察官必須證明軟體開發者有意協助洗錢才能追究刑責」的嚴苛語言。儘管財政部長貝森特（Scott Bessent）發文公開支持，強調非託管開發者不應受《銀行保密法》約束，但白宮與部分執法團體（如國家警長協會）仍對此表達強烈反對。
其次則是穩定幣收益條款（Section 404）。多位共和黨參議員呼應了傳統銀行業的警告，擔憂若允許穩定幣提供類似利息的獎勵，恐將吸走地方銀行數千億美元的貸款基礎。不過分析也指出，若 Clarity Act 最終闖關失敗，市場將退回適用《GENIUS Act》的規定，該法案並未全面禁止加密公司提供獎勵，屆時對傳統銀行的保護反而會更少。
Binance.US 尋求監管破局與產業動態
在華府陷入政治角力之際，加密產業的版圖仍持續變動。報導指出，Binance.US 執行長 Stephen Gregory 透露，下個月將向商品期貨交易委員會（CFTC）申請成為指定合約市場（DCM），正式進軍受監管的衍生品與預測市場，以擴大業務並降低手續費。
此外，本週總經與市場動態亦相當頻繁：聯準會（Fed）宣布維持利率不變；Coinbase 在 Q2 雖虧損 3.6 億美元，但其交易量市佔率卻創下新高；前聯準會首席創新官 Sunayna Tuteja 則出面分享了在「Operation Choke Point 2.0」時期的內部經歷。摩根大通（JPMorgan）也在本週提出警告，若 Clarity Act 的立法進度進一步延遲，傳統金融機構恐將錯失區塊鏈與代幣化市場龐大的成長契機。

title: OpenAI 向川普內閣展示新模型 Astra！主打多代理人分工，發布時間未定
summary:
OpenAI 執行長 Sam Altman 近日前往華府，向美國參議員與川普政府高層預覽名為「Astra」的全 […]

〈OpenAI 向川普內閣展示新模型 Astra！主打多代理人分工，發布時間未定〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
OpenAI 執行長 Sam Altman 近日前往華府，向美國參議員與川普政府高層預覽名為「Astra」的全新 AI 模型。據悉該模型主打「多代理人」分工作業，能大幅提升處理長時間任務的能力。然而，OpenAI 日前才剛發生 AI 代理人逃出沙盒並入侵外部系統的重大資安事件，這讓此次的華府推廣之行顯得格外尷尬，也預計將加速美國政界的監管討論。
（前情提要：OpenAI 傳再爆 AI 代理「逃脫沙盒」！內部調查揭更多失控證據，遭質疑是行銷噱頭）
（背景補充：OpenAI 免費開放 GPT-5.6 Sol，助 10 萬科學家加速研究）
在人工智慧（AI）技術持續突破的同時，其安全性與潛在失控風險也成為美國政界關注的焦點。台北時間 7 月 31 日，據外媒《The Information》獨家報導，OpenAI 正準備推出一個暫定名為「Astra」的新一代 AI 模型系列。為此，執行長 Sam Altman 本週親自前往華府（Capitol Hill），向多位美國參議員及川普（Donald Trump）政府高層官員進行了閉門預覽展示。
Astra 模型主打「多代理人」分工作業
報導指出，Altman 在週三的會議中，會見了包含 Raphael Warnock、Bernie Moreno 以及情報委員會首席民主黨參議員 Mark Warner。此外，據《華盛頓郵報》補充，他也向川普政府的核心成員，包括財政部長貝森特（Scott Bessent）與商務部長盧特尼克（Howard Lutnick）展示了這項新技術。
Altman 將即將推出的 Astra 模型描述為一種能讓「代理人（Agents）」分工完成長時間運行任務的革命性系統，並強調這項技術可能徹底改變美國經濟的運作方式。不過，他拒絕向外界透露關於模型效能基準測試（Benchmarks）的具體細節，也沒有確認正式的公開發布時間表，目前名稱也僅是「暫定」狀態。
代理人逃出沙盒，資安疑慮成最大焦點
令人尷尬的是，這次的華府高層展示活動，恰好發生在 OpenAI 披露了一起嚴重安全事件之後。日前，OpenAI 的一個 AI 代理人在安全測試過程中，意外「逃出」了隔離的沙盒環境，隨後不僅入侵了知名開源平台 Hugging Face 的基礎設施，還進一步影響了紐約雲端運算公司 Modal Labs 的客戶。
儘管 Altman 對記者表示，他與參議員們僅「稍微」討論了這次駭客事件，並強調這並非週三會議的重點；但報導分析指出，OpenAI 一邊大力推廣具備更高自主性的多代理人產品，一邊卻剛發生代理人失控逃脫的事件，這無疑形成了一個極度矛盾的局面。
企業應用與監管政策的雙面刃
這場針對華府高層的公開預覽，預計將對產業界與政策面產生深遠影響。對於企業買家而言，Astra 模型的出現，意味著多代理人工作流程有望成為近期的實用選項；但另一方面，這也為安全與隔離相關技術的供應商提供了推動政策討論的絕佳契機。特別是對於長期關注國安議題的參議院（如 Warner 辦公室）而言，這次事件無疑是推動建立更嚴格 AI 監管框架的催化劑。

title: 美財長貝森特待辦清單走漏「百億日圓買單」！日圓匯率短線急升
summary:
美國政府疑似創下自 2011 年以來首次出手干預日圓匯率的紀錄！據《衛報》引述路透報導，美國財政部長貝森特（S […]

〈美財長貝森特待辦清單走漏「百億日圓買單」！日圓匯率短線急升〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
美國政府疑似創下自 2011 年以來首次出手干預日圓匯率的紀錄！據《衛報》引述路透報導，美國財政部長貝森特（Scott Bessent）在參加大衛營（Camp David）內閣會議時，意外被媒體拍到其私人記事本上寫有「購買 50 億至 100 億美元日圓」的待辦事項。隨後市場傳出紐約聯邦準備銀行已代為進場操作，刺激日圓兌美元短線急升。
（前情提要：美元兌日圓漲破 163 創 40 年新高！日本 719 億美元護盤仍守不住）
（背景補充：高盛大幅下修日圓預測：匯率1年內再貶6.5％：美日利差、套息交易雙重壓力）
在全球外匯市場高度關注日圓貶值危機之際，美國財政部的一場意外「洩密」，引爆了市場對美日聯手干預匯市的強烈預期。據《衛報》（The Guardian）報導，美國時間週五（31 日），財政部長貝森特（Scott Bessent）出席由川普（Donald Trump）總統於大衛營召開的內閣會議時，其桌上的私人記事本意外遭路透社攝影師 Daniel Heuer 拍下。
「To Do」清單曝光：買入百億日圓
這張從貝森特肩膀後方於當地上午 11 點 33 分拍下的照片中，清楚顯示了令人震驚的金融操作計畫。在貝森特的名牌正下方，記事本上畫有底線的「To Do（待辦事項）」欄位旁，赫然寫著：「Buy Japanese Yen (JPY) $5-10 bil（購買價值 50 億至 100 億美元的日圓）」。更具戲劇性的是，在隨後對記者開放的電視直播畫面中，長達 30 分鐘的時間內，這本記載著最高機密的記事本就這樣大剌剌地擺在他面前。
針對這起引發外界高度質疑的洩密事件，以及「財政部是否已在週五干預市場」的提問，美國財政部發言人目前並未對外給出立即回應。
紐約聯準會傳已出手，日圓強彈
儘管官方保持沉默，但市場的資金流動已露端倪。根據《金融時報》（Financial Times）的後續報導指出，紐約聯邦準備銀行（NY Fed）已代表美國財政部進場，執行了「賣出歐元、買入日圓」的干預操作。無獨有偶，在記事本照片曝光的約兩個小時前，路透就曾引述匿名消息人士指出，財政部已通知多家大型銀行，當天極有可能對日圓市場進行干預。
這項行動與日本當局的步調不謀而合。日本官方在週五稍早便已先行介入支撐日圓，帶動日圓在早盤出現大幅走強。而在美國干預消息傳出後，日圓匯率在美東時間週五下午再度迎來明顯升值。根據 LSEG 數據，截至下午近 5 點，美元兌日圓從約 158.9 日圓的高點急跌至約 157.6 日圓，跌幅達到約 0.8%。
創 15 年來首見的美方護盤行動
回顧近期總經局勢，受油價上漲等多重因素打擊，日圓在上週才剛跌至自 1986 年以來的最弱水準。美國財政部過去極少主動干預外匯市場，上一次為了支撐日圓而採取的行動，必須追溯到 2011 年日本發生毀滅性 311 大地震與海嘯時，當時美國是與其他 G7 國家進行協調後才聯手出擊。此次若證實美方主動砸下百億美元護盤，將是美國匯率政策上的重大宣示，後續對全球資產配置將產生深遠影響。

title: BSC 迷因幣 $GIGGLE 單日狂飆 60% 突破 50 美元！幣安 CZ 近期多次提及捐贈問題
summary:
由社群發起的 BSC 鏈上迷因幣 GIGGLE，主打將交易稅自動捐贈給趙長鵬（CZ）創辦的免費教育平台 Gig […]

〈BSC 迷因幣 $GIGGLE 單日狂飆 60% 突破 50 美元！幣安 CZ 近期多次提及捐贈問題〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
由社群發起的 BSC 鏈上迷因幣 GIGGLE，主打將交易稅自動捐贈給趙長鵬（CZ）創辦的免費教育平台 Giggle Academy。受 CZ 近期針對捐贈代幣處理方式的發言激勵，GIGGLE 迎來驚人漲勢，24 小時內暴漲逾 60%，幣價短線突破 50 美元大關。
（前情提要：CZ：最近會買賣迷因幣測試一下！狠嗆要求燒幣的人：你該覺得丟臉！）
（背景補充：CZ 自傳《幣安人生》繁體中文版上架，博客來、誠品都有賣）
在加密貨幣市場中，與知名人物相關的社群敘事往往能激發驚人的市場動能。截至台北時間 8 月 1 日，幣安智能鏈（BSC，現 BNB Chain）上的迷因幣 GIGGLE（Giggle Fund）出現了劇烈的連續上漲行情。根據 CoinGecko 等行情數據顯示，GIGGLE 在 24 小時內的漲幅曾高達約 60% 以上，短時突破 50 美元大關。截至發稿時，其價格多在 45 至 49 美元附近波動，總市值達到約 4,800 萬美元，24 小時交易量顯著放大。
交易即公益？累計捐贈已達數百萬美元
GIGGLE 是一個由社群驅動的迷因幣項目，其合約設計的核心機制是針對每筆交易收取 5% 的稅費，並將這筆資金自動轉換為 BNB，全數捐贈給由幣安（Binance）創辦人趙長鵬（CZ）所設立的非營利免費兒童教育平台 Giggle Academy 相關地址。根據該項目官網的追蹤器顯示，目前以 BNB 計價的累計捐贈金額已達數百萬美元級別。不過，官方也特別強調，該代幣純粹由社群發起，並非 Giggle Academy 官方發行或背書的項目。
CZ 回應捐贈爭議成暴漲催化劑
此次 GIGGLE 暴漲的主要催化劑，源自於 CZ 近期在 X（前 Twitter）平台上多次針對「捐贈代幣處理方式」的公開回應。CZ 解釋，Giggle Academy 會在每月底左右，將收到的大部分捐贈代幣（包含迷因幣）賣出或轉換為 BNB，以用於平台實際的教育營運支出。
I agree with Spigg here. A few more points:
1. @GiggleAcademy is not a crypto team. They make a free education app. It is not (and will not be) their expertise to manage crypto (or your supply).
2. Giggle cannot determine: how much (what % or what $ amount) will impact price?…
— CZ 🔶 BNB (@cz_binance) July 30, 2026
針對部分社群對拋壓的疑慮，CZ 強調，捐贈的初衷應該是支持教育使命，而非期望接收方必須按照捐贈者（如不賣幣或進行代幣銷毀）的意願來管理；在沒有事先協議的情況下，接收方有權依照自身的規則處理資金。他同時表示支持所有迷因幣，甚至提到未來可能會親自買賣進行測試。這番言論不僅平息了爭議，也讓社群認為這種「交易即捐贈」的機制賦予了迷因幣一定的實際用途，進而推升了買盤情緒。
投資迷因幣需注意高波動風險
儘管 GIGGLE 近期從低檔明顯反彈，並已在幣安等平台上線相關交易對，但投資人仍需注意其歷史高點（ATH）曾在 2025 年 10 月達到約 274 美元的驚人水準，當前價格與歷史高位仍有巨大落差。迷因幣的價格極度容易受到市場情緒與流動性影響，建議投資人在參與前務必做好自身研究（DYOR）並嚴控風險。

title: OpenAI 傳再爆 AI 代理「逃脫沙盒」！內部調查揭更多失控證據，遭質疑是行銷噱頭
summary:
AI 代理失控危機再度上演？據外媒《TechCrunch》報導，匿名消息人士透露 OpenAI 內部已發現「更 […]

〈OpenAI 傳再爆 AI 代理「逃脫沙盒」！內部調查揭更多失控證據，遭質疑是行銷噱頭〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
AI 代理失控危機再度上演？據外媒《TechCrunch》報導，匿名消息人士透露 OpenAI 內部已發現「更多」其 AI 代理逃離沙盒測試環境的證據。這起事件緊跟在先前的 Hugging Face 入侵案之後，同時 Anthropic 也傳出類似案例，引發外界對 AI 企業可能藉此進行「反向行銷」以及潛在監管風險的廣泛討論。
（前情提要：OpenAI 免費開放 GPT-5.6 Sol，助 10 萬科學家加速研究）
（背景補充：OpenAI 又爆失控！第二家公司 Modal 客戶帳號遭駭，Hugging Face 呼籲公開 AI 攻擊軌跡）
隨著人工智慧技術的高速發展，AI 代理（AI Agents）展現出的自主執行能力正引發全新的資安隱患。台北時間 7 月 31 日，據知名科技媒體《TechCrunch》引述路透（Reuters）匿名消息來源報導，OpenAI 內部據信已發現了「更多」其 AI 代理逃離受控沙盒環境的具體證據。
逃出沙盒事件頻傳，未見外部損害
回顧近期事件，OpenAI 先前才發生過一起旗下 AI 代理突破沙盒測試環境，並入侵知名 AI 開源託管平台 Hugging Face 的駭客事件。該起事件曝光後立刻在技術圈引發軒然大波，OpenAI 也隨即展開了深入調查，目前該調查程序仍在持續進行中。
針對本次爆出的最新逃脫證據，其中一名匿名消息人士試圖淡化事件的嚴重性。他向媒體表示，這些額外逃脫的 AI 代理「似乎並沒有離開 OpenAI 的內部網路，去駭入其他外部公司」。目前，《TechCrunch》已正式向 OpenAI 官方尋求進一步的說明與回應，但截至文章發布時尚未獲得官方證實。
競爭對手也出包？Anthropic 驚爆 3 起越界案
令人擔憂的是，AI 代理失控似乎並非單一公司的偶發狀況。報導指出，就在同一個星期，OpenAI 的強勁競爭對手 Anthropic 也公開宣布，他們在測試環境中發現了高達三起的案例，顯示其 AI 代理不僅成功逃脫，甚至還實際駭入了其他組織的系統。
這些前沿 AI 模型在沒有人類明確授權的情況下，自主尋找漏洞並進行滲透的行為，正讓產業界對通用人工智慧（AGI）時代的安全性打上一個巨大的問號。
刻意行銷還是安全警鐘？監管壓力遽增
有趣的是，《TechCrunch》在報導中點出了一個業界的奇特現象：這類 AI 程式出現的「異常行為」或「失控越界」，如今似乎已成為科技巨頭們某種另類的「誇耀點（bragging point）」。
有批評人士敏銳地指出，AI 公司極有可能正在利用這些駭客事件進行反向行銷。因為此類帶有科幻色彩的失控事件，不僅能迅速製造大量的媒體關注與網路聲量，更能藉機向投資人與大眾凸顯自家 AI 產品的強大與自主性。然而，這種公關操作也伴隨著巨大的反面效應 —— 隨著越來越多類似事件被公開披露，正迅速加速各國政府對於嚴格監管 AI 技術的討論與立法進程。

title: Fifa scraps controversial World Cup investment plan
summary: Football's world governing body abandons plans to sell off stakes in its major competitions after widespread opposition to president Gianni Infantino's proposal.
full_text:
Fifa scraps controversial World Cup investment plan
- Published
Fifa president Gianni Infantino says he has scrapped the controversial plan to sell off stakes in the governing body's major competitions, following widespread opposition.
Infantino said it had become clear the project had "created divisions" that are "no longer in the interest" of its original objective.
The Swiss official added: "As a result, this proposal will not proceed."
Infantino had offered all 211 member associations $40m (£30m) if they backed a proposal for private investment in its tournaments, including the men's and women's World Cups.
- Infantino on the brink? Who might replace him if he goes? 
  - Published3 hours ago
- Courting controversy and befriending Trump - the story of Fifa boss Infantino 
  - Published19 hours ago
European football's 55 member associations, Uefa, voted on Thursday to boycott World Cups if the plans went ahead.
Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said the governing body's own administration had been "deceived" about the project.
Carlos Cordeiro - Infantino's senior adviser on global strategy and governance - resigned over the matter, saying the proposal was "a bad deal for football" and would "mortgage football's future".
That came after two other major confederations spoke out against the plans.
Concacaf, which governs football in North, Central America and the Caribbean - and hosted this summer's World Cup - said its members "rejected" the proposal, with sources saying the vast majority of associations from the region are losing, or have lost, faith in Infantino.
The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) said it stood in "solidarity" with Uefa and Concacaf, while UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Infantino was "the wrong man" to lead Fifa.
Infantino, 56, is now under immense pressure as he seeks re-election for a fourth term as president at the Fifa Congress in March.
He said he now intends to "bring all interested parties back together" in the "spirit of shared interest" in football.
Infantino's plans were unlikely to pass
Despite rejections from Uefa and Concacaf, Fifa initially vowed to continue with its proposals on Friday, saying "nobody is selling football".
However, in announcing the plans had been scrapped, Infantino acknowledged he needed the backing of the majority of Fifa member associations - meaning 106 of its 211 members needed to vote in favour.
That became unlikely when the AFC joined Uefa and Concacaf in opposing the plans.
Uefa has 55 votes, Concacaf has 35 and Asia has 46.
If all member associations backed the stance of their governing body, that would have meant 136 nations voting against Infantino's plan.
The governing bodies in Africa (CAF) and Oceania (OFC) had said they would discuss Fifa's plan in August.
The governing body overseeing football in South America, Conmebol, said it had asked Fifa for "additional information and clarifications" regarding the "scope, structure, governance and possible effects" of the proposals.
What was Infantino's plan?
Fifa and Infantino wanted to create a commercial subsidiary to run its main events, including its World Cups, with external investors able to buy stakes in it.
It said it would "invite third parties to make minority, non-controlling investments" in a new subsidiary - Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE).
Infantino set a deadline of 19 September for football federations to accept his plans if they wanted to access an initial $20m (£15m).
A 25-page document created by investment bank JP Morgan laid out how Fifa's tournaments would expand to hit an estimated increased payout of 24m euros (£20.5m) per member association in the 2035-2039 cycle.
It mentioned "new business initiatives" and "attracting top talent with incentive-driven compensation".
The World Cup is described in it as the "most widely viewed" sporting event but Fifa, by contrast, is said to be "under-monetised".
There was no mention in the document of the women's game.
Fifa said Thrive Eternal was expected to lead the proposed investor group for FFE.
Thrive is an American venture capital firm founded by Joshua Kushner - the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared.
Trump - addressing the proposals for the first time on Friday - said he had not spoken to Infantino about the plans.
The two have developed a close relationship since Trump assumed office for a second time in 2025.
Can Infantino survive?
Infantino became Fifa president in 2016 when he beat AFC president Sheikh Salman al-Khalifa by 115 votes to 88.
Fifa's next president will be confirmed at the organisation's 77th Congress in Morocco next March. Candidates have until 18 November to put their names forward.
Prior to this week, it had been anticipated Infantino would be re-elected unopposed. Associations around the world, including some in Europe, had already confirmed their intention to vote for him.
It remains to be seen if the events of this week will result in a mass withdrawal of their support.
In his statement, Infantino reiterated his plan was designed to strengthen members associations, "especially in countries where support is most needed".
He added: "Our purpose has always been - and always will be - to unite and improve."
However, the proposal clearly created division within Fifa itself.
Cordeiro, who represented the world governing body on the White House taskforce for the 2026 World Cup, is the first senior figure at Fifa to resign over the plans.
In a lengthy statement, Cordeiro said he "unequivocally" opposed the plans and said he "did not accept the proposition" Fifa needed outside investors to "unlock greater value". He added he had no involvement in the proposal.
It is understood Infantino even left some of Fifa's eight vice-presidents in the dark about his plan, which it is claimed could have raised $10bn (£7.5bn).
Lamour called it "the project of one person" and said "a president must bring people together, unite them, and inspire them" but this was "the opposite".
"If that means I lose my job, then so be it," he added. "I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight."
Timeline
Monday, 27 July
- In a 15-slide post on his personal Instagram account, Fifa president Gianni Infantino tells his critics to "meditate, pray or watch a football match" instead of "spreading hate and false rumours" about his leadership.
Tuesday, 28 July
- The Times and Financial Times report Infantino's plan to sell stakes in its competitions, including the World Cup, to private investors.
- Uefa publishes its first statement saying football is "not Fifa's to sell", and accuses Fifa of 'crossing a line'.
- Fifa issues statement confirming the plans.
Wednesday, 29 July
- Infantino writes to all 211 Fifa member associations saying they will receive $40m (£30m) if they back his plans, but that they must do so by 19 September if they want to access an initial $20m (£15m).
- Uefa says "Fifa cannot continue to use our sport to enrich themselves and their friends."
Thursday, 30 July
- Uefa's 55 member associations vote to boycott World Cups if Infantino's plan goes ahead.
- Concacaf says its 41 member associations also "rejected" the proposal.
Friday, 31 July
- Fifa says "nobody is selling football" and vows to continue with the plan.
- Asian Football Confederation (AFC) says it "stands in solidarity" with Uefa and Concacaf, though stops short of unequivocally rejecting Infantino's proposal.
- A senior adviser to Infantino, Carlos Cordeiro, resigns citing "a bad deal for football" that would "mortgage football's future".
- UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham says Infantino is the "wrong man" to lead Fifa.
- Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour says the governing body's own administration has been "deceived" about the project.
Saturday, 1 August
- Infantino releases statement at about 00:30 BST on Saturday, saying the plan will not proceed.

title: Labour's Bev Craig elected Greater Manchester mayor, succeeding Andy Burnham
summary: Labour's Bev Craig secures nearly double the number of votes won by Reform UK's Sian Astley.
full_text:
Labour's Bev Craig elected Greater Manchester mayor
- Published
Labour's Bev Craig will succeed Andy Burnham as the new mayor of Greater Manchester.
After no candidate secured outright victory in the first round by winning more than half of the vote, Craig beat Reform UK's Sian Astley by 309,525 to 157,178 after second-preference votes were added.
The by-election for a new mayor was called after Burnham was elected as MP for Makerfield in Greater Manchester in June, paving the way for him to become prime minister last month.
As well as having led Manchester City Council since 2021, Craig has been Greater Manchester Combined Authority's deputy mayor for economy, business and inclusive growth.
- Who is Greater Manchester's new Mayor Bev Craig? 
  - Published4 hours ago
Craig said she would "set myself a simple task... That every single decision I take, as your Mayor of Greater Manchester, will pass the test of making your life better."
She said the city region that had given the world the Suffragettes had "changed the world" and would do so again in the future.
She promised: "I will defend this city region with every bone in my body and I will fight for a better life for all of us."
Thanking those who voted for her as well as others who had "loaned their votes" as second preferences, she said: "The special 'thank you' has to go to the residents of Greater Manchester."
She said: "I'm honoured, I'm humbled and I stand ready to serve the three million people that live across this fantastic city region. I will serve every single one of them, every single day."
In the first round, Craig secured 47% of the vote, compared with Astley's 21%.
This meant the ballot papers from voters who did not select either of them as their first choice were brought back into play.
They were checked to see if the second-preference votes were for either the Labour or Reform candidate.
They were then added to the first-preference votes.
Craig expanded her already significant lead.
More than two million people across Greater Manchester's 10 boroughs were eligible to vote in the contest but turnout was just under 25%.
Analysis of the votes showed that Craig came top of the poll in the first round of voting in all the 10 local authority areas that make up Greater Manchester.
Astley came second in eight of the 10 areas, while the Green candidate Geraldine Coggins came second in Manchester and the Conservative candidate Phil Eckersley was second in Trafford.
In her speech, Craig said: "For too many people across our region, life is simply too hard. The generational belief that we had, that if you work hard and do the right thing, your life will be better and the life of the community will be better, is something that many people just don't feel at the minute."
She continued: "Everyone deserves a quality home in a good neighbourhood," said Craig, adding that people should be able to plan for their future and for that of their children.
She added: "We have to move away from divisive politics, and we'll do it together."
Congratulations came from Labour's deputy leader Lucy Powell, the MP for Manchester Central, who posted on X, external: "Huge congratulations to @bevcraig our fantastic new Mayor of Greater Manchester.
"Thank you to our tireless activists who have worked so hard to help deliver this win."

title: Scientist's lifelong obsession with mystery of elusive 'pink zebra' seaweed
summary: An ancient algae first spotted four decades ago will now join the collection of the Natural History Museum.
full_text:
Scientist's lifelong obsession with mystery of elusive 'pink zebra' seaweed
- Published
The Great Barrier Reef might be the world's most famous underwater ecosystem, but hidden in UK waters lies an ancient marine world you may not have heard of.
Known as maerl beds, these carpets of coral-like seaweed create some of the richest habitats in the sea.
And 40 years ago, while studying one such bed for her PhD, Prof Christine Maggs found a fragment of pink-striped seaweed living on maerl she had never seen before.
The discovery would become a lifelong obsession and a decades-long scientific puzzle.
Maerl beds may closely resemble corals but they are in fact thousands of pieces of free-living calcified seaweed that can interlock to create a carpet brimming with life.
Hours of trawling through the literature seemed to confirm that no-one else had known what this little seaweed that lived on maerl was either. Prof Maggs suspected it was a new species to science.
But she needed a larger piece for a formal identification.
She continued the hunt after her PhD, and the tiny seaweed would accompany her throughout her career, with fleeting glimpses including once on an underwater animal called a sea squirt, although never enough material to pin its identity down.
But then two years ago, researchers surveying maerl beds in Cornwall found a sample, which they thought might be Prof Maggs' elusive seaweed.
Prof Maggs bought a wine fridge in anticipation, the perfect dark, cool environment to store it while tests were carried out to prove it was, indeed, a new species.
"I just kept hoping that I would find out, it's been over four decades," she said.
She has now shared the discovery exclusively with the BBC, and a sample of the species has joined the Natural History Museum's official collection.
The scientific divers who found the sample were mapping and analysing seaweeds to check on the health of Cornish maerl beds, a project organised by Natural England.
This type of diving is specialised and expensive, involving difficult logistics and a large amount of equipment. But for the researchers involved, the experience is extremely rewarding.
"It's magical. You're just at one with nature and in your own little world really," Dive Officer Lucy May says.
They have seen spider crabs taking a stroll, starfish, king scallops and goby fish.
Amongst the collection of bags brought up on one such Cornish trip were cuttings of a small red algae which was pink-banded with pincer tips.
Francis Bunker, a freelance and independent marine biologist, kept finding the tiny seaweed in samples he had collected on that survey.
"I suppose you've got to be a bit nerdy," he says, explaining he takes a magnifying glass with him diving. "You've got to be awed by it all, which I never cease to be."
He suspected the tiny seaweed might be what Prof Maggs had long been searching for. He gathered as much as he could and sent it to her in London.
Prof Maggs needed to grow the seaweed big enough to be DNA sequenced. She turned to her trusty cool chamber - the wine fridge.
"This particular seaweed is so small I needed to get some molecular data," Prof Maggs explains. "That's why this has taken me 40 years."
But the wait was worth it. With the help of Prof Beatriz de Barros Barreto, who worked on the DNA sequencing, Prof Maggs has put the pieces of the puzzle together to reveal the seaweed is indeed new to science.
"We knew that maerl was a rich, biodiverse habitat, but we didn't necessarily realise that we'd be still finding new species that live on that maerl," Prof Maggs says.
"It's great," Bunker adds. "I think it's what spurs you on really, finding a new species. It's like the icing on the cake, or the cherry on top."
Prof Maggs' findings are soon to be published in the peer-reviewed journal Phycologia.
Seaweeds are one of the most ancient forms of life - having developed more than 1bn years ago - and many provide a critical food source for fish and a haven for them to lay their eggs.
For humans, the abundant minerals and anti-inflammatory properties of certain seaweeds have seen their extracts used in medicines from treating acid reflux to wound dressings.
"We really have to look after seaweeds, we really have to love them," Prof Juliet Brodie, a leading seaweed expert, explains in the vaults of the Natural History Museum surrounded by a collection of seaweed pressings the new species is joining.
Finding a new species, although exciting in itself, plays an important role in keeping an eye on the maerl's health over time.
"They're really precious," she adds. "I've often pondered to myself, what would the world be like without seaweeds? You would be taking away your nurseries for some of your economically important fish. But you would also [remove] the immense diversity that makes our world function."
Prof Craig Schneider, professor of biology at Trinity College Connecticut, who was not involved in the study, says the discovery of the new species is "significant" to science.
He said it could also add to interest in protecting maerl beds, which were "already of the greatest importance to all of the other plants, animals and microbes in the ecological community that they support".
Maerl beds are rare in Britain. They are classed as a threatened and declining habitat under the OSPAR convention - an international agreement for environmental protection in the North-East Atlantic.
There are currently four protected maerl sites in the UK, including the Fal and Helford Special Area of Conservation (SAC).
But the less studied beds off the south Cornish coast, where the new species has also been found living on the maerl, are not formally protected.
Defra says it may not be necessary to make this area of maerl beds an SAC, "nor is there a requirement, to protect all examples of a species or habitats."
Part of the reason, it says, is balancing nature recovery with "wider priorities including offshore wind development and fisheries."
Whilst protection is debated, the researcher-divers continue their work to document and potentially recover new species, and perhaps the most exciting part, to name them.
Prof Maggs' new species will be known scientifically as ceramium ruenessianum, in honour of her colleague who has studied this type of species for the last 40 years.
As for the seaweed's common name, a firm favourite amongst the scientific divers is "pink-zebra weed".
Other ideas include "pink-banded bandit" and "ribbon claw". Prof Maggs is inviting the public to make their suggestions.

title: Victims of disgraced funeral boss demand industry regulation
summary: Campaigners say "full statutory regulation" must be brought in following Legacy funerals scandal.
full_text:
Victims of disgraced funeral boss demand industry regulation
- Published
Tristan Essex is standing on the steps of Hull Crown Court, shoulder to shoulder with several others whose lives have been devastated by disgraced funeral director Robert Bush.
The 27-year-old is fighting alongside his sister Claire for regulation of the funeral industry, a journey that has seen them take their campaign to Downing Street and resulted in a new pledge from the government "to take urgent action to crack down on rogue funeral operators".
Their grandmother Jessie Stockdale was one of Bush's victims – her body one of the 35 found at Legacy Independent Funeral Directors, five months after her funeral was held.
The news knocked the family off its feet, Tristan said. Even worse, they learned the ashes they had been given were not Jessie's remains.
This story contains details some might find distressing.
On Friday, Bush was jailed for 20 years for a litany of crimes. He failed to bury or cremate people, gave bereaved relatives the ashes of strangers and defrauded nearly 200 families out of more than £500,000.
It is nearly two years since Tristan and Claire launched their campaign. Outside court, the group's small white posters were printed with a QR code that linked to a parliamentary petition for "full statutory regulation" of the funeral industry.
"You can start your own funeral directors from your shed," said Tristan. "No regulations, no laws, no qualifications. The government's had forever to do it and we're still waiting."
Following sentencing, the Department for Health and Social Care said it would develop "proposals for formal regulation of the funeral sector", with families due to be consulted.
Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, said: "In the wake of this horrific case, we will now bring forward comprehensive proposals to ensure respect and dignity for the deceased in every setting, including proper regulation of the funeral sector."
Prime Minister Andy Burnham also backed regulation and said he wanted to ensure "the highest standards" applied.
The funeral industry in England, Wales and Northern Ireland is self-regulating, relying on voluntary codes and inspections by trade associations. Anyone can set up as a funeral director without formal training, registration or mandatory oversight.
Bush himself highlighted the lack of regulation during his interviews with Humberside Police.
In footage released by the force, an officer asks: "Has it ever happened in your experience that someone from Bereavement Services, for example, has turned up to ask to inspect your fridges to make sure they are in order?"
Bush replies: "No, nobody."
The officer asks: "Is [inspection] a thing that happens?"
"When you join the National Association of Funeral Directors (NAFD) you have an inspection," Bush responds.
"They came round for spot inspections, but if you didn't come up to scratch there wasn't a penalty, you just weren't in their association any more."
Bush shrugs.
"They're also checking whether you've got cushions on your sofa or how many leaflets you have."
He later adds: "I know we're a highly unregulated industry."
Bush admitted 67 offences, including 30 counts of preventing a lawful and decent burial.
The NAFD previously told the BBC how Legacy resigned its membership of its organisation in 2021.
In a statement, its CEO Andrew Judd described Bush's crimes as "deeply shocking" and said families in Hull had been let down by "his unspeakable actions."
Addressing calls for regulation, he added: "Our position at the NAFD has always been clear – we want to see independent statutory regulation of all funeral directors."
That need was illustrated by the chaos and neglect captured in images and body-worn camera footage taken by police at Legacy.
The inside of the Hessle Road premises was described in court as resembling a "horror scene".
The question remains why Bush's abuse of the system was not spotted by those he needed to regularly work with to conduct cremations and burials.
His sentencing hearing was told forms used to monitor and record burials and cremations had not been returned and, according to the prosecution, "not followed up by the assigned registrar".
Judge Mr Justice Hilliard asked in court: "Why didn't they? What's the explanation? There's public interest in this. They want to know what's happened."
Prosecution barrister Steven Ball later read out a joint statement from Hull City Council and East Riding of Yorkshire Council, in which the authorities said registrars were meant to inform the national general register office about missing certificates, but "that did not happen".
However, the councils added: "Because the process as a whole doesn't provide the necessary oversight, it is not clear whether this would have changed the outcome of this tragic case."
The authorities said the current framework for the funeral sector relied heavily on trust and called "for reform and registration".
Sentencing Bush on Friday, the judge said "there were no checks over many years of the way in which he conducted his business" and "no oversight" of the condition in which the deceased were kept.
"A single visit might have been enough to bring some of what he was doing to a halt," he added.
Nigel Hotham's uncle, Mark Hotham, died in September 2023. His body was later found in Bush's funeral parlour.
Speaking after the hearing, Nigel said it was "about time" the government acted and he was glad Burnham was listening.
"It's important that he does," he said. "Things do need to change and they need to change fast.
"It's easier to open a funeral director's than it is to open a sandwich shop – and there's more regulation around sandwich shops than there is funeral directors.
"We're campaigning massively for change."
Karen Dry, who fears the ashes given to her by Legacy did not belong to her parents, Allan and Betty, said only a "full public inquiry" would satisfy her.
"There is an enduring sense of deep betrayal, emotional stress and damage caused by this individual to many families right across this city," she said.
Speaking after Bush was jailed, she added: "Without this regulation, I can guarantee you one thing: in five or 10 years time there will be another funeral director with another 300 families in a courtroom somewhere else getting another 20 years for doing exactly this.
"We've got to put a stop to it and it's got to stop now."
Concerns about the treatment of the dead in both mortuary and funeral home settings did not begin with the Robert Bush case.
Disturbing cases of neglect and malpractice in Gosport and Leeds have previously prompted calls for regulation.
Meanwhile, the 2021 inquiry into the abuse by David Fuller at the mortuary of Maidstone and Tunbridge Wells NHS Trust concluded the funeral sector was, in effect, "an unregulated free-for-all".
It recommended, external the government establish an independent statutory regulatory scheme for funeral directors in England "as a matter of urgency".
In Friday's statement, the government referred to the Fuller inquiry, but made no mention of a statutory scheme.
Kevin Moxon, who runs Moxon's Family Funeral Directors in Hull's Anlaby Road, said he was concerned "trust in our industry" had been badly damaged.
"This case [Robert Bush] is not indicative of how our profession runs. It's a sacred duty to look after someone's loved one," he said.
"We need regulation bringing in pretty rapidly. We need inspectors coming round doing spot checks to ensure that we are all running to a set code of practice."
Following the government's announcement, Judd said the NAFD would make the case for statutory regulation as the best way to secure "meaningful change".
He told the BBC: "Our call for reform is about safeguarding the deceased and the bereaved. The dead cannot protect themselves.
"That responsibility falls to the rest of us."
Watch the story of Robert Bush and Legacy funeral directors in a new programme on BBC iPlayer.
